abstract: We consider the problem of decoding block coded data, using a physical dynamical system. We sketch out a decompression algorithm for fractal block codes and then show how to implement a recurrent neural network using physically simple but highly-nonlinear, analog circuit models of neurons and synapses. The nonlinear system has many fixed points, but we have at our disposal a procedure to choose the parameters in such a way that only one solution, the desired solution, is stable. As a partial proof of the concept, we present experimental data from a small system a 16-neuron analog CMOS chip fabricated in a 2m analog p-well process. This chip operates in the subthreshold regime and, for each choice of parameters, converges to a unique stable state. Each state exhibits a qualitatively fractal shape.

paragraphs: The paper explores decoding compressed block data by allowing a physical system to settle into a solution. Starting from a decompression algorithm for fractal block codes, the authors construct a recurrent neural network using simple analog circuit models. The circuit dynamics perform the computation through their evolution toward a stable state.

The neuron and synapse models are strongly nonlinear, and the resulting system has many fixed points: states at which it could remain unchanged. The crucial contribution is a parameter-selection procedure that makes only the desired solution stable. This distinguishes the existence of a possible solution from the stability needed for the physical decoder to reach a useful outcome.

As a partial demonstration, the authors present measurements from a 16-neuron analog CMOS chip operating in the subthreshold regime. For each parameter choice, it converges to a unique stable state with a qualitatively fractal shape. These observations support the proposed connection between fractal decoding and analog dynamics, while the paper explicitly presents the small chip as a partial proof of concept.
summary.tldr: A small analog recurrent network demonstrates how carefully chosen dynamics can settle into a stable solution inspired by fractal decompression.

title: An Analog Neural Network Inspired by Fractal Block Coding

paragraphs: The paper develops an analytical framework for estimating how localized structural damage affects a neural network's function. It studies a spatially organized associative memory, where function is assessed through the capacity to retrieve stored information. The motivating question is how the geometry and distribution of damage relate to the resulting memory impairment.

The analysis varies lesion area, shape, and number. This makes the pattern of damage part of the explanation, allowing several aspects of a lesion configuration to be examined together. Although the mathematical results rely on approximations, the abstract reports good agreement with simulations. That agreement supports the framework as a way to estimate retrieval damage in the modeled network.

The authors connect the results to features of multi-infarct dementia, particularly the association between infarct count and dementia after stroke. They also discuss a proposed multiplicative interaction between Alzheimer's disease and multi-infarct dementia. These connections give the computational study its clinical motivation: a model of localized damage can help interpret how different patterns of injury relate to functional loss.
summary.tldr: An associative-memory analysis links lesion area, shape, and number to retrieval damage, with approximate predictions supported by simulations.

title: Patterns of damage in neural networks: The effects of lesion area, shape and number

abstract: The auditory system of the barn owl contains several spatial maps. In young barn owls raised with optical prisms over their eyes, these auditory maps are shifted to stay in register with the visual map, suggesting that the visual input imposes a frame of reference on the auditory maps. However, the optic tectum, the first site of convergence of visual with auditory information, is not the site of plasticity for the shift of the auditory maps; the plasticity occurs instead in the inferior colliculus, which contains an auditory map and projects into the optic tectum. We explored a model of the owl remapping in which a global reinforcement signal whose delivery is controlled by visual foveation. A hebb learning rule gated by rein(cid:173) forcement learned to appropriately adjust auditory maps. In addi(cid:173) tion, reinforcement learning preferentially adjusted the weights in the inferior colliculus, as in the owl brain, even though the weights were allowed to change throughout the auditory system. This ob(cid:173) servation raises the possibility that the site of learning does not have to be genetically specified, but could be determined by how the learning procedure interacts with the network architecture. 126 Alexandre Pouget, Cedric Deffayet, Te"ence J. paragraphs: Young barn owls raised with optical prisms shift their auditory spatial maps to align with altered visual information. The puzzling detail is where this adaptation occurs. The first convergence of visual and auditory information is in the optic tectum, but the relevant plasticity occurs earlier, in the inferior colliculus.

The authors model this remapping with a global reinforcement signal controlled by visual foveation. A Hebbian learning rule, gated by that signal, adjusts the auditory maps appropriately. Although weights are permitted to change throughout the auditory system, the learning procedure preferentially changes weights in the inferior colliculus, matching the location observed in the owl.

This result offers an explanation for how a learning signal can produce anatomically selective adaptation without restricting all change to a predetermined site. The authors suggest that the location of learning could emerge from the interaction between the learning procedure and network architecture. Their model supports that possibility by reproducing both map adjustment and its preferred anatomical location.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-gated learning model reproduces auditory remapping and preferentially changes the same brain region implicated in barn owls.

title: Reinforcement Learning Predicts the Site of Plasticity for Auditory Remapping in the Barn Owl

abstract: vVe analyze the convergence properties of three spike-triggered data analysis techniques. All of our results are obtained in the set(cid:173) ting of a (possibly multidimensional) linear-nonlinear (LN) cascade model for stimulus-driven neural activity. We start by giving exact rate of convergence results for the common spike-triggered average (STA) technique. Next, we analyze a spike-triggered covariance method, variants of which have been recently exploited successfully by Bialek, Simoncelli, and colleagues. These first two methods suf(cid:173) fer from extraneous conditions on their convergence; therefore, we introduce an estimator for the LN model parameters which is de(cid:173) signed to be consistent under general conditions. We provide an algorithm for the computation of this estimator and derive its rate of convergence. We close with a brief discussion of the efficiency of these estimators and an application to data recorded from the primary motor cortex of awake, behaving primates.

paragraphs: The paper studies how reliably three spike-triggered analysis techniques recover properties of stimulus-driven neural activity as data accumulate. All results are developed within a linear-nonlinear cascade model, which may be multidimensional. This model setting is the common basis for comparing the estimators and interpreting their convergence guarantees.

The authors first derive exact convergence rates for the spike-triggered average, then analyze a spike-triggered covariance method. Both techniques require additional conditions for convergence. To address those requirements, the paper introduces an estimator of the cascade model's parameters designed to be consistent under general conditions, meaning that it approaches the correct parameters as the amount of data grows under those conditions.

The work provides a computational algorithm for the new estimator and derives its convergence rate. It also discusses estimator efficiency and applies the analysis to recordings from primary motor cortex in awake, behaving primates. The contribution combines guarantees about estimation with a procedure for carrying it out, while keeping those guarantees anchored to the stated model framework.
summary.tldr: Within linear-nonlinear neural models, the paper analyzes spike-triggered estimators and develops an alternative designed for consistency under general conditions.

title: Convergence Properties of Some Spike-Triggered Analysis Techniques

abstract: Why are sensory modalities segregated the way they are? In this paper we show that sensory modalities are well designed for self-supervised cross-modal learning. Using the Minimizing-Disagreement algorithm on an unsupervised speech categorization task with visual (moving lips) and auditory (sound signal) inputs, we show that very informative auditory dimensions actually harm performance when moved to the visual side of the network. It is better to throw them away than to consider them part of the “visual input”. We explain this ﬁnding in terms of the statistical structure in sensory inputs.

Using the Minimizing-Disagreement algorithm on an unsupervised speech categorization task with visual (moving lips) and auditory (sound signal) inputs, we show that very informative auditory dimensions actually harm performance when moved to the visual side of the network. It is better to throw them away than to consider them part of the “visual input”. We explain this ﬁnding in terms of the statistical structure in sensory inputs.

paragraphs: This paper asks why sensory inputs are separated into modalities in the way they are. It examines that question through self-supervised learning between vision and hearing. The authors use the Minimizing-Disagreement algorithm for unsupervised speech categorization, with moving lips providing visual information and the sound signal providing auditory information.

The striking experiment changes which side of the network receives certain auditory dimensions. Although those dimensions are highly informative, moving them to the visual side harms performance. In the studied setting, discarding them works better than treating them as part of the visual input. Their usefulness therefore depends on how they are grouped with the other sensory information.

The authors explain this result through the statistical structure of sensory inputs and argue that the usual modality separation is well suited to cross-modal learning. The finding shows why informative features alone do not determine success: the relationships within and between the input groups also matter. Its evidence comes from the reported speech-categorization task and the specific reassignment of auditory information.
summary.tldr: In cross-modal speech learning, moving informative auditory features to the visual input harms performance more than discarding them.

title: Sensory Modality Segregation

abstract: In contrast to the equivalence of linear blind source separation and linear independent component analysis it is not possible to recover the origi- nal source signal from some unknown nonlinear transformations of the sources using only the independence assumption. Integrating the ob- jectives of statistical independence and temporal slowness removes this indeterminacy leading to a new method for nonlinear blind source sepa- ration. The principle of temporal slowness is adopted from slow feature analysis, an unsupervised method to extract slowly varying features from a given observed vectorial signal. The performance of the algorithm is demonstrated on nonlinearly mixed speech data.
originalAbstract: In contrast to the equivalence of linear blind source separation and linear independent component analysis it is not possible to recover the origi- nal source signal from some unknown nonlinear transformations of the sources using only the independence assumption. Integrating the ob- jectives of statistical independence and temporal slowness removes this indeterminacy leading to a new method for nonlinear blind source sepa- ration. The principle of temporal slowness is adopted from slow feature analysis, an unsupervised method to extract slowly varying features from a given observed vectorial signal. The performance of the algorithm is demonstrated on nonlinearly mixed speech data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover source signals after they have been mixed through unknown nonlinear transformations. It identifies an ambiguity that statistical independence alone cannot resolve: independent recovered components need not identify the original sources for some nonlinear transformations. This makes nonlinear separation different from the linear relationship between source separation and independent component analysis.

The authors combine independence with temporal slowness, the objective of extracting features that change slowly over time. The slowness principle comes from slow feature analysis, an unsupervised method for processing observed vector-valued signals. The combined method therefore uses both statistical relationships and the way a signal evolves over time.

The paper states that integrating these objectives removes the identified indeterminacy and produces a new nonlinear source-separation method. Performance is demonstrated on nonlinearly mixed speech data. The significance is that temporal information supplies an additional separation criterion where independence by itself is insufficient, with the speech experiment illustrating the resulting algorithm.
summary.tldr: Combining statistical independence with temporal slowness addresses an ambiguity in nonlinear source separation and is demonstrated on mixed speech.

title: Nonlinear Blind Source Separation by Integrating Independent Component Analysis and Slow Feature Analysis

abstract: This paper addresses the bottom-up influence of local image information on human eye movements. Most existing computational models use a set of biologically plausible linear filters, e.g., Gabor or Difference-of-Gaussians filters as a front-end, the outputs of which are nonlinearly combined into a real number that indicates visual saliency. Unfortunately, this requires many design parameters such as the number, type, and size of the front-end filters, as well as the choice of nonlinearities, weighting and normalization schemes etc., for which biological plausibility cannot always be justified. As a result, these parameters have to be chosen in a more or less ad hoc way. Here, we propose to learn a visual saliency model directly from human eye movement data. The model is rather simplistic and essentially parameter-free, and therefore contrasts recent developments in the field that usually aim at higher prediction rates at the cost of additional parameters and increasing model complexity. Experimental results show that--despite the lack of any biological prior knowledge--our model performs comparably to existing approaches, and in fact learns image features that resemble findings from several previous studies. In particular, its maximally excitatory stimuli have center-surround structure, similar to receptive fields in the early human visual system.

paragraphs: This paper studies how local image information attracts human eye movements. Many computational saliency models begin with filters chosen to resemble biological visual processing, then combine their outputs into an attention score. That design requires decisions about filter types, sizes, weights, and nonlinear transformations, some of which lack a clear biological justification.

The authors instead learn a saliency model directly from human eye movement data. Their approach is deliberately simple and described as essentially parameter-free. The aim is to let the relationship between images and observed gaze guide the model, reducing reliance on the many manually chosen components used by existing approaches.

Experiments show performance comparable to existing models despite the absence of built-in biological knowledge. The learned features also resemble earlier findings about vision: patterns that most strongly activate the model have a center-surround organization similar to early visual receptive fields. The result shows that such structure can emerge from learning to predict eye movements, without being explicitly supplied as a prior.
summary.tldr: A simple saliency model learned from eye movements matches existing approaches and develops features resembling early visual receptive fields.

title: A Nonparametric Approach to Bottom-Up Visual Saliency

abstract: Graph matching is a fundamental problem in Computer Vision and Machine Learning. We present two contributions. First, we give a new spectral relaxation technique for approximate solutions to matching problems, that naturally incorporates one-to-one or one-to-many constraints within the relaxation scheme. The second is a normalization procedure for existing graph matching scoring functions that can dramatically improve the matching accuracy. It is based on a reinterpretation of the graph matching compatibility matrix as a bipartite graph on edges for which we seek a bistochastic normalization. We evaluate our two contributions on a comprehensive test set of random graph matching problems, as well as on image correspondence problem. Our normalization procedure can be used to improve the performance of many existing graph matching algorithms, including spectral matching, graduated assignment and semidefinite programming.

First, we give a new spectral relaxation technique for approximate solutions to matching problems, that naturally incorporates one-to-one or one-to-many constraints within the relaxation scheme. The second is a normalization procedure for existing graph matching scoring functions that can dramatically improve the matching accuracy. It is based on a reinterpretation of the graph matching compatibility matrix as a bipartite graph on edges for which we seek a bistochastic normalization. We evaluate our two contributions on a comprehensive test set of random graph matching problems, as well as on image correspondence problem. Our normalization procedure can be used to improve the performance of many existing graph matching algorithms, including spectral matching, graduated assignment and semidefinite programming.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between elements of different graphs. This paper contributes two ways to improve that process. The first is a spectral relaxation for finding approximate matches. It incorporates one-to-one or one-to-many correspondence constraints directly into the relaxed problem, so those requirements participate in the approximation itself.

The second contribution changes how candidate matches are scored. The authors reinterpret the compatibility matrix used in graph matching as a bipartite graph whose elements represent edges, and seek a bistochastic normalization. This normalization balances the matrix in both directions. It provides a way to adjust existing scoring functions rather than requiring every matching algorithm to be replaced.

The authors evaluate both contributions on random graph-matching problems and image correspondence. They report that normalization can dramatically improve matching accuracy and can benefit several existing approaches, including spectral matching, graduated assignment, and semidefinite programming. The broader significance is that improving the balance of the scoring function can help multiple matching procedures, alongside the separate benefit of the new relaxation.
summary.tldr: A constrained spectral relaxation and a balancing procedure for compatibility scores improve approximate graph matching.

title: Balanced Graph Matching

abstract: We present polynomial-time algorithms for the exact computation of lowest- energy states, worst margin violators, partition functions, and marginals in binary undirected graphical models. Our approach provides an interesting alternative to the well-known graph cut paradigm in that it does not impose any submodularity constraints; instead we require planarity to establish a correspondence with perfect matchings in an expanded dual graph. Maximum-margin parameter estimation for a boundary detection task shows our approach to be efﬁcient and effective.
originalAbstract: We present polynomial-time algorithms for the exact computation of lowest- energy states, worst margin violators, partition functions, and marginals in binary undirected graphical models. Our approach provides an interesting alternative to the well-known graph cut paradigm in that it does not impose any submodularity constraints; instead we require planarity to establish a correspondence with perfect matchings in an expanded dual graph. Maximum-margin parameter estimation for a boundary detection task shows our approach to be efﬁcient and effective.

paragraphs: The paper develops exact inference algorithms for binary undirected graphical models under a planarity requirement. These models describe interacting variables with two possible states. The algorithms compute lowest-energy configurations, partition functions, and marginal probabilities, covering both the search for a best configuration and calculations about the model's probability distribution.

The approach uses a correspondence between the graphical model and perfect matchings in an expanded dual graph. This transformation leads to polynomial-time algorithms. Its structural requirement differs from the submodularity constraints used in the graph-cut paradigm: the method does not impose those constraints, but relies on planarity to establish the matching correspondence.

The algorithms also identify worst margin violators, configurations needed for maximum-margin parameter estimation. The authors use that learning procedure in a boundary detection task and report that the approach is efficient and effective. The contribution connects an exact combinatorial inference method to parameter learning, showing how the same planar structure can support several computations required to train and use the model.
summary.tldr: A perfect-matching formulation enables polynomial-time exact inference for planar binary graphical models without imposing submodularity constraints.

title: Efficient Exact Inference in Planar Ising Models

abstract: We propose a multiple incremental decremental algorithm of Support Vector Machine (SVM). Conventional single cremental decremental SVM can update the trained model efficiently when single data point is added to or removed from the training set. When we add and/or remove multiple data points, this algorithm is time-consuming because we need to repeatedly apply it to each data point. The roposed algorithm is computationally more efficient when multiple data points are added and/or removed simultaneously. The single incremental decremental algorithm is built on an optimization technique called parametric programming. We extend the idea and introduce multi-parametric programming for developing the proposed algorithm. Experimental results on synthetic and real data sets indicate that the proposed algorithm can significantly reduce the computational cost of multiple incremental decremental operation. Our approach is especially useful for online SVM learning in which we need to remove old data points and add new data points in a short amount of time.

Conventional single cremental decremental SVM can update the trained model efficiently when single data point is added to or removed from the training set. When we add and/or remove multiple data points, this algorithm is time-consuming because we need to repeatedly apply it to each data point. The roposed algorithm is computationally more efficient when multiple data points are added and/or removed simultaneously. The single incremental decremental algorithm is built on an optimization technique called parametric programming. We extend the idea and introduce multi-parametric programming for developing the proposed algorithm. Experimental results on synthetic and real data sets indicate that the proposed algorithm can significantly reduce the computational cost of multiple incremental decremental operation. Our approach is especially useful for online SVM learning in which we need to remove old data points and add new data points in a short amount of time.

paragraphs: The paper addresses updating a trained support vector machine when several training examples are added or removed. Existing incremental and decremental methods efficiently handle a single example. Applying those updates repeatedly becomes time-consuming when the change involves many examples, creating a bottleneck for models whose training data must be refreshed frequently.

The proposed algorithm handles multiple additions or removals simultaneously. It extends the parametric-programming idea underlying the single-example method into multi-parametric programming. This changes the optimization machinery so that a group of training-set changes can be treated together, making multiple-example updates computationally more efficient.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets indicate that the method can substantially reduce the cost of these updates. The authors highlight online SVM learning as a particularly useful setting: old examples must be removed while new examples are incorporated within a short time. The contribution concerns making those model-maintenance operations faster when data changes arrive in groups.
summary.tldr: A multi-parametric SVM update algorithm reduces computation when multiple training examples are added or removed together.

title: Multiple Incremental Decremental Learning of Support Vector Machines

abstract: We consider reinforcement learning in partially observable domains where the agent can query an expert for demonstrations. Our nonparametric Bayesian approach combines model knowledge, inferred from expert information and independent exploration, with policy knowledge inferred from expert trajectories. We introduce priors that bias the agent towards models with both simple representations and simple policies, resulting in improved policy and model learning.
originalAbstract: We consider reinforcement learning in partially observable domains where the agent can query an expert for demonstrations. Our nonparametric Bayesian approach combines model knowledge, inferred from expert information and independent exploration, with policy knowledge inferred from expert trajectories. We introduce priors that bias the agent towards models with both simple representations and simple policies, resulting in improved policy and model learning.

paragraphs: The paper considers reinforcement learning when the agent cannot fully observe its environment and can ask an expert for demonstrations. In this setting, learning involves both understanding the environment and deciding how to act. The authors develop a nonparametric Bayesian approach that brings information about these two tasks into a common learning framework.

The approach combines model knowledge obtained from expert information and the agent's own exploration with policy knowledge inferred from expert trajectories. Demonstrations therefore contribute information about behavior as well as information useful for modeling the domain. Independent exploration supplies another source of evidence about the environment in which the policy must operate.

The authors introduce priors that favor models having both simple representations and simple policies. These preferences guide learning toward explanations that are economical in how they describe the environment and the behavior associated with it. The paper reports improvements in both policy and model learning, supporting the use of policy simplicity alongside representational simplicity when incorporating expert demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Bayesian priors favoring simple models and policies improve learning from expert demonstrations and exploration in partially observable environments.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Policy Priors for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) are an increasingly popular framework for modeling neural spike trains. They have been linked to the theory of stochastic point processes and researchers have used this relation to assess goodness-of-fit using methods from point-process theory, e.g. the time-rescaling theorem. However, high neural firing rates or coarse discretization lead to a breakdown of the assumptions necessary for this connection. Here, we show how goodness-of-fit tests from point-process theory can still be applied to GLMs by constructing equivalent surrogate point processes out of time-series observations. Furthermore, two additional tests based on thinning and complementing point processes are introduced. They augment the instruments available for checking model adequacy of point processes as well as discretized models.

They have been linked to the theory of stochastic point processes and researchers have used this relation to assess goodness-of-fit using methods from point-process theory, e.g. the time-rescaling theorem. However, high neural firing rates or coarse discretization lead to a breakdown of the assumptions necessary for this connection. Here, we show how goodness-of-fit tests from point-process theory can still be applied to GLMs by constructing equivalent surrogate point processes out of time-series observations. Furthermore, two additional tests based on thinning and complementing point processes are introduced. They augment the instruments available for checking model adequacy of point processes as well as discretized models.

paragraphs: Generalized linear models are used to describe neural spike trains, and their relationship to point processes provides tools for checking model fit. One such tool uses time rescaling. However, the connection depends on assumptions that can break down when neural firing rates are high or observations are divided into coarse time intervals.

The paper shows how to retain point-process goodness-of-fit methods by constructing equivalent surrogate point processes from time-series observations. This construction supplies a way to apply those checks to GLMs despite the problem caused by discretization. The contribution concerns how model adequacy is assessed, making the representation used for testing an explicit part of the procedure.

The authors also introduce two further tests based on thinning and complementing point processes. These expand the available checks for both point-process models and discretized models. Together, the surrogate construction and additional tests address a concrete mismatch between observation format and testing assumptions, providing more ways to evaluate whether a fitted spike-train model adequately describes its data.
summary.tldr: Surrogate point processes and new thinning and complementing tests extend goodness-of-fit checking to discretized neural models.

title: Rescaling, thinning or complementing? On goodness-of-fit procedures for point process models and Generalized Linear Models

abstract: We define a copula process which describes the dependencies between arbitrarily many random variables independently of their marginal distributions. As an example, we develop a stochastic volatility model, Gaussian Copula Process Volatility (GCPV), to predict the latent standard deviations of a sequence of random variables. To make predictions we use Bayesian inference, with the Laplace approximation, and with Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative. We find our model can outperform GARCH on simulated and financial data. And unlike GARCH, GCPV can easily handle missing data, incorporate covariates other than time, and model a rich class of covariance structures.
originalAbstract: We define a copula process which describes the dependencies between arbitrarily many random variables independently of their marginal distributions. As an example, we develop a stochastic volatility model, Gaussian Copula Process Volatility (GCPV), to predict the latent standard deviations of a sequence of random variables. To make predictions we use Bayesian inference, with the Laplace approximation, and with Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative. We find our model can outperform GARCH on simulated and financial data. And unlike GARCH, GCPV can easily handle missing data, incorporate covariates other than time, and model a rich class of covariance structures.

paragraphs: A joint statistical model must describe both the behavior of individual variables and their relationships with one another. This paper introduces a copula process that separates those two concerns. It describes dependence among arbitrarily many random variables independently of their marginal distributions, allowing the relationship structure to be modeled separately from each variable's own distribution.

The authors demonstrate the idea with Gaussian Copula Process Volatility, a model for predicting the unobserved standard deviations of a sequence of variables. These latent standard deviations represent the changing scale of variability. Predictions use Bayesian inference, with a Laplace approximation as one approach and Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative.

The model can outperform GARCH on the simulated and financial data considered. The authors also emphasize its ability to accommodate missing observations, use covariates beyond time, and represent a rich range of covariance structures. Together, these properties show how separating dependence from marginal behavior can support a flexible volatility model, alongside the reported predictive benefits.
summary.tldr: Copula processes separate dependence from marginal distributions and enable a flexible Bayesian volatility model that can outperform GARCH.

title: Copula Processes

abstract: In this paper, we propose the first exact algorithm for minimizing the difference of two submodular functions (D.S.), i.e., the discrete version of the D.C. programming problem. The developed algorithm is a branch-and-bound-based algorithm which responds to the structure of this problem through the relationship between submodularity and convexity. The D.S. programming problem covers a broad range of applications in machine learning because this generalizes the optimization of a wide class of set functions. The authors present what they describe as the first exact algorithm for this problem.

The method uses branch and bound and exploits the relationship between submodularity and convexity. Its design therefore draws on the mathematical structure of the objective rather than treating it as an arbitrary set function. The central contribution is exact optimization for the stated problem, providing a way to obtain solutions beyond those returned by existing approximate approaches.

The authors empirically investigate the algorithm and apply it to feature selection and discriminative structure learning. These examples illustrate differences between exact solutions from the proposed method and approximate solutions from existing algorithms. The experiments make the distinction in solution type concrete for learning tasks, while the abstract's main claim concerns the development of an exact algorithm for the broader optimization formulation.
summary.tldr: A branch-and-bound algorithm exactly minimizes differences of submodular functions by exploiting their connection to convexity.

title: Prismatic Algorithm for Discrete D.C. Programming Problem

abstract: We describe the tradeoff between the performance in a visual recognition problem and the control authority that the agent can exercise on the sensing process. We focus on the problem of “visual search” of an object in an otherwise known and static scene, propose a measure of control authority, and relate it to the expected risk and its proxy (conditional entropy of the posterior density). We show this analytically, as well as empirically by simulation using the simplest known model that captures the phenomenology of image formation, including scaling and occlusions. We show that a “passive” agent given a training set can provide no guarantees on performance beyond what is afforded by the priors, and that an “omnipotent” agent, capable of infinite control authority, can achieve arbitrarily good performance (asymptotically).

This makes sensing control part of the recognition problem: performance depends on the observations an agent can obtain as well as the information it already has.

The authors propose a measure of control authority and relate it to expected recognition risk. They also connect control to conditional entropy of the posterior distribution, used as a proxy for that risk. The relationship is studied analytically and through simulations using an image-formation model that includes scaling and occlusion.

An agent with unlimited control authority can approach arbitrarily good performance asymptotically. The latter conclusion depends on an idealized control capability and concerns limiting behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper relates visual recognition guarantees to sensing control, from passive observation to asymptotically powerful unlimited control.

title: Controlled Recognition Bounds for Visual Learning and Exploration

abstract: In text analysis documents are represented as disorganized bags of words, models of count features are typically based on mixing a small number of topics \cite{lda,sam}. Recently, it has been observed that for many text corpora documents evolve into one another in a smooth way, with some features dropping and new ones being introduced. The counting grid \cite{cgUai} models this spatial metaphor literally: it is multidimensional grid of word distributions learned in such a way that a document's own distribution of features can be modeled as the sum of the histograms found in a window into the grid. The major drawback of this method is that it is essentially a mixture and all the content much be generated by a single contiguous area on the grid. This may be problematic especially for lower dimensional grids. In this paper, we overcome to this issue with the \emph{Componential Counting Grid} which brings the componential nature of topic models to the basic counting grid. We also introduce a generative kernel based on the document's grid usage and a visualization strategy useful for understanding large text corpora. We evaluate our approach on document classification and multimodal retrieval obtaining state of the art results on standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: Counting grids represent documents using a spatial arrangement of word distributions. A document's word counts are modeled by combining the histograms inside a window on that grid. This captures the observation that documents in many collections can change smoothly into one another as some words disappear and others enter.

The original approach requires all of a document's content to come from one contiguous grid region. That restriction can be problematic, particularly when the grid has few dimensions. The proposed Componential Counting Grid allows a document to draw on multiple windows, bringing the ability to combine separate components from topic models into the grid representation.

The authors also construct a generative kernel from how documents use the grid and introduce a visualization approach for understanding large text collections. These additions make the representation useful beyond fitting word counts. Evaluations on document classification and multimodal retrieval report state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, supporting the practical value of allowing multiple regions to contribute to a document.
summary.tldr: Componential Counting Grids model documents with multiple grid windows, improving flexibility and achieving strong classification and retrieval results.

title: Documents as multiple overlapping windows into grids of counts

abstract: We present a recurrent neuronal network, modeled as a continuous-time dynamical system, that can solve constraint satisfaction problems. Discrete variables are represented by coupled Winner-Take-All (WTA) networks, and their values are encoded in localized patterns of oscillations that are learned by the recurrent weights in these networks. Constraints over the variables are encoded in the network connectivity. Although there are no sources of noise, the network can escape from local optima in its search for solutions that satisfy all constraints by modifying the effective network connectivity through oscillations. If there is no solution that satisfies all constraints, the network state changes in a pseudo-random manner and its trajectory approximates a sampling procedure that selects a variable assignment with a probability that increases with the fraction of constraints satisfied by this assignment. External evidence, or input to the network, can force variables to specific values. When new inputs are applied, the network re-evaluates the entire set of variables in its search for the states that satisfy the maximum number of constraints, while being consistent with the external input. Our results demonstrate that the proposed network architecture can perform a deterministic search for the optimal solution to problems with non-convex cost functions. The network is inspired by canonical microcircuit models of the cortex and suggests possible dynamical mechanisms to solve constraint satisfaction problems that can be present in biological networks, or implemented in neuromorphic electronic circuits.

paragraphs: This paper presents a continuous-time recurrent neural network for constraint satisfaction. Connections between the networks encode the constraints, turning the search for a compatible assignment into the evolution of a dynamical system.

The system contains no noise sources, yet oscillations can change its effective connectivity and allow it to escape local optima. When no assignment satisfies every constraint, its state follows a pseudo-random trajectory that approximates sampling. Assignments satisfying a larger fraction of constraints receive higher probability under this approximate sampling behavior.

Inspired by cortical microcircuit models, the architecture suggests possible mechanisms for biological computation and possible implementations in neuromorphic circuits.
summary.tldr: Coupled neural oscillators use deterministic dynamics to search constraint assignments and can escape local optima without injected noise.

title: Recurrent networks of coupled Winner-Take-All oscillators for solving constraint satisfaction problems

abstract: We present the Convex Polytope Machine (CPM), a novel non-linear learning algorithm for large-scale binary classification tasks. The CPM finds a large margin convex polytope separator which encloses one class. We develop a stochastic gradient descent based algorithm that is amenable to massive datasets, and augment it with a heuristic procedure to avoid sub-optimal local minima. Our experimental evaluations of the CPM on large-scale datasets from distinct domains (MNIST handwritten digit recognition, text topic, and web security) demonstrate that the CPM trains models faster, sometimes several orders of magnitude, than state-of-the-art similar approaches and kernel-SVM methods while achieving comparable or better classification performance. Our empirical results suggest that, unlike prior similar approaches, we do not need to control the number of sub-classifiers (sides of the polytope) to avoid overfitting.

Its multiple sides provide the component boundaries of the classifier, allowing the decision rule to use a geometric enclosure rather than relying on a single separating boundary.

The authors develop a stochastic-gradient training algorithm suitable for massive datasets. They supplement it with a heuristic intended to avoid poor local minima. This combination addresses the practical optimization challenge of fitting the polytope, while the heuristic remains a practical device rather than a stated guarantee of finding a global optimum.

Experiments cover handwritten-digit recognition, text topics, and web security. The reported models train faster than comparable approaches and kernel SVMs, sometimes by several orders of magnitude, while attaining comparable or better classification performance. The results also suggest that controlling the number of polytope sides is unnecessary for avoiding overfitting in the evaluated settings. That last observation is empirical, rather than a universal guarantee about model size.
summary.tldr: The Convex Polytope Machine learns a nonlinear enclosure for one class, with substantially faster training and competitive accuracy in reported experiments.

title: Large-Margin Convex Polytope Machine

abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings of rhythm perception might contain enough information to distinguish different rhythm types/genres or even identify the rhythms themselves. We apply convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze and classify EEG data recorded within a rhythm perception study in Kigali, Rwanda which comprises 12 East African and 12 Western rhythmic stimuli – each presented in a loop for 32 seconds to 13 participants. We investigate the impact of the data representation and the pre-processing steps for this classification tasks and compare different network structures. Using CNNs, we are able to recognize individual rhythms from the EEG with a mean classification accuracy of 24.4% (chance level 4.17%) over all subjects by looking at less than three seconds from a single channel. Aggregating predictions for multiple channels, a mean accuracy of up to 50% can be achieved for individual subjects.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether EEG recorded during rhythm perception contains enough information to identify the rhythm being heard. The reported single-channel result uses less than three seconds of signal. Across subjects, mean accuracy for recognizing individual rhythms reaches 24.4%, compared with a chance level of 4.17%.

Combining predictions from multiple channels can raise mean accuracy to as much as 50% for individual subjects. That result concerns individual subjects and is distinct from the average across all subjects for the single-channel setting. Together, the findings show that the recorded EEG carries information useful for distinguishing the presented rhythms and that aggregating channels can improve recognition in the reported cases.
summary.tldr: CNNs identify presented rhythms from short EEG segments above chance, with further gains from combining channels for individual subjects.

title: Using Convolutional Neural Networks to Recognize Rhythm ￼Stimuli from Electroencephalography Recordings

abstract: We propose a class of closed-form estimators for GLMs under high-dimensional sampling regimes. Our class of estimators is based on deriving closed-form variants of the vanilla unregularized MLE but which are (a) well-defined even under high-dimensional settings, and (b) available in closed-form. We then perform thresholding operations on this MLE variant to obtain our class of estimators. We derive a unified statistical analysis of our class of estimators, and show that it enjoys strong statistical guarantees in both parameter error as well as variable selection, that surprisingly match those of the more complex regularized GLM MLEs, even while our closed-form estimators are computationally much simpler. We derive instantiations of our class of closed-form estimators, as well as corollaries of our general theorem, for the special cases of logistic, exponential and Poisson regression models. We corroborate the surprising statistical and computational performance of our class of estimators via extensive simulations.

paragraphs: Estimating generalized linear models in high dimensions can call for computationally complex regularized maximum-likelihood procedures. This paper develops a simpler alternative: estimators that can be expressed in closed form. The goal is to retain strong statistical behavior while reducing the computational work needed to obtain parameter estimates and identify relevant variables.

The construction begins with modified versions of the ordinary, unregularized maximum-likelihood estimator. These variants are designed to remain well-defined in high-dimensional settings and to have explicit formulas. Thresholding operations then turn them into the proposed estimator family. This separates the initial calculation from the operation that selects which estimated effects to retain.

A unified analysis provides guarantees for both parameter estimation error and variable selection that match those of the more complex regularized GLM estimators considered. The authors work out specific versions for logistic, exponential, and Poisson regression, and support the statistical and computational findings with extensive simulations. The contribution is a common construction showing that simpler computation can preserve strong guarantees across these models.
summary.tldr: Closed-form, thresholded GLM estimators match strong guarantees of more complex regularized estimators while simplifying computation.

title: Closed-form Estimators for High-dimensional Generalized Linear Models

abstract: For massive and heterogeneous modern data sets, it is of fundamental interest to provide guarantees on the accuracy of estimation when computational resources are limited. In the application of learning to rank, we provide a hierarchy of rank-breaking mechanisms ordered by the complexity in thus generated sketch of the data. This allows the number of data points collected to be gracefully traded off against computational resources available, while guaranteeing the desired level of accuracy. Theoretical guarantees on the proposed generalized rank-breaking implicitly provide such trade-offs, which can be explicitly characterized under certain canonical scenarios on the structure of the data.

paragraphs: Learning to rank involves estimating an ordering from observed ranking information. With large, heterogeneous datasets, the useful question is not only how accurately an estimator can learn, but how much computation achieving that accuracy requires. This paper studies that relationship by changing how the ranking data is summarized before estimation.

The authors introduce a hierarchy of generalized rank-breaking mechanisms. These mechanisms produce sketches of the original data with different levels of complexity. Organizing the sketches into a hierarchy provides a way to adjust the computational demands of estimation while considering how much data must be collected to support a desired accuracy.

The theoretical guarantees describe a tradeoff between sample quantity and available computation. That tradeoff is implicit in the general analysis and becomes explicit for certain canonical data structures. The contribution is thus a framework for reasoning about resource choices in ranking problems: the complexity of the processed data and the number of observations can be considered together while maintaining the stated accuracy guarantees.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of ranking-data sketches provides theoretical tradeoffs between computational resources, sample size, and estimation accuracy.

title: Computational and Statistical Tradeoffs in Learning to Rank

abstract: Towards learning programs from data, we introduce the problem of sampling programs from posterior distributions conditioned on that data. Within this setting, we propose an algorithm that uses a symbolic solver to efficiently sample programs. The proposal combines constraint-based program synthesis with sampling via random parity constraints. We give theoretical guarantees on how well the samples approximate the true posterior, and have empirical results showing the algorithm is efficient in practice, evaluating our approach on 22 program learning problems in the domains of text editing and computer-aided programming.

paragraphs: Learning programs from data can be framed as uncertainty over which program explains the observations. This paper focuses on sampling programs from the posterior distribution conditioned on those data. The target is a distribution of plausible programs, so the task requires more than finding a single program that satisfies the available examples.

The authors propose an algorithm that combines constraint-based program synthesis with sampling through random parity constraints. A symbolic solver is the computational engine for generating program samples. This connects machinery for satisfying program constraints with a probabilistic objective: producing samples that approximate the desired posterior over programs.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees describing how closely the generated samples approximate that posterior. It also evaluates the algorithm on 22 program-learning problems involving text editing and computer-aided programming, reporting practical efficiency. These two forms of evidence address different parts of the contribution: whether the samples represent the intended distribution and whether the sampling procedure is computationally useful on the tested problems.
summary.tldr: Symbolic solving and random parity constraints enable efficient approximate posterior sampling of programs, supported by theoretical guarantees and 22 evaluated problems.

title: Sampling for Bayesian Program Learning

abstract: The design of revenue-maximizing combinatorial auctions, i.e. multi item auctions over bundles of goods, is one of the most fundamental problems in computational economics, unsolved even for two bidders and two items for sale. In the traditional economic models, it is assumed that the bidders' valuations are drawn from an underlying distribution and that the auction designer has perfect knowledge of this distribution. Despite this strong and oftentimes unrealistic assumption, it is remarkable that the revenue-maximizing combinatorial auction remains unknown. In recent years, automated mechanism design has emerged as one of the most practical and promising approaches to designing high-revenue combinatorial auctions. The most scalable automated mechanism design algorithms take as input samples from the bidders' valuation distribution and then search for a high-revenue auction in a rich auction class. In this work, we provide the first sample complexity analysis for the standard hierarchy of deterministic combinatorial auction classes used in automated mechanism design. In particular, we provide tight sample complexity bounds on the number of samples needed to guarantee that the empirical revenue of the designed mechanism on the samples is close to its expected revenue on the underlying, unknown distribution over bidder valuations, for each of the auction classes in the hierarchy. In addition to helping set automated mechanism design on firm foundations, our results also push the boundaries of learning theory. In particular, the hypothesis functions used in our contexts are defined through multi stage combinatorial optimization procedures, rather than simple decision boundaries, as are common in machine learning.

paragraphs: Automated mechanism design searches for high-revenue auctions using sampled bidder valuations. This is especially relevant for combinatorial auctions, where bidders value bundles of multiple goods and the underlying valuation distribution may be unknown. The paper asks how many samples are needed for revenue measured on those samples to reliably reflect expected revenue.

The authors analyze the standard hierarchy of deterministic auction classes used in automated mechanism design. For each class, they provide tight sample complexity bounds ensuring that empirical revenue is close to expected revenue under the underlying distribution. This gives a statistical foundation for selecting auctions from data: a strong result on the observed sample can be related to performance beyond that sample.

The guarantee concerns revenue estimation and generalization within the analyzed classes, rather than solving the unrestricted revenue-maximization problem. The analysis also extends learning-theory techniques to unusually complicated functions. Here, the functions being studied are defined by multistage combinatorial optimization procedures, so controlling their behavior requires going beyond the simple decision boundaries common in learning-theory examples.
summary.tldr: Tight sample bounds explain when revenue observed during automated auction design reliably reflects expected revenue for standard deterministic auction classes.

title: Sample Complexity of Automated Mechanism Design

abstract: Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) is a popular machine learning algorithm, and has quite a few effective implementations such as XGBoost and pGBRT. Although many engineering optimizations have been adopted in these implementations, the efficiency and scalability are still unsatisfactory when the feature dimension is high and data size is large. A major reason is that for each feature, they need to scan all the data instances to estimate the information gain of all possible split points, which is very time consuming. To tackle this problem, we propose two novel techniques: \emph{Gradient-based One-Side Sampling} (GOSS) and \emph{Exclusive Feature Bundling} (EFB). With GOSS, we exclude a significant proportion of data instances with small gradients, and only use the rest to estimate the information gain. We prove that, since the data instances with larger gradients play a more important role in the computation of information gain, GOSS can obtain quite accurate estimation of the information gain with a much smaller data size. With EFB, we bundle mutually exclusive features (i.e., they rarely take nonzero values simultaneously), to reduce the number of features. We prove that finding the optimal bundling of exclusive features is NP-hard, but a greedy algorithm can achieve quite good approximation ratio (and thus can effectively reduce the number of features without hurting the accuracy of split point determination by much). We call our new GBDT implementation with GOSS and EFB \emph{LightGBM}. Our experiments on multiple public datasets show that, LightGBM speeds up the training process of conventional GBDT by up to over 20 times while achieving almost the same accuracy.

paragraphs: Training gradient-boosted decision trees becomes expensive when many examples and features must be examined to choose splits. This paper introduces LightGBM, which attacks that workload along both dimensions. Its two techniques reduce the examples used to estimate split quality and the number of features considered during that process.

These are reported experimental gains, with the largest speedup describing the upper end of the results. The contribution combines two targeted reductions in split-search work into an efficient tree-boosting implementation.
summary.tldr: LightGBM accelerates boosted-tree training through gradient-based example sampling and bundling of rarely co-active features.

title: LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree

abstract: Computational models in fields such as computational neuroscience are often evaluated via stochastic simulation or numerical approximation. Fitting these models implies a difficult optimization problem over complex, possibly noisy parameter landscapes. Bayesian optimization (BO) has been successfully applied to solving expensive black-box problems in engineering and machine learning. Here we explore whether BO can be applied as a general tool for model fitting. First, we present a novel hybrid BO algorithm, Bayesian adaptive direct search (BADS), that achieves competitive performance with an affordable computational overhead for the running time of typical models. We then perform an extensive benchmark of BADS vs. many common and state-of-the-art nonconvex, derivative-free optimizers, on a set of model-fitting problems with real data and models from six studies in behavioral, cognitive, and computational neuroscience. With default settings, BADS consistently finds comparable or better solutions than other methods, including `vanilla' BO, showing great promise for advanced BO techniques, and BADS in particular, as a general model-fitting tool.

When model evaluations rely on stochastic simulation or numerical approximation, the search landscape can be complicated and noisy. This paper asks whether Bayesian optimization can become a practical general-purpose tool for this kind of model fitting.

The authors introduce Bayesian adaptive direct search, or BADS, a hybrid Bayesian optimization algorithm. Its design targets competitive optimization performance while keeping the algorithm's own computational overhead affordable relative to typical model runtimes. That balance matters because choosing the next evaluation also takes time, and this cost contributes to the overall fitting effort.

The evaluation compares BADS with many derivative-free, nonconvex optimizers on real-data model-fitting problems from six neuroscience studies. With default settings, BADS consistently finds solutions comparable to or better than those of the alternatives, including vanilla Bayesian optimization. The findings support BADS as a promising broadly useful fitting tool, based on its performance across the tested behavioral, cognitive, and computational neuroscience problems.
summary.tldr: BADS combines practical computational overhead with consistently competitive model-fitting results across problems from six neuroscience studies.

title: Practical Bayesian Optimization for Model Fitting with Bayesian Adaptive Direct Search

abstract: A conjugate Gamma-Poisson model for Dynamic Matrix Factorization incorporated with metadata influence (mGDMF for short) is proposed to effectively and efficiently model massive, sparse and dynamic data in recommendations. Modeling recommendation problems with a massive number of ratings and very sparse or even no ratings on some users/items in a dynamic setting is very demanding and poses critical challenges to well-studied matrix factorization models due to the large-scale, sparse and dynamic nature of the data. Our proposed mGDMF tackles these challenges by introducing three strategies: (1) constructing a stable Gamma-Markov chain model that smoothly drifts over time by combining both static and dynamic latent features of data; (2) incorporating the user/item metadata into the model to tackle sparse ratings; and (3) undertaking stochastic variational inference to efficiently handle massive data. mGDMF is conjugate, dynamic and scalable. Experiments show that mGDMF significantly (both effectively and efficiently) outperforms the state-of-the-art static and dynamic models on large, sparse and dynamic data.

The method combines three mechanisms. A stable Gamma-Markov chain allows latent features to drift smoothly over time while retaining both static and dynamic information. User and item metadata provide information where ratings are sparse. Stochastic variational inference makes learning manageable for large datasets, and the model retains a conjugate probabilistic structure.

The reported experiments show significant improvements in both effectiveness and efficiency over the static and dynamic models considered on large, sparse, changing data. The contribution is the integration of these capabilities within one recommendation model. Temporal structure addresses evolving behavior, metadata supplements scarce interactions, and scalable inference supports fitting the resulting model to massive collections of observations.
summary.tldr: mGDMF combines evolving latent factors, metadata, and scalable inference to model large, sparse recommendation datasets.

title: Gamma-Poisson Dynamic Matrix Factorization Embedded with Metadata Influence

abstract: A central problem in dynamical system modeling is state discovery—that is, finding a compact summary of the past that captures the information needed to predict the future. Predictive State Representations (PSRs) enable clever spectral methods for state discovery; however, while consistent in the limit of infinite data, these methods often suffer from poor performance in the low data regime. In this paper we develop a novel algorithm for incorporating domain knowledge, in the form of an imperfect state representation, as side information to speed spectral learning for PSRs. We prove theoretical results characterizing the relevance of a user-provided state representation, and design spectral algorithms that can take advantage of a relevant representation. Our algorithm utilizes principal angles to extract the relevant components of the representation, and is robust to misspecification. Empirical evaluation on synthetic HMMs, an aircraft identification domain, and a gene splice dataset shows that, even with weak domain knowledge, the algorithm can significantly outperform standard PSR learning.

The supplied knowledge takes the form of a proposed state representation that may contain useful information without being fully correct. The authors characterize theoretically when that representation is relevant and design spectral algorithms that exploit its relevant parts. Their method uses principal angles to identify those components and is robust to misspecification of the supplied representation.

Experiments include synthetic hidden Markov models, aircraft identification, and a gene splice dataset. Even weak domain knowledge can yield substantial improvements over standard predictive-state learning in these evaluations. The findings support treating an imperfect state description as useful side information: the algorithm can extract relevant structure while completing the representation through learning.
summary.tldr: A spectral learning method extracts useful parts of imperfect state descriptions to improve predictive state discovery with limited data.

title: Completing State Representations using Spectral Learning

abstract: Inferring intent from observed behavior has been studied extensively within the frameworks of Bayesian inverse planning and inverse reinforcement learning. These methods infer a goal or reward function that best explains the actions of the observed agent, typically a human demonstrator. Another agent can use this inferred intent to predict, imitate, or assist the human user. However, a central assumption in inverse reinforcement learning is that the demonstrator is close to optimal. While models of suboptimal behavior exist, they typically assume that suboptimal actions are the result of some type of random noise or a known cognitive bias, like temporal inconsistency. In this paper, we take an alternative approach, and model suboptimal behavior as the result of internal model misspecification: the reason that user actions might deviate from near-optimal actions is that the user has an incorrect set of beliefs about the rules -- the dynamics -- governing how actions affect the environment. Our insight is that while demonstrated actions may be suboptimal in the real world, they may actually be near-optimal with respect to the user's internal model of the dynamics. By estimating these internal beliefs from observed behavior, we arrive at a new method for inferring intent. We demonstrate in simulation and in a user study with 12 participants that this approach enables us to more accurately model human intent, and can be used in a variety of applications, including offering assistance in a shared autonomy framework and inferring human preferences.

paragraphs: Inferring a person's goal from their actions often assumes they act nearly optimally. When behavior looks inefficient, existing models may attribute it to randomness or a known bias. This paper considers another explanation: the person may misunderstand how actions affect the environment, so their decisions reflect an incorrect internal model of its dynamics.

The key idea is that behavior can be poor under the real rules yet sensible under the rules the person believes. The proposed method estimates those internal beliefs from observed actions and uses them to infer intent. This separates what someone wants from their understanding of how to achieve it, giving apparently suboptimal actions an informative interpretation.

Simulation experiments and a study with 12 participants show more accurate modeling of human intent. The approach also supports applications in shared-autonomy assistance and preference inference. These findings suggest that accounting for mistaken beliefs can improve how another agent interprets and assists a user, especially when observed actions are near-optimal under the user's internal model.
summary.tldr: Inferring a person's mistaken beliefs about environmental dynamics can improve intent prediction and support more useful assistance.

title: Where Do You Think You're Going?: Inferring Beliefs about Dynamics from Behavior

abstract: By providing a simple and efficient way of computing low-variance gradients of continuous random variables, the reparameterization trick has become the technique of choice for training a variety of latent variable models. However, it is not applicable to a number of important continuous distributions. We introduce an alternative approach to computing reparameterization gradients based on implicit differentiation and demonstrate its broader applicability by applying it to Gamma, Beta, Dirichlet, and von Mises distributions, which cannot be used with the classic reparameterization trick. Our experiments show that the proposed approach is faster and more accurate than the existing gradient estimators for these distributions.

paragraphs: Training a latent-variable model often requires gradients involving continuous random variables. The reparameterization trick is useful because it provides an efficient way to compute gradients with low variance. However, the classic form does not apply to several important distributions, restricting where that training technique can be used.

The paper introduces an alternative way to compute reparameterization gradients through implicit differentiation. This changes the mathematical route used to obtain the gradients and broadens the range of supported distributions. The authors demonstrate the approach on Gamma, Beta, Dirichlet, and von Mises distributions, which they identify as incompatible with the classic reparameterization trick.

Experiments show the proposed method to be faster and more accurate than existing gradient estimators for those distributions. The result matters because the choice of random-variable distribution is part of how a latent-variable model is specified. Extending efficient gradient computation to additional distributions makes the training approach applicable to a broader set of such models, with the reported speed and accuracy benefits established by the experiments.
summary.tldr: Implicit differentiation extends reparameterization gradients to additional continuous distributions, with faster and more accurate estimation in the reported experiments.

title: Implicit Reparameterization Gradients

abstract: In recent years, unfolding iterative algorithms as neural networks has become an empirical success in solving sparse recovery problems. However, its theoretical understanding is still immature, which prevents us from fully utilizing the power of neural networks. In this work, we study unfolded ISTA (Iterative Shrinkage Thresholding Algorithm) for sparse signal recovery. We introduce a weight structure that is necessary for asymptotic convergence to the true sparse signal. With this structure, unfolded ISTA can attain a linear convergence, which is better than the sublinear convergence of ISTA/FISTA in general cases. Furthermore, we propose to incorporate thresholding in the network to perform support selection, which is easy to implement and able to boost the convergence rate both theoretically and empirically. Extensive simulations, including sparse vector recovery and a compressive sensing experiment on real image data, corroborate our theoretical results and demonstrate their practical usefulness. We have made our codes publicly available: https://github.com/xchen-tamu/linear-lista-cpss.

It focuses on unfolded ISTA, connecting its learned network structure to convergence toward the true sparse signal. The aim is to turn empirical success into mathematical guidance for choosing weights and thresholds.

The authors identify a weight structure necessary for asymptotic convergence to the true signal. With that structure, unfolded ISTA can achieve linear convergence, improving on the general sublinear convergence of ISTA and FISTA. The distinction matters: the structural condition is necessary for the stated asymptotic goal, while linear convergence is a capability established for the structured approach.

They further introduce thresholding that performs support selection, helping identify which signal entries belong in the sparse solution. This addition is easy to implement and improves convergence rates both theoretically and empirically. Simulations for sparse vector recovery and a compressive-sensing experiment on real images support the analysis and demonstrate the practical value of the proposed weights and thresholds.
summary.tldr: Structured weights and support-selecting thresholds give unfolded ISTA theoretical and empirical improvements in sparse-recovery convergence.

title: Theoretical Linear Convergence of Unfolded ISTA and Its Practical Weights and Thresholds

abstract: Many applications of machine learning involve the analysis of large data frames -- matrices collecting heterogeneous measurements (binary, numerical, counts, etc.) across samples -- with missing values. Low-rank models, as studied by Udell et al. (2016), are popular in this framework for tasks such as visualization, clustering and missing value imputation. Yet, available methods with statistical guarantees and efficient optimization do not allow explicit modeling of main additive effects such as row and column, or covariate effects. In this paper, we introduce a low-rank interaction and sparse additive effects (LORIS) model which combines matrix regression on a dictionary and low-rank design, to estimate main effects and interactions simultaneously. We provide statistical guarantees in the form of upper bounds on the estimation error of both components. Then, we introduce a mixed coordinate gradient descent (MCGD) method which provably converges sub-linearly to an optimal solution and is computationally efficient for large scale data sets. We show on simulated and survey data that the method has a clear advantage over current practices.

paragraphs: Large data tables can mix binary measurements, numbers, and counts while also containing missing entries. Low-rank models are useful for analyzing such tables, but the paper identifies a gap in methods combining statistical guarantees and efficient optimization: they do not explicitly represent additive row, column, or covariate effects alongside interactions.

LORIS combines low-rank interactions with sparse additive effects. It uses matrix regression on a dictionary together with a low-rank design to estimate both components simultaneously. This separates two kinds of structure within one model: main effects described by the additive component and interactions represented through the low-rank component.

The authors provide upper bounds on the estimation errors of both components. They also introduce mixed coordinate gradient descent, an algorithm with a proved sublinear convergence rate to an optimal solution and computational efficiency for large datasets. Results on simulated and survey data show an advantage over current practices. The contribution therefore includes a richer model, statistical error analysis, and an optimization method for fitting it.
summary.tldr: LORIS jointly estimates sparse additive effects and low-rank interactions in heterogeneous tables, with statistical and optimization guarantees.

title: Low-rank Interaction with Sparse Additive Effects Model for Large Data Frames

abstract: Layer normalization (LayerNorm) has been successfully applied to various deep neural networks to help stabilize training and boost model convergence because of its capability in handling re-centering and re-scaling of both inputs and weight matrix. However, the computational overhead introduced by LayerNorm makes these improvements expensive and significantly slows the underlying network, e.g. RNN in particular. In this paper, we hypothesize that re-centering invariance in LayerNorm is dispensable and propose root mean square layer normalization, or RMSNorm. RMSNorm regularizes the summed inputs to a neuron in one layer according to root mean square (RMS), giving the model re-scaling invariance property and implicit learning rate adaptation ability. RMSNorm is computationally simpler and thus more efficient than LayerNorm. We also present partial RMSNorm, or pRMSNorm where the RMS is estimated from p% of the summed inputs without breaking the above properties. Extensive experiments on several tasks using diverse network architectures show that RMSNorm achieves comparable performance against LayerNorm but reduces the running time by 7%~64% on different models. Source code is available at https://github.com/bzhangGo/rmsnorm.
