paragraphs: Layer normalization can stabilize neural-network training, but its computational overhead can slow the underlying model, particularly recurrent networks. This paper investigates whether its recentering behavior is necessary. The authors hypothesize that it can be removed while keeping the useful effects of controlling scale.

They propose RMSNorm, which normalizes summed inputs using their root mean square. The method retains rescaling invariance and provides implicit learning-rate adaptation while requiring simpler computation than LayerNorm. A further variant, partial RMSNorm, estimates the root mean square from only a percentage of the summed inputs, preserving those stated properties.

Experiments across several tasks and network architectures show performance comparable to LayerNorm with running-time reductions ranging from 7% to 64%, depending on the model. These results support the proposed simplification in the evaluated settings. The contribution separates two roles bundled into LayerNorm and shows that retaining scale normalization alone can offer a favorable performance-and-runtime trade-off without requiring the full original computation.
summary.tldr: RMSNorm removes LayerNorm’s recentering operation while achieving comparable experimental performance and reducing runtime by 7%–64% across tested models.

title: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization

abstract: We consider combinatorial online learning with subset choices when only relative feedback information from subsets is available, instead of bandit or semi-bandit feedback which is absolute. Specifically, we study two regret minimisation problems over subsets of a finite ground set $[n]$, with subset-wise relative preference information feedback according to the Multinomial logit choice model. In the first setting, the learner can play subsets of size bounded by a maximum size and receives top-$m$ rank-ordered feedback, while in the second setting the learner can play subsets of a fixed size $k$ with a full subset ranking observed as feedback. For both settings, we devise instance-dependent and order-optimal regret algorithms with regret $O(\frac{n}{m} \ln T)$ and $O(\frac{n}{k} \ln T)$, respectively. We derive fundamental limits on the regret performance of online learning with subset-wise preferences, proving the tightness of our regret guarantees. Our results also show the value of eliciting more general top-$m$ rank-ordered feedback over single winner feedback ($m=1$). Our theoretical results are corroborated with empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions in which a learner chooses groups of items and observes their relative preferences rather than absolute rewards. The goal is to keep regret small: the accumulated cost of learning while making choices. Preferences follow a Multinomial logit model, which supplies the probabilistic structure used by the algorithms and analysis.

Two feedback settings are considered. In one, the learner chooses subsets up to a maximum size and observes the ordered top m items. In the other, every chosen subset contains exactly k items, and the learner observes its complete ranking. The authors develop algorithms with instance-dependent regret scaling as O((n/m) ln T) and O((n/k) ln T), respectively.

Matching fundamental limits establish that these regret rates are optimal in order for the studied settings. The dependence on m explains the value of requesting richer rankings: observing several leading items can improve regret relative to observing only a winner. Empirical evaluations support the theoretical results, connecting the feedback advantage to the algorithms’ observed behavior.
summary.tldr: Under a Multinomial logit preference model, ranking-based subset selection admits order-optimal regret that improves with richer feedback.

title: Combinatorial Bandits with Relative Feedback

abstract: We propose a new way of constructing invertible neural networks by combining simple building blocks with a novel set of composition rules. This leads to a rich set of invertible architectures, including those similar to ResNets. Inversion is achieved with a locally convergent iterative procedure that is parallelizable and very fast in practice. Additionally, the determinant of the Jacobian can be computed analytically and efficiently, enabling their generative use as flow models. To demonstrate their flexibility, we show that our invertible neural networks are competitive with ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification. When trained as generative models, our invertible networks achieve competitive likelihoods on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32, with bits per dimension of 0.98, 3.32 and 4.06 respectively.

paragraphs: Invertible neural networks must support recovering an input from its transformed representation. MintNet proposes a construction based on simple building blocks and new composition rules, producing a broad range of invertible architectures, including designs resembling ResNets. The aim is to combine architectural flexibility with operations needed for both classification and generation.

The inverse is computed through a parallelizable iterative procedure that is locally convergent and reported to be fast in practice. The network’s Jacobian determinant can also be calculated analytically and efficiently. That determinant makes the architecture usable as a flow model, where transformations support evaluating the probability assigned to data.

For classification, the networks are competitive with ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10. As generative models, they achieve reported competitive likelihoods of 0.98, 3.32, and 4.06 bits per dimension on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet 32×32, respectively. These results demonstrate flexibility across the two uses, while the inversion guarantee remains specifically local rather than a claim of convergence from every starting point.
summary.tldr: MintNet constructs flexible invertible networks with efficient Jacobian determinants and a fast, locally convergent inversion procedure.

title: MintNet: Building Invertible Neural Networks with Masked Convolutions

abstract: To deepen our understanding of graph neural networks, we investigate the representation power of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) through the looking glass of graph moments, a key property of graph topology encoding path of various lengths. We find that GCNs are rather restrictive in learning graph moments. Without careful design, GCNs can fail miserably even with multiple layers and nonlinear activation functions. We analyze theoretically the expressiveness of GCNs, arriving at a modular GCN design, using different propagation rules. Our modular design is capable of distinguishing graphs from different graph generation models for surprisingly small graphs, a notoriously difficult problem in network science. Our investigation suggests that, depth is much more influential than width and deeper GCNs are more capable of learning higher order graph moments. Additionally, combining GCN modules with different propagation rules is critical to the representation power of GCNs.

paragraphs: This paper examines what graph convolutional networks can learn about graph structure through graph moments, which encode paths of different lengths. It finds that these networks can be restrictive in their ability to learn such properties. Multiple layers and nonlinear activations alone do not prevent failures when the architecture is poorly designed.

The authors analyze expressiveness theoretically and develop a modular architecture combining different propagation rules. Propagation determines how information travels through the graph, so changing these rules changes the structural information available to the model. The proposed design can distinguish graphs from different graph-generation models even when the graphs are small, a difficult setting highlighted by the paper.

The investigation suggests that depth matters more than width for this task, with deeper networks better able to learn higher-order graph moments. It also identifies combining modules with different propagation rules as critical to representation power. The findings provide architectural guidance tied to learning graph topology, rather than asserting that increasing depth alone solves every expressive limitation.
summary.tldr: Analysis through graph moments motivates modular graph networks and highlights the importance of depth and varied propagation rules.

title: Understanding the Representation Power of Graph Neural Networks in Learning Graph Topology

abstract: We consider the problem of identifying multiway block structure from a large noisy tensor. Such problems arise frequently in applications such as genomics, recommendation system, topic modeling, and sensor network localization. We propose a tensor block model, develop a unified least-square estimation, and obtain the theoretical accuracy guarantees for multiway clustering. The statistical convergence of the estimator is established, and we show that the associated clustering procedure achieves partition consistency. A sparse regularization is further developed for identifying important blocks with elevated means. The proposal handles a broad range of data types, including binary, continuous, and hybrid observations. Through simulation and application to two real datasets, we demonstrate the outperformance of our approach over previous methods.

paragraphs: A tensor organizes observations along several dimensions, and useful groups may exist along more than one of those dimensions. This paper studies how to recover that multiway block structure when the observed tensor is large and noisy. Such structure appears in settings including genomics, recommendation, topic modeling, and sensor network localization.

The authors introduce a tensor block model and a unified least-squares estimator. They establish statistical convergence and theoretical accuracy guarantees for the resulting clustering method, including partition consistency. This connects the fitted numerical model to the recovery of the underlying grouping, rather than assessing the model only by how closely it fits observed entries.

The method also includes sparse regularization to identify important blocks with elevated means, allowing the analysis to highlight particular groups of entries. It accommodates binary, continuous, and hybrid observations. Simulations and applications to two real datasets show better performance than the previous methods considered. The contribution combines a flexible model for several data types with theoretical support for recovering groups across multiple dimensions.
summary.tldr: Tensor block models recover multiway clusters from noisy data, with statistical guarantees and a sparse extension for identifying elevated blocks.

title: Multiway clustering via tensor block models

abstract: Contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms are widely used in sequential decision tasks such as news article recommendation systems, web page ad placement algorithms, and mobile health. Most of the existing algorithms have regret proportional to a polynomial function of the context dimension, $d$. In many applications however, it is often the case that contexts are high-dimensional with only a sparse subset of size $s_0 (\ll d)$ being correlated with the reward. We consider the stochastic linear contextual bandit problem and propose a novel algorithm, namely the Doubly-Robust Lasso Bandit algorithm, which exploits the sparse structure of the regression parameter as in Lasso, while blending the doubly-robust technique used in missing data literature. The high-probability upper bound of the regret incurred by the proposed algorithm does not depend on the number of arms and scales with $\mathrm{log}(d)$ instead of a polynomial function of $d$. The proposed algorithm shows good performance when contexts of different arms are correlated and requires less tuning parameters than existing methods.

Most of the existing algorithms have regret proportional to a polynomial function of the context dimension, $d$. In many applications however, it is often the case that contexts are high-dimensional with only a sparse subset of size $s_0 (\ll d)$ being correlated with the reward. We consider the stochastic linear contextual bandit problem and propose a novel algorithm, namely the Doubly-Robust Lasso Bandit algorithm, which exploits the sparse structure of the regression parameter as in Lasso, while blending the doubly-robust technique used in missing data literature. The high-probability upper bound of the regret incurred by the proposed algorithm does not depend on the number of arms and scales with $\mathrm{log}(d)$ instead of a polynomial function of $d$. The proposed algorithm shows good performance when contexts of different arms are correlated and requires less tuning parameters than existing methods.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits repeatedly choose among actions using available context and learn from the resulting rewards. Many algorithms become harder to use effectively as the number of context features grows. This paper considers stochastic linear contextual bandits where the context is high-dimensional but only a small subset of features is associated with reward.

The proposed Doubly-Robust Lasso Bandit combines sparse regression with a doubly robust technique from missing-data research. Lasso supplies the mechanism for exploiting sparsity in the regression parameter. Combining these ideas addresses a setting where a large feature description contains only a much smaller amount of reward-relevant information.

The authors establish a high-probability regret upper bound that depends logarithmically on the context dimension and does not depend on the number of arms. This improves the dimensional dependence relative to polynomial dependence described for many existing algorithms. They also report good performance when contexts across different arms are correlated and fewer tuning parameters than existing methods. These benefits are stated for the sparse stochastic linear setting studied.
summary.tldr: Combining Lasso with doubly robust estimation yields a sparse linear bandit algorithm with logarithmic dimensional dependence in its high-probability regret bound.

title: Doubly-Robust Lasso Bandit

abstract: Multilabel classification is a challenging problem arising in applications ranging from information retrieval to image tagging. A popular approach to this problem is to employ a reduction to a suitable series of binary or multiclass problems (e.g., computing a softmax based cross-entropy over the relevant labels). While such methods have seen empirical success, less is understood about how well they approximate two fundamental performance measures: precision@$k$ and recall@$k$. In this paper, we study five commonly used reductions, including the one-versus-all reduction, a reduction to multiclass classification, and normalised versions of the same, wherein the contribution of each instance is normalised by the number of relevant labels. Our main result is a formal justification of each reduction: we explicate their underlying risks, and show they are each consistent with respect to either precision or recall. Further, we show that in general no reduction can be optimal for both measures. We empirically validate our results, demonstrating scenarios where normalised reductions yield recall gains over unnormalised counterparts.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification allows each example to have several relevant labels. A common training strategy reduces the task to binary or multiclass problems, but the resulting loss may favor a particular evaluation measure. This paper asks how five common reductions relate to precision at k and recall at k.

The analysis includes one-versus-all and multiclass reductions, along with normalized variants that scale each example's contribution by its number of relevant labels. The authors identify the risks underlying these objectives and prove that each reduction is consistent with either precision or recall. This gives a formal interpretation of what the training loss is aligned to optimize.

A further result shows that, in general, a reduction cannot be optimal for both measures. Consequently, choosing a loss involves the intended evaluation criterion, not just a convenient way to organize training. Experiments support the analysis by demonstrating cases where normalized reductions improve recall over unnormalized alternatives. Those gains are scenario-dependent, consistent with the paper's distinction between the two objectives.
summary.tldr: Five common multilabel reductions align with either precision or recall, and no reduction is generally optimal for both.

title: Multilabel reductions: what is my loss optimising?

abstract: How well does a classic deep net architecture like AlexNet or VGG19 classify on a standard dataset such as CIFAR-10 when its “width”— namely, number of channels in convolutional layers, and number of nodes in fully-connected internal layers — is allowed to increase to infinity? Such questions have come to the forefront in the quest to theoretically understand deep learning and its mysteries about optimization and generalization. They also connect deep learning to notions such as Gaussian processes and kernels. A recent paper [Jacot et al., 2018] introduced the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) which captures the behavior of fully-connected deep nets in the infinite width limit trained by gradient descent; this object was implicit in some other recent papers. An attraction of such ideas is that a pure kernel-based method is used to capture the power of a fully-trained deep net of infinite width. The current paper gives the first efficient exact algorithm for computing the extension of NTK to convolutional neural nets, which we call Convolutional NTK (CNTK), as well as an efficient GPU implementation of this algorithm. This results in a significant new benchmark for performance of a pure kernel-based method on CIFAR-10, being 10% higher than the methods reported in [Novak et al., 2019], and only 6% lower than the performance of the corresponding finite deep net architecture (once batch normalization etc. are turned off). Theoretically, we also give the first non-asymptotic proof showing that a fully-trained sufficiently wide net is indeed equivalent to the kernel regression predictor using NTK.

The practical challenge is computing the convolutional version of this kernel efficiently and exactly.

summary.tldr: An efficient exact convolutional neural tangent kernel algorithm enables strong kernel classification results alongside a sufficiently-wide-network equivalence proof.

title: On Exact Computation with an Infinitely Wide Neural Net

abstract: Many real-world problems, including multi-speaker text-to-speech synthesis, can greatly benefit from the ability to meta-learn large models with only a few task- specific components. Updating only these task-specific modules then allows the model to be adapted to low-data tasks for as many steps as necessary without risking overfitting. Unfortunately, existing meta-learning methods either do not scale to long adaptation or else rely on handcrafted task-specific architectures. Here, we propose a meta-learning approach that obviates the need for this often sub-optimal hand-selection. In particular, we develop general techniques based on Bayesian shrinkage to automatically discover and learn both task-specific and general reusable modules. Empirically, we demonstrate that our method discovers a small set of meaningful task-specific modules and outperforms existing meta- learning approaches in domains like few-shot text-to-speech that have little task data and long adaptation horizons. We also show that existing meta-learning methods including MAML, iMAML, and Reptile emerge as special cases of our method.

paragraphs: Adapting a large model to a task with little data can benefit from changing only a small set of task-specific components. The challenge is deciding which components should vary and which should be shared. This paper addresses that choice in meta-learning, especially when adaptation needs to continue for many optimization steps.

The proposed approach uses Bayesian shrinkage to discover both reusable modules and modules that should specialize to individual tasks. This removes the need to hand-select the task-specific architecture. It targets a practical gap described by the authors: existing approaches either struggle with long adaptation or depend on manually designed choices about which parts of the model can change.

Experiments show that the method discovers a small set of meaningful task-specific modules and outperforms existing meta-learning approaches in settings such as few-shot text-to-speech. These settings combine scarce task data with long adaptation horizons. The authors also show that MAML, iMAML, and Reptile are special cases of their formulation, connecting the proposed modular approach to established methods within a common framework.
summary.tldr: Bayesian shrinkage lets a meta-learning system discover which modules to share and which to adapt, improving low-data tasks with long adaptation.

title: Modular Meta-Learning with Shrinkage

abstract: Binary source code matching, especially on function-level, has a critical role in the field of computer security. Given binary code only, finding the corresponding source code improves the accuracy and efficiency in reverse engineering. Given source code only, related binary code retrieval contributes to known vulnerabilities confirmation. However, due to the vast difference between source and binary code, few studies have investigated binary source code matching. Previously published studies focus on code literals extraction such as strings and integers, then utilize traditional matching algorithms such as the Hungarian algorithm for code matching. Nevertheless, these methods have limitations on function-level, because they ignore the potential semantic features of code and a lot of code lacks sufficient code literals. Also, these methods indicate a need for expert experience for useful feature identification and feature engineering, which is timeconsuming. This paper proposes an end-to-end cross-modal retrieval network for binary source code matching, which achieves higher accuracy and requires less expert experience. We adopt Deep Pyramid Convolutional Neural Network (DPCNN) for source code feature extraction and Graph Neural Network (GNN) for binary code feature extraction. We also exploit neural network-based models to capture code literals, including strings and integers. Furthermore, we implement "norm weighted sampling" for negative sampling. We evaluate our model on two datasets, where it outperforms other methods significantly.

paragraphs: Matching a compiled function to its source code can support reverse engineering, while retrieving binaries related to known source code can help confirm vulnerabilities. The difficulty is that source and binary code look very different. Earlier approaches described in the paper rely heavily on matching literals such as strings and integers, which may be scarce within individual functions.

CodeCMR treats the task as retrieval across two different forms of code. It uses a Deep Pyramid Convolutional Neural Network to extract source-code features and a Graph Neural Network to extract binary-code features. Neural models also capture strings and integers, so those clues remain part of the approach alongside learned code representations.

The end-to-end network additionally uses a negative-sampling procedure called norm weighted sampling. Across two evaluated datasets, the authors report substantially better performance than the compared methods and reduced dependence on expert feature engineering. The main practical significance is a way to match functions using learned representations when literal-based evidence alone provides an incomplete basis for retrieval.
summary.tldr: CodeCMR learns source and binary code representations to improve function-level matching with less expert feature engineering.

title: CodeCMR: Cross-Modal Retrieval For Function-Level Binary Source Code Matching

abstract: In this paper we propose the first multi-armed bandit algorithm based on re-sampling that achieves asymptotically optimal regret simultaneously for different families of arms (namely Bernoulli, Gaussian and Poisson distributions). Unlike Thompson Sampling which requires to specify a different prior to be optimal in each case, our proposal RB-SDA does not need any distribution-dependent tuning. RB-SDA belongs to the family of Sub-sampling Duelling Algorithms (SDA) which combines the sub-sampling idea first used by the BESA and SSMC algorithms with different sub-sampling schemes. In particular, RB-SDA uses Random Block sampling. We perform an experimental study assessing the flexibility and robustness of this promising novel approach for exploration in bandit models.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose the first multi-armed bandit algorithm based on re-sampling that achieves asymptotically optimal regret simultaneously for different families of arms (namely Bernoulli, Gaussian and Poisson distributions). Unlike Thompson Sampling which requires to specify a different prior to be optimal in each case, our proposal RB-SDA does not need any distribution-dependent tuning. RB-SDA belongs to the family of Sub-sampling Duelling Algorithms (SDA) which combines the sub-sampling idea first used by the BESA and SSMC algorithms with different sub-sampling schemes. In particular, RB-SDA uses Random Block sampling. We perform an experimental study assessing the flexibility and robustness of this promising novel approach for exploration in bandit models.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit learner must decide how much to explore uncertain choices while seeking high rewards. This paper develops a resampling-based approach that works across several reward-distribution families without distribution-dependent tuning. The central question is whether that flexibility can coexist with asymptotically optimal regret, a measure of long-run losses from learning.

The proposed algorithm, RB-SDA, belongs to a family called Sub-sampling Duelling Algorithms. This family combines earlier subsampling ideas with different schemes for choosing subsamples, and RB-SDA specifically uses Random Block sampling. Its exploration procedure therefore draws on resampled observations, with the sampling scheme forming a central part of the algorithm's design.

The authors prove asymptotically optimal regret for Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Poisson arms using the same proposal without distribution-specific tuning. They contrast this with Thompson Sampling, which requires different priors to achieve optimality in those cases. An experimental study assesses the approach's flexibility and robustness. The guarantee concerns the named distribution families and asymptotic regret, giving a precise scope to the method's adaptability.
summary.tldr: RB-SDA achieves asymptotically optimal regret for Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Poisson bandits without distribution-dependent tuning.

title: Sub-sampling for Efficient Non-Parametric Bandit Exploration

abstract: Entropy regularization, smoothing of Q-values and neural network function approximator are key components of the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, such as Soft Actor-Critic~\cite{haarnoja2018soft}. Despite the widespread use, the impact of these core techniques on the convergence of RL algorithms is not yet fully understood. In this work, we analyse these techniques from error propagation perspective using the approximate dynamic programming framework. In particular, our analysis shows that (1) value smoothing results in increased stability of the algorithm in exchange for slower convergence, (2) entropy regularization reduces overestimation errors at the cost of modifying the original problem, (3) we study a combination of these techniques that describes the Soft Actor-Critic algorithm.
originalAbstract: Entropy regularization, smoothing of Q-values and neural network function approximator are key components of the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, such as Soft Actor-Critic~\cite{haarnoja2018soft}. Despite the widespread use, the impact of these core techniques on the convergence of RL algorithms is not yet fully understood. In this work, we analyse these techniques from error propagation perspective using the approximate dynamic programming framework. In particular, our analysis shows that (1) value smoothing results in increased stability of the algorithm in exchange for slower convergence, (2) entropy regularization reduces overestimation errors at the cost of modifying the original problem, (3) we study a combination of these techniques that describes the Soft Actor-Critic algorithm.

paragraphs: Modern reinforcement-learning algorithms combine techniques such as entropy regularization, smoothing of Q-values, and neural function approximation. Their widespread use does not by itself explain how they affect convergence. This paper studies their effects through approximate dynamic programming, focusing on how errors propagate through successive value updates.

The analysis identifies a tradeoff for value smoothing: it increases algorithmic stability but slows convergence. Entropy regularization has a different effect, reducing overestimation errors while changing the original optimization problem. These findings distinguish two mechanisms that may appear together in an algorithm but influence learning in different ways.

The authors also analyze a combination of the techniques that describes Soft Actor-Critic. This connects the theoretical framework to a widely used algorithm and helps interpret the role of its components. The contribution is an account of what those components trade away as well as what they improve: stability comes with slower progress, while reduced overestimation comes with a modified objective.
summary.tldr: An error-propagation analysis shows how value smoothing and entropy regularization trade convergence speed and the original objective for stability and reduced overestimation.

title: On the Convergence of Smooth Regularized Approximate Value Iteration Schemes

abstract: We present simple differentially private estimators for the parameters of multivariate sub-Gaussian data that are accurate at small sample sizes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms both theoretically and empirically using synthetic and real-world datasets---showing that their asymptotic error rates match the state-of-the-art theoretical bounds, and that they concretely outperform all previous methods. Specifically, previous estimators either have weak empirical accuracy at small sample sizes, perform poorly for multivariate data, or require the user to provide strong a priori estimates for the parameters.
originalAbstract: We present simple differentially private estimators for the parameters of multivariate sub-Gaussian data that are accurate at small sample sizes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms both theoretically and empirically using synthetic and real-world datasets---showing that their asymptotic error rates match the state-of-the-art theoretical bounds, and that they concretely outperform all previous methods. Specifically, previous estimators either have weak empirical accuracy at small sample sizes, perform poorly for multivariate data, or require the user to provide strong a priori estimates for the parameters.

paragraphs: CoinPress addresses a basic statistical task under privacy constraints: estimating the mean and covariance of data with multiple variables. The mean summarizes typical values, while covariance describes how variables vary together. The paper develops simple estimators that satisfy differential privacy and remain accurate with small sample sizes for multivariate sub-Gaussian data.

The motivation is a gap between theoretical accuracy and practical usefulness. According to the authors, earlier estimators can struggle with small datasets or multiple variables, or require users to supply strong prior estimates of the parameters. Those requirements matter because estimating the parameters is precisely the task the user wants to perform.

The authors support their methods with both mathematical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real datasets. Their asymptotic error rates match leading theoretical bounds, while the reported empirical comparisons outperform previous methods. These findings connect two different goals: maintaining favorable error behavior as sample size grows and delivering useful accuracy when data are limited. The stated distributional setting is central to those results.
summary.tldr: CoinPress provides differentially private mean and covariance estimators with strong theoretical rates and improved empirical accuracy at small sample sizes.

title: CoinPress: Practical Private Mean and Covariance Estimation

abstract: Task-oriented dialogue is often decomposed into three tasks: understanding user input, deciding actions, and generating a response. While such decomposition might suggest a dedicated model for each sub-task, we find a simple, unified approach leads to state-of-the-art performance on the MultiWOZ dataset. SimpleTOD is a simple approach to task-oriented dialogue that uses a single, causal language model trained on all sub-tasks recast as a single sequence prediction problem. This allows SimpleTOD to fully leverage transfer learning from pre-trained, open domain, causal language models such as GPT-2. SimpleTOD improves over the prior state-of-the-art in joint goal accuracy for dialogue state tracking, and our analysis reveals robustness to noisy annotations in this setting. SimpleTOD also improves the main metrics used to evaluate action decisions and response generation in an end-to-end setting: inform rate by 8.1 points, success rate by 9.7 points, and combined score by 7.2 points.

paragraphs: A task-oriented dialogue system needs to understand a user’s request, choose an action, and generate a response. These responsibilities often motivate separate models. SimpleTOD asks whether one language model can perform them together by expressing all of the subtasks as parts of a single sequence prediction problem.

The model is causal: it predicts subsequent sequence content from what has already appeared. This shared formulation allows the system to benefit from pretraining in open-domain language modeling, including models such as GPT-2. The architectural contribution is the unification itself, making the dialogue subtasks compatible with the same training and prediction mechanism.

On MultiWOZ, SimpleTOD improves the previous state of the art in joint goal accuracy for tracking dialogue state. The authors also report robustness to noisy annotations in that setting. In end-to-end evaluation, inform rate increases by 8.1 points, success rate by 9.7 points, and the combined score by 7.2 points. Together, these results show that a simple unified formulation can improve both state tracking and the evaluated action-and-response outcomes.
summary.tldr: SimpleTOD treats dialogue understanding, action selection, and response generation as one language-modeling problem and improves MultiWOZ results.

title: A Simple Language Model for Task-Oriented Dialogue

abstract: Given a multi-microphone recording of an unknown number of speakers talking concurrently, we simultaneously localize the sources and separate the individual speakers. At the core of our method is a deep network, in the waveform domain, which isolates sources within an angular region $\theta \pm w/2$, given an angle of interest $\theta$ and angular window size $w$. By exponentially decreasing $w$, we can perform a binary search to localize and separate all sources in logarithmic time. Our algorithm also allows for an arbitrary number of potentially moving speakers at test time, including more speakers than seen during training. Experiments demonstrate state of the art performance for both source separation and source localization, particularly in high levels of background noise.

At the core of our method is a deep network, in the waveform domain, which isolates sources within an angular region $\theta \pm w/2$, given an angle of interest $\theta$ and angular window size $w$. By exponentially decreasing $w$, we can perform a binary search to localize and separate all sources in logarithmic time. Our algorithm also allows for an arbitrary number of potentially moving speakers at test time, including more speakers than seen during training. Experiments demonstrate state of the art performance for both source separation and source localization, particularly in high levels of background noise.

paragraphs: When several people speak simultaneously, a microphone array records a mixture of their voices. This paper jointly tackles two tasks: determining where the speakers are and separating their speech. The method does not require the number of speakers in the recording to be known in advance.

Its core is a neural network that operates directly on waveforms and isolates sound sources inside a specified angular window. The inputs include a direction of interest and the width of the region around it. Repeatedly shrinking that width exponentially enables a binary search that localizes and separates sources in logarithmic time, tying the separation procedure to spatial refinement.

At test time, the algorithm accommodates an arbitrary number of potentially moving speakers, including more speakers than appeared during training. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for both separation and localization, particularly under high background noise. The findings show how a direction-selective network can be reused within a search procedure to address recordings whose speaker count and locations vary.
summary.tldr: A direction-selective waveform network uses progressively narrower angular windows to locate and separate an unknown number of speakers.

title: The Cone of Silence: Speech Separation by Localization

abstract: We introduce regularized Frank-Wolfe, a general and effective algorithm for inference and learning of dense conditional random fields (CRFs). The algorithm optimizes a nonconvex continuous relaxation of the CRF inference problem using vanilla Frank-Wolfe with approximate updates, which are equivalent to minimizing a regularized energy function. Our proposed method is a generalization of existing algorithms such as mean field or concave-convex procedure. This perspective not only offers a unified analysis of these algorithms, but also allows an easy way of exploring different variants that potentially yield better performance. We illustrate this in our empirical results on standard semantic segmentation datasets, where several instantiations of our regularized Frank-Wolfe outperform mean field inference, both as a standalone component and as an end-to-end trainable layer in a neural network. We also show that dense CRFs, coupled with our new algorithms, produce significant improvements over strong CNN baselines.

The algorithm optimizes a nonconvex continuous relaxation of the CRF inference problem using vanilla Frank-Wolfe with approximate updates, which are equivalent to minimizing a regularized energy function. Our proposed method is a generalization of existing algorithms such as mean field or concave-convex procedure. This perspective not only offers a unified analysis of these algorithms, but also allows an easy way of exploring different variants that potentially yield better performance. We illustrate this in our empirical results on standard semantic segmentation datasets, where several instantiations of our regularized Frank-Wolfe outperform mean field inference, both as a standalone component and as an end-to-end trainable layer in a neural network. We also show that dense CRFs, coupled with our new algorithms, produce significant improvements over strong CNN baselines.

paragraphs: Dense conditional random fields model dependencies among predictions, making their inference procedure an important part of the overall system. This paper introduces regularized Frank-Wolfe as a general approach to both inference and learning in these models. It works with a continuous, nonconvex relaxation of the original inference problem.

The algorithm uses ordinary Frank-Wolfe with approximate updates that are equivalent to minimizing a regularized energy function. This perspective encompasses existing approaches, including mean field and the concave-convex procedure. It therefore provides a common basis for analyzing methods that might otherwise appear separate. It also offers a straightforward route to exploring alternative regularized variants that could perform better.

Experiments on standard semantic segmentation datasets show that several variants outperform mean field inference. The gains appear both when the inference algorithm is used independently and when it is incorporated as an end-to-end trainable neural network layer. Dense CRFs using the new algorithms also significantly improve on strong convolutional network baselines. These results give practical support to the broader optimization framework and its flexibility.
summary.tldr: Regularized Frank-Wolfe unifies dense-CRF inference methods and yields variants that improve semantic segmentation in the reported experiments.

title: Regularized Frank-Wolfe for Dense CRFs: Generalizing Mean Field and Beyond

abstract: The problem of reducing processing time of large deep learning models is a fundamental challenge in many real-world applications. Early exit methods strive towards this goal by attaching additional Internal Classifiers (ICs) to intermediate layers of a neural network. ICs can quickly return predictions for easy examples and, as a result, reduce the average inference time of the whole model. However, if a particular IC does not decide to return an answer early, its predictions are discarded, with its computations effectively being wasted. To solve this issue, we introduce Zero Time Waste (ZTW), a novel approach in which each IC reuses predictions returned by its predecessors by (1) adding direct connections between ICs and (2) combining previous outputs in an ensemble-like manner. We conduct extensive experiments across various datasets and architectures to demonstrate that ZTW achieves a significantly better accuracy vs. inference time trade-off than other recently proposed early exit methods.
originalAbstract: The problem of reducing processing time of large deep learning models is a fundamental challenge in many real-world applications. Early exit methods strive towards this goal by attaching additional Internal Classifiers (ICs) to intermediate layers of a neural network. ICs can quickly return predictions for easy examples and, as a result, reduce the average inference time of the whole model. However, if a particular IC does not decide to return an answer early, its predictions are discarded, with its computations effectively being wasted. To solve this issue, we introduce Zero Time Waste (ZTW), a novel approach in which each IC reuses predictions returned by its predecessors by (1) adding direct connections between ICs and (2) combining previous outputs in an ensemble-like manner. We conduct extensive experiments across various datasets and architectures to demonstrate that ZTW achieves a significantly better accuracy vs. inference time trade-off than other recently proposed early exit methods.

paragraphs: Early-exit neural networks attach classifiers to intermediate layers so that easy inputs can receive a prediction before the full network runs. This reduces average inference time. However, when an intermediate classifier does not return an answer, its prediction is typically discarded even though the computation needed to produce it has already been performed.

Zero Time Waste, or ZTW, makes those earlier predictions available to later internal classifiers. It adds direct connections between classifiers and combines previous outputs in an ensemble-like manner. This allows subsequent decisions to reuse work done along the way, making the sequence of intermediate classifiers a source of accumulated predictive information.

Across experiments involving several datasets and architectures, ZTW achieves a significantly better accuracy-versus-inference-time trade-off than the compared recent early-exit methods. The result supports treating intermediate predictions as reusable evidence throughout inference. For applications balancing response time and prediction quality, the reported improvement means the early-exit design can make more effective use of computation already spent on an input.
summary.tldr: ZTW reuses earlier internal predictions in early-exit networks, improving the reported trade-off between accuracy and inference time.

title: Zero Time Waste: Recycling Predictions in Early Exit Neural Networks

abstract: Acquisition of data is a difficult task in many applications of machine learning, and it is only natural that one hopes and expects the population risk to decrease (better performance) monotonically with increasing data points. It turns out, somewhat surprisingly, that this is not the case even for the most standard algorithms that minimize the empirical risk. Non-monotonic behavior of the risk and instability in training have manifested and appeared in the popular deep learning paradigm under the description of double descent. These problems highlight the current lack of understanding of learning algorithms and generalization. It is, therefore, crucial to pursue this concern and provide a characterization of such behavior. In this paper, we derive the first consistent and risk-monotonic (in high probability) algorithms for a general statistical learning setting under weak assumptions, consequently answering some questions posed by Viering et. al. 2019 on how to avoid non-monotonic behavior of risk curves. We further show that risk monotonicity need not necessarily come at the price of worse excess risk rates. To achieve this, we derive new empirical Bernstein-like concentration inequalities of independent interest that hold for certain non-i.i.d.~processes such as Martingale Difference Sequences.

paragraphs: Adding training data does not always improve a learned model's population risk, its expected error on the underlying distribution. Even standard empirical risk minimization can produce increases along the learning curve. This paper asks how to design algorithms that avoid such non-monotonic behavior while still learning effectively as more data becomes available.

The authors derive algorithms that are both consistent and risk-monotonic with high probability in a general statistical learning setting under weak assumptions. Consistency describes their eventual learning behavior, while risk monotonicity addresses how performance evolves with increasing data. The high-probability qualification matters: the result does not promise monotonic improvement in every individual run.

The paper further shows that enforcing risk monotonicity need not worsen excess-risk convergence rates. Its analysis develops empirical Bernstein-like concentration inequalities that apply to certain dependent processes, including martingale difference sequences. These tools support learning guarantees beyond independent, identically distributed quantities. The contribution establishes that more reliable learning curves can coexist with strong rates of statistical improvement under the studied conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs consistent algorithms with high-probability risk monotonicity and shows this property need not worsen excess-risk rates.

title: Risk Monotonicity in Statistical Learning

abstract: When learning tasks over time, artificial neural networks suffer from a problem known as Catastrophic Forgetting (CF). This happens when the weights of a network are overwritten during the training of a new task causing forgetting of old information. To address this issue, we propose MetA Reusable Knowledge or MARK, a new method that fosters weight reusability instead of overwriting when learning a new task. Specifically, MARK keeps a set of shared weights among tasks. We envision these shared weights as a common Knowledge Base (KB) that is not only used to learn new tasks, but also enriched with new knowledge as the model learns new tasks. Key components behind MARK are two-fold. On the one hand, a metalearning approach provides the key mechanism to incrementally enrich the KB with new knowledge and to foster weight reusability among tasks. On the other hand, a set of trainable masks provides the key mechanism to selectively choose from the KB relevant weights to solve each task. By using MARK, we achieve state of the art results in several popular benchmarks, surpassing the best performing methods in terms of average accuracy by over 10% on the 20-Split-MiniImageNet dataset, while achieving almost zero forgetfulness using 55% of the number of parameters. Furthermore, an ablation study provides evidence that, indeed, MARK is learning reusable knowledge that is selectively used by each task.

paragraphs: Neural networks can forget earlier tasks when training on a new task overwrites useful weights. MARK addresses this by encouraging reusable knowledge across a sequence of tasks. It maintains shared weights as a common knowledge base that supports new learning and is enriched as additional tasks arrive.

Two mechanisms organize that knowledge base. A meta-learning procedure incrementally incorporates new knowledge and encourages weights to remain useful across tasks. Trainable masks then select which shared weights each task should use. These components address complementary needs: building reusable representations and giving individual tasks access to the parts relevant to them.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. On 20-Split-MiniImageNet, MARK exceeds the best-performing compared methods by over 10% in average accuracy, with almost no forgetting while using 55% of the number of parameters. An ablation study provides evidence that the shared knowledge is genuinely reused and selectively accessed by tasks. The findings support the method's intended mechanism as well as its measured performance, linking retention and parameter efficiency through selective reuse.
summary.tldr: MARK combines a meta-learned shared knowledge base with task-specific masks to improve continual learning through selective weight reuse.

title: Optimizing Reusable Knowledge for Continual Learning via Metalearning

abstract: Perhaps the single most important use case for differential privacy is to privately answer numerical queries, which is usually achieved by adding noise to the answer vector. The central question is, therefore, to understand which noise distribution optimizes the privacy-accuracy trade-off, especially when the dimension of the answer vector is high. Accordingly, an extensive literature has been dedicated to the question and the upper and lower bounds have been successfully matched up to constant factors (Bun et al.,2018; Steinke & Ullman, 2017). In this paper, we take a novel approach to address this important optimality question. We first demonstrate an intriguing central limit theorem phenomenon in the high-dimensional regime. More precisely, we prove that a mechanism is approximately Gaussian Differentially Private (Dong et al., 2021) if the added noise satisfies certain conditions. In particular, densities proportional to $\mathrm{e}^{-\|x\|_p^\alpha}$, where $\|x\|_p$ is the standard $\ell_p$-norm, satisfies the conditions. Taking this perspective, we make use of the Cramer--Rao inequality and show an "uncertainty principle"-style result: the product of privacy parameter and the $\ell_2$-loss of the mechanism is lower bounded by the dimension. Furthermore, the Gaussian mechanism achieves the constant-sharp optimal privacy-accuracy trade-off among all such noises. Our findings are corroborated by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Answering many numerical questions privately usually means adding noise to the collection of answers. The central design choice is how to distribute that noise so that it protects the data while keeping answers useful. This paper studies that trade-off when the answer vector has many dimensions, seeking sharper conclusions than bounds that agree only up to constant factors.

The authors prove a central-limit-type result: under specified conditions on the noise, the resulting mechanism is approximately Gaussian differentially private. This describes the mechanism’s privacy behavior, rather than requiring the added noise itself to be Gaussian. The conditions cover a family of noise densities defined using powers of standard p-norms.

Using this perspective and the Cramer–Rao inequality, the paper derives a lower bound linking the privacy parameter, squared-Euclidean-style error, and dimension. Within the noise class covered by the analysis, Gaussian noise achieves the optimal privacy–accuracy trade-off with sharp constants. Numerical experiments support these theoretical findings. The scope of the optimality claim is the analyzed noise family.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional privacy theorem establishes sharp optimality of Gaussian noise within a specified class of private query-answering mechanisms.

title: A Central Limit Theorem for Differentially Private Query Answering

abstract: Graph neural network (GNN)'s success in graph classification is closely related to the Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) algorithm. By iteratively aggregating neighboring node features to a center node, both 1-WL and GNN obtain a node representation that encodes a rooted subtree around the center node. These rooted subtree representations are then pooled into a single representation to represent the whole graph. However, rooted subtrees are of limited expressiveness to represent a non-tree graph. To address it, we propose Nested Graph Neural Networks (NGNNs). NGNN represents a graph with rooted subgraphs instead of rooted subtrees, so that two graphs sharing many identical subgraphs (rather than subtrees) tend to have similar representations. The key is to make each node representation encode a subgraph around it more than a subtree. To achieve this, NGNN extracts a local subgraph around each node and applies a base GNN to each subgraph to learn a subgraph representation. The whole-graph representation is then obtained by pooling these subgraph representations. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis showing that NGNN is strictly more powerful than 1-WL. In particular, we proved that NGNN can discriminate almost all r-regular graphs, where 1-WL always fails. Moreover, unlike other more powerful GNNs, NGNN only introduces a constant-factor higher time complexity than standard GNNs. NGNN is a plug-and-play framework that can be combined with various base GNNs. We test NGNN with different base GNNs on several benchmark datasets. NGNN uniformly improves their performance and shows highly competitive performance on all datasets.

paragraphs: Standard graph neural networks repeatedly aggregate neighboring features, producing node representations associated with rooted subtrees. Those representations can miss distinctions in graphs whose structure is not tree-like. Nested Graph Neural Networks address this expressive limitation by making local subgraphs the building blocks of a whole-graph representation.

For each node, NGNN extracts a surrounding subgraph and applies a base graph neural network to that subgraph. It then pools the resulting subgraph representations to describe the complete graph. The framework can wrap different base networks, allowing an existing architecture to represent richer local structure through the nested construction.

The authors prove that NGNN is strictly more expressive than the 1-WL procedure underlying standard message-passing expressiveness. In particular, it distinguishes almost all regular graphs of the studied kind where 1-WL fails. They report only a constant-factor increase in time complexity over standard GNNs. Across tested base networks and benchmark datasets, NGNN consistently improves performance and remains highly competitive, connecting the theoretical increase in expressiveness to empirical gains.
summary.tldr: NGNN pools learned local-subgraph representations to exceed 1-WL expressiveness and improve tested graph classifiers with constant-factor additional time complexity.

title: Nested Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The emergence of the Internet-of-Things (IoT) sheds light on applying the machine teaching (MT) algorithms for online personalized education on home devices. This direction becomes more promising during the COVID-19 pandemic when in-person education becomes infeasible. However, as one of the most influential and practical MT paradigms, iterative machine teaching (IMT) is prohibited on IoT devices due to its inefficient and unscalable algorithms. IMT is a paradigm where a teacher feeds examples iteratively and intelligently based on the learner's status. In each iteration, current IMT algorithms greedily traverse the whole training set to find an example for the learner, which is computationally expensive in practice. We propose a novel teaching framework, Locality Sensitive Teaching (LST), based on locality sensitive sampling, to overcome these challenges. LST has provable near-constant time complexity, which is exponentially better than the existing baseline. With at most 425.12x speedups and 99.76% energy savings over IMT, LST is the first algorithm that enables energy and time efficient machine teaching on IoT devices. Owing to LST's substantial efficiency and scalability, it is readily applicable in real-world education scenarios.

paragraphs: Iterative machine teaching selects examples based on a learner's current state, adapting instruction as learning proceeds. A computational bottleneck arises when the teacher scans the entire training set at every iteration to choose the next example. The paper targets this repeated search cost, which makes existing approaches difficult to use efficiently on Internet-of-Things devices.

Locality Sensitive Teaching replaces that expensive selection process with a framework based on locality sensitive sampling. The authors prove near-constant time complexity, an exponential improvement over the existing baseline's complexity. This changes the computational burden of selecting teaching examples, making the teaching procedure more suitable for devices with limited time and energy resources.

The reported evaluation reaches speedups of up to 425.12 times and energy savings of up to 99.76% relative to iterative machine teaching. These are maximum reported improvements, so they describe the strongest observed gains. The paper presents the framework as enabling efficient machine teaching on IoT devices, motivated by personalized education at home. Its main demonstrated benefit is the substantial reduction in the computational and energy costs of adaptive example selection.
summary.tldr: Locality Sensitive Teaching accelerates adaptive example selection with provable near-constant complexity and large reported time and energy savings.

title: Locality Sensitive Teaching

abstract: Tuning hyperparameters is a crucial but arduous part of the machine learning pipeline. Hyperparameter optimization is even more challenging in federated learning, where models are learned over a distributed network of heterogeneous devices; here, the need to keep data on device and perform local training makes it difficult to efficiently train and evaluate configurations. In this work, we investigate the problem of federated hyperparameter tuning. We first identify key challenges and show how standard approaches may be adapted to form baselines for the federated setting. Then, by making a novel connection to the neural architecture search technique of weight-sharing, we introduce a new method, FedEx, to accelerate federated hyperparameter tuning that is applicable to widely-used federated optimization methods such as FedAvg and recent variants. Theoretically, we show that a FedEx variant correctly tunes the on-device learning rate in the setting of online convex optimization across devices. Empirically, we show that FedEx can outperform natural baselines for federated hyperparameter tuning by several percentage points on the Shakespeare, FEMNIST, and CIFAR-10 benchmarks—obtaining higher accuracy using the same training budget.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning requires training and evaluating alternative configurations, which becomes harder when data remains distributed across heterogeneous devices. Local training and restrictions on moving data complicate the usual tuning workflow. This paper identifies those challenges and adapts standard approaches to establish baselines for selecting hyperparameters in the federated setting.

The proposed method, FedEx, connects federated tuning to weight-sharing techniques used in neural architecture search. That connection provides a way to accelerate the search within a limited training budget. FedEx applies to widely used federated optimization methods, including FedAvg and recent variants, making tuning part of the distributed learning process.

Separately, experiments on Shakespeare, FEMNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that FedEx can improve accuracy over natural tuning baselines by several percentage points with the same training budget. The theory supports a particular optimization setting, while the experiments demonstrate practical benefits across the reported benchmarks.
summary.tldr: FedEx uses a connection to weight-sharing to accelerate federated hyperparameter tuning and can improve accuracy within the same training budget.

title: Federated Hyperparameter Tuning: Challenges, Baselines, and Connections to Weight-Sharing

abstract: Annealed importance sampling (AIS) and related algorithms are highly effective tools for marginal likelihood estimation, but are not fully differentiable due to the use of Metropolis-Hastings correction steps. Differentiability is a desirable property as it would admit the possibility of optimizing marginal likelihood as an objective using gradient-based methods. To this end, we propose Differentiable AIS (DAIS), a variant of AIS which ensures differentiability by abandoning the Metropolis-Hastings corrections. As a further advantage, DAIS allows for mini-batch gradients. We provide a detailed convergence analysis for Bayesian linear regression which goes beyond previous analyses by explicitly accounting for the sampler not having reached equilibrium. Using this analysis, we prove that DAIS is consistent in the full-batch setting and provide a sublinear convergence rate. Furthermore, motivated by the problem of learning from large-scale datasets, we study a stochastic variant of DAIS that uses mini-batch gradients. Surprisingly, stochastic DAIS can be arbitrarily bad due to a fundamental incompatibility between the goals of last-iterate convergence to the posterior and elimination of the accumulated stochastic error. This is in stark contrast with other settings such as gradient-based optimization and Langevin dynamics, where the effect of gradient noise can be washed out by taking smaller steps. This indicates that annealing-based marginal likelihood estimation with stochastic gradients may require new ideas.

paragraphs: Annealed importance sampling estimates marginal likelihood, a quantity useful for assessing probabilistic models. Its Metropolis-Hastings corrections prevent full differentiability, complicating the use of its estimates as gradient-based learning objectives. Differentiable AIS, or DAIS, removes those corrections to make the procedure differentiable and also permits gradients computed from mini-batches of data.

The authors analyze convergence for Bayesian linear regression while explicitly accounting for a sampler that has not reached equilibrium. In the full-batch setting, they prove consistency and a sublinear convergence rate. This establishes that the differentiable construction can approach the desired result in the analyzed setting despite abandoning the usual correction steps.

The stochastic version has a more troubling behavior: mini-batch gradient noise can make DAIS arbitrarily bad. The analysis identifies a conflict between making the final iterate approach the posterior and removing stochastic errors accumulated along the process. Smaller steps do not resolve this conflict as they can in other settings. The result points to a substantive obstacle for scaling annealing-based marginal-likelihood estimation through stochastic gradients.
summary.tldr: DAIS makes annealed importance sampling differentiable, but its analysis reveals that mini-batch gradient noise can cause arbitrarily poor estimates.

title: Differentiable Annealed Importance Sampling and the Perils of Gradient Noise

abstract: The bandit problem with graph feedback, proposed in [Mannor and Shamir, NeurIPS 2011], is modeled by a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ where $V$ is the collection of bandit arms, and once an arm is triggered, all its incident arms are observed. A fundamental question is how the structure of the graph affects the min-max regret. We propose the notions of the fractional weak domination number $\delta^*$ and the $k$-packing independence number capturing upper bound and lower bound for the regret respectively. We show that the two notions are inherently connected via aligning them with the linear program of the weakly dominating set and its dual --- the fractional vertex packing set respectively. Based on this connection, we utilize the strong duality theorem to prove a general regret upper bound $O\left(\left(\delta^*\log |V|\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}}\right)$ and a lower bound $\Omega\left(\left(\delta^*/\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}}\right)$ where $\alpha$ is the integrality gap of the dual linear program. Therefore, our bounds are tight up to a $\left(\log |V|\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ factor on graphs with bounded integrality gap for the vertex packing problem including trees and graphs with bounded degree. Moreover, we show that for several special families of graphs, we can get rid of the $\left(\log |V|\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ factor and establish optimal regret.

paragraphs: In a bandit problem with graph feedback, choosing an action can reveal information about other actions according to a directed graph. The paper asks how this observation structure determines minimax regret. Its aim is to characterize learning difficulty through graph properties that capture both achievable performance and unavoidable error.

The authors introduce fractional weak domination and a packing-based independence quantity. These correspond to a linear program for weak domination and its dual packing problem. Strong duality connects the two descriptions, supporting upper and lower regret bounds with the same two-thirds power dependence on the number of rounds.

The remaining difference between the bounds depends on a logarithmic factor and the dual problem's integrality gap. For graphs with bounded integrality gap, including trees and bounded-degree graphs, the bounds match up to the cube root of a logarithmic factor in the number of actions. For several special graph families, that factor can also be removed. The results make the observation graph's role explicit and identify cases where the optimal regret can be established.
summary.tldr: Linked graph domination and packing quantities yield nearly matching regret bounds for bandits with graph feedback.

title: Understanding Bandits with Graph Feedback

abstract: This article proposes novel rules for false discovery rate control (FDRC) geared towards online anomaly detection in time series. Online FDRC rules allow to control the properties of a sequence of statistical tests. In the context of anomaly detection, the null hypothesis is that an observation is normal and the alternative is that it is anomalous. FDRC rules allow users to target a lower bound on precision in unsupervised settings. The methods proposed in this article overcome short-comings of previous FDRC rules in the context of anomaly detection, in particular ensuring that power remains high even when the alternative is exceedingly rare (typical in anomaly detection) and the test statistics are serially dependent (typical in time series). We show the soundness of these rules in both theory and experiments.

paragraphs: Online anomaly detection repeatedly decides whether each new observation is normal or unusual. Treating those decisions as statistical tests creates a need to control false discoveries across the sequence. This paper proposes false discovery rate control rules designed specifically for that ongoing time-series setting.

In each test, normality is the null hypothesis and an anomaly is the alternative. Controlling false discoveries lets users target a lower bound on precision in an unsupervised setting: it connects the testing procedure to the reliability of the anomalies it flags. The paper focuses on keeping detection power high while providing that control.

Two conditions make this difficult in practice: genuine anomalies may be extremely rare, and nearby test statistics may depend on one another. The proposed rules address shortcomings of previous methods under these characteristic conditions. The authors support the rules with theoretical results and experiments. Their contribution is therefore a testing framework tailored to detecting rare events in dependent streams while managing the reliability of reported detections.
summary.tldr: The paper designs online false discovery controls that retain detection power for rare anomalies in serially dependent time series.

title: Online false discovery rate control for anomaly detection in time series

abstract: We present a slot-wise, object-based transition model that decomposes a scene into objects, aligns them (with respect to a slot-wise object memory) to maintain a consistent order across time, and predicts how those objects evolve over successive frames. The model is trained end-to-end without supervision using transition losses at the level of the object-structured representation rather than pixels. Thanks to the introduction of our novel alignment module, the model deals properly with two issues that are not handled satisfactorily by other transition models, namely object persistence and object identity. We show that the combination of an object-level loss and correct object alignment over time enables the model to outperform a state-of-the-art baseline, and allows it to deal well with object occlusion and re-appearance in partially observable environments.

paragraphs: Predicting a changing scene becomes difficult when objects disappear from view and later return. This paper develops an object-based transition model that separates a scene into object slots and predicts how those objects evolve across frames. A central challenge is keeping each slot associated with the same object over time.

The model introduces an alignment module that matches objects to a slot-wise memory, maintaining consistent ordering across observations. Training is end-to-end and unsupervised. Its transition losses operate on the structured object representation rather than on pixels, connecting the prediction objective to the objects whose evolution the model is intended to track.

The authors show that combining object-level losses with correct temporal alignment outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline. The model also handles occlusion and reappearance well in partially observable environments. These findings emphasize the importance of both persistence and identity: useful prediction requires maintaining an object’s representation through changes in visibility and preserving which object that representation refers to across time.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised object-transition model uses memory-based alignment and object-level losses to track identity through occlusion and predict scene changes.

title: Unsupervised Object-Based Transition Models For 3D Partially Observable Environments

abstract: Despite achieving remarkable efficiency, traditional network pruning techniques often follow manually-crafted heuristics to generate pruned sparse networks. Such heuristic pruning strategies are hard to guarantee that the pruned networks achieve test accuracy comparable to the original dense ones. Recent works have empirically identified and verified the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH): a randomly-initialized dense neural network contains an extremely sparse subnetwork, which can be trained to achieve similar accuracy to the former. Due to the lack of theoretical evidence, they often need to run multiple rounds of expensive training and pruning over the original large networks to discover the sparse subnetworks with low accuracy loss. By leveraging dynamical systems theory and inertial manifold theory, this work theoretically verifies the validity of the LTH. We explore the possibility of theoretically lossless pruning as well as one-time pruning, compared with existing neural network pruning and LTH techniques. We reformulate the neural network optimization problem as a gradient dynamical system and reduce this high-dimensional system onto inertial manifolds to obtain a low-dimensional system regarding pruned subnetworks. We demonstrate the precondition and existence of pruned subnetworks and prune the original networks in terms of the gap in their spectrum that make the subnetworks have the smallest dimensions.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that a randomly initialized dense network contains a very sparse subnetwork that can be trained to similar accuracy. The authors recast neural network optimization as a gradient dynamical system. They then use inertial manifold theory to reduce that high-dimensional system to a lower-dimensional one associated with a pruned subnetwork. This connects the search for a smaller network to the mathematical structure of the training dynamics, rather than relying solely on manually chosen pruning heuristics.

The analysis identifies preconditions and establishes the existence of pruned subnetworks within that framework. Spectral gaps guide pruning toward subnetworks of the smallest dimensions supported by the approach. The stated possibilities of theoretically lossless and one-time pruning depend on this analysis and its preconditions; they should not be read as an unconditional promise for arbitrary networks. The contribution is a theoretical route for reasoning about sparse trainable subnetworks.
summary.tldr: Inertial manifold theory provides conditions for sparse subnetworks and a theoretical framework for exploring lossless, one-time pruning.

title: Validating the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis with Inertial Manifold Theory

abstract: Existing fine-tuning methods either tune all parameters of the pre-trained model (full fine-tuning), which is not efficient, or only tune the last linear layer (linear probing), which suffers a significant accuracy drop compared to the full fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose a new parameter-efficient fine-tuning method termed as SSF, representing that researchers only need to Scale and Shift the deep Features extracted by a pre-trained model to catch up with the performance of full fine-tuning. In this way, SSF also surprisingly outperforms other parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches even with a smaller number of tunable parameters. Furthermore, different from some existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., Adapter or VPT) that introduce the extra parameters and computational cost in the training and inference stages, SSF only adds learnable parameters during the training stage, and these additional parameters can be merged into the original pre-trained model weights via re-parameterization in the inference phase. With the proposed SSF, our model obtains 2.46% (90.72% vs. 88.54%) and 11.48% (73.10% vs. 65.57%) performance improvement on FGVC and VTAB-1k in terms of Top-1 accuracy compared to the full fine-tuning but only fine-tuning about 0.3M parameters. We also conduct amounts of experiments in various model families (CNNs, Transformers, and MLPs) and datasets. Results on 26 image classification datasets in total and 3 robustness & out-of-distribution datasets show the effectiveness of SSF. Code is available at https://github.com/dongzelian/SSF.
