paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained model often involves updating all its parameters or training only its final linear layer. The former is expensive, while the latter can sacrifice accuracy. This paper proposes SSF, a method that learns how to scale and shift the model's deep features using a small set of trainable parameters.

The learned adjustments can be merged into the original model weights through reparameterization for inference. Consequently, the extra learnable parameters are needed during training without remaining as additional inference-time components. This gives the method an efficiency advantage that extends beyond reducing the number of parameters being optimized.

With about 0.3 million tuned parameters, SSF reports 90.72% versus 88.54% top-1 accuracy for full fine-tuning on FGVC, and 73.10% versus 65.57% on VTAB-1k. It also outperforms other parameter-efficient approaches with fewer tunable parameters in the reported comparisons. Experiments across convolutional networks, transformers, and MLPs, covering 26 classification datasets and three robustness or distribution-shift datasets, provide evidence for the method across varied evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SSF adapts pretrained models through learned feature scales and shifts that can be merged into model weights, achieving strong accuracy with few tuned parameters.

title: Scaling & Shifting Your Features: A New Baseline for Efficient Model Tuning

abstract: To improve the sustainability and resilience of modern food systems, designing improved crop management strategies is crucial. The increasing abundance of data on agricultural systems suggests that future strategies could benefit from adapting to environmental conditions, but how to design these adaptive policies poses a new frontier. A natural technique for learning policies in these kinds of sequential decision-making problems is reinforcement learning (RL). To obtain the large number of samples required to learn effective RL policies, existing work has used mechanistic crop growth models (CGMs) as simulators. These solutions focus on single-year, single-crop simulations for learning strategies for a single agricultural management practice. However, to learn sustainable long-term policies we must be able to train in multi-year environments, with multiple crops, and consider a wider array of management techniques. We introduce CYCLESGYM, an RL environment based on the multi-year, multi-crop CGM Cycles. CYCLESGYM allows for long-term planning in agroecosystems, provides modular state space and reward constructors and weather generators, and allows for complex actions. For RL researchers, this is a novel benchmark to investigate issues arising in real-world applications. For agronomists, we demonstrate the potential of RL as a powerful optimization tool for agricultural systems management in multi-year case studies on nitrogen (N) fertilization and crop planning scenarios.

paragraphs: Crop management involves decisions whose consequences unfold over time and depend on environmental conditions. Reinforcement learning can learn such decision policies, but it needs many training examples. Prior work has used crop growth simulators, often restricting learning to one crop, one year, and one management practice.

CyclesGym expands that setting through an environment built on the Cycles crop growth model. It supports multiple crops and years, enabling policies to consider longer-term agricultural consequences. Modular tools define the information available to the learner and the rewards used to assess decisions. Weather generators and support for complex actions allow a wider range of management scenarios.

The paper presents multi-year case studies involving nitrogen fertilization and crop planning to demonstrate reinforcement learning’s potential as an agricultural optimization tool. For researchers, the environment provides a benchmark grounded in agricultural decision problems. Its main contribution is the ability to investigate coordinated, long-term management in simulation, extending beyond the narrow planning scope of the earlier environments described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: CyclesGym supports reinforcement learning for multi-year, multi-crop management, demonstrated through fertilization and crop-planning case studies.

title: Learning Long-Term Crop Management Strategies with CyclesGym

abstract: Research in Neuroscience, as in many scientific disciplines, is undergoing a renaissance based on deep learning. Unique to Neuroscience, deep learning models can be used not only as a tool but interpreted as models of the brain. The central claims of recent deep learning-based models of brain circuits are that they make novel predictions about neural phenomena or shed light on the fundamental functions being optimized. We show, through the case-study of grid cells in the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit, that one may get neither. We begin by reviewing the principles of grid cell mechanism and function obtained from first-principles modeling efforts, then rigorously examine the claims of deep learning models of grid cells. Using large-scale architectural and hyperparameter sweeps and theory-driven experimentation, we demonstrate that the results of such models may be more strongly driven by particular, non-fundamental, and post-hoc implementation choices than fundamental truths about neural circuits or the loss function(s) they might optimize. We discuss why these models cannot be expected to produce accurate models of the brain without the addition of substantial amounts of inductive bias, an informal No Free Lunch result for Neuroscience. Based on first principles work, we provide hypotheses for what additional loss functions will produce grid cells more robustly. In conclusion, circumspection and transparency, together with biological knowledge, are warranted in building and interpreting deep learning models in Neuroscience.

paragraphs: Deep-learning models in neuroscience are sometimes interpreted as explanations of brain circuits, including what those circuits optimize. This paper examines that interpretation through models of grid cells in the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit. It asks whether the models deliver new neural predictions or reveal fundamental functions, rather than merely producing a familiar-looking result.

The authors first review insights from first-principles modeling, then investigate deep-learning claims using broad architecture and hyperparameter sweeps alongside theory-driven experiments. Their results show that model behavior may depend more strongly on particular implementation choices, including post-hoc choices, than on fundamental properties of neural circuits or the proposed learning objectives.

The paper argues that accurate brain models require substantial inductive bias informed by biology, framing this as an informal no-free-lunch result. It also proposes hypotheses about additional loss functions that could make grid cells emerge more robustly. The implication is a call for transparent implementation choices and biological grounding when interpreting learned representations as scientific evidence about neural mechanisms.
summary.tldr: A grid-cell case study shows that implementation choices can drive neural-model results, complicating claims about brain function.

title: No Free Lunch from Deep Learning in Neuroscience: A Case Study through Models of the Entorhinal-Hippocampal Circuit

abstract: We develop an eigenspace estimation algorithm for distributed environments with arbitrary node failures, where a subset of computing nodes can return structurally valid but otherwise arbitrarily chosen responses. Notably, this setting encompasses several important scenarios that arise in distributed computing and data-collection environments such as silent/soft errors, outliers or corrupted data at certain nodes, and adversarial responses. Our estimator builds upon and matches the performance of a recently proposed non-robust estimator up to an additive $\tilde{O}(\sigma \sqrt{\alpha})$ error, where $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the existing estimator and $\alpha$ is the fraction of corrupted nodes.

paragraphs: The paper studies eigenspace estimation when computation is distributed across nodes and some nodes return unreliable answers. The failure model allows responses that have the expected structure but contain arbitrarily chosen information. This matters because an answer can look valid to a receiving system while still being corrupted or deliberately misleading.

The authors develop a communication-efficient estimator for this setting by building on an existing non-robust estimator. The same formulation covers silent or soft computational errors, outliers, corrupted data at individual nodes, and adversarial responses. Treating these cases together makes the result relevant to several distinct sources of unreliable distributed information.

The main guarantee compares the robust method directly with its non-robust starting point. Its performance matches that estimator up to an additional error of order sigma times the square root of alpha, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here, sigma squared is the existing estimator's variance and alpha is the fraction of corrupted nodes. The bound therefore describes a controlled cost of robustness in terms of both the original estimator's variability and the amount of corruption.
summary.tldr: A distributed eigenspace estimator tolerates arbitrarily corrupted node responses with an additive error controlled by estimator variance and the corrupted-node fraction.

title: Communication-efficient distributed eigenspace estimation with arbitrary node failures

abstract: Explaining machine learning models is an important and increasingly popular area of research interest. The Shapley value from game theory has been proposed as a prime approach to compute feature importance towards model predictions on images, text, tabular data, and recently graph neural networks (GNNs) on graphs. In this work, we revisit the appropriateness of the Shapley value for GNN explanation, where the task is to identify the most important subgraph and constituent nodes for GNN predictions. We claim that the Shapley value is a non-ideal choice for graph data because it is by definition not structure-aware. We propose a Graph Structure-aware eXplanation (GStarX) method to leverage the critical graph structure information to improve the explanation. Specifically, we define a scoring function based on a new structure-aware value from the cooperative game theory proposed by Hamiache and Navarro (HN). When used to score node importance, the HN value utilizes graph structures to attribute cooperation surplus between neighbor nodes, resembling message passing in GNNs, so that node importance scores reflect not only the node feature importance, but also the node structural roles. We demonstrate that GStarX produces qualitatively more intuitive explanations, and quantitatively improves explanation fidelity over strong baselines on chemical graph property prediction and text graph sentiment classification. Code: https://github.com/ShichangZh/GStarX

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network involves identifying which nodes and subgraphs matter to its prediction. The Shapley value offers a game-theoretic way to assign importance, but the authors argue that its definition does not account for graph structure. This matters because a node's contribution can depend on its connections and its role among neighboring nodes.

GStarX instead builds its scoring function from the Hamiache–Navarro value, a structure-aware concept from cooperative game theory. It distributes the extra value arising from cooperation between neighboring nodes. This process resembles message passing in graph neural networks, allowing importance scores to reflect both node features and the structural relationships through which nodes contribute together.

The authors evaluate the method on chemical graph property prediction and sentiment classification using text graphs. They report explanations that are qualitatively more intuitive and quantitatively more faithful to model predictions than strong baselines. The contribution is an explanation mechanism that incorporates the graph's organization directly into attribution, rather than evaluating node information without an explicit account of structural cooperation.
summary.tldr: GStarX uses structure-aware cooperative-game values to explain GNN predictions through node features and graph roles, improving evaluated explanation fidelity.

title: GStarX: Explaining Graph Neural Networks with Structure-Aware Cooperative Games

abstract: Existing work in continual learning (CL) focuses on mitigating catastrophic forgetting, i.e., model performance deterioration on past tasks when learning a new task. However, the training efficiency of a CL system is under-investigated, which limits the real-world application of CL systems under resource-limited scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel framework called Sparse Continual Learning (SparCL), which is the first study that leverages sparsity to enable cost-effective continual learning on edge devices. SparCL achieves both training acceleration and accuracy preservation through the synergy of three aspects: weight sparsity, data efficiency, and gradient sparsity. Specifically, we propose task-aware dynamic masking (TDM) to learn a sparse network throughout the entire CL process, dynamic data removal (DDR) to remove less informative training data, and dynamic gradient masking (DGM) to sparsify the gradient updates. Each of them not only improves efficiency, but also further mitigates catastrophic forgetting. SparCL consistently improves the training efficiency of existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) CL methods by at most 23X less training FLOPs, and, surprisingly, further improves the SOTA accuracy by at most 1.7%. SparCL also outperforms competitive baselines obtained from adapting SOTA sparse training methods to the CL setting in both efficiency and accuracy. We also evaluate the effectiveness of SparCL on a real mobile phone, further indicating the practical potential of our method.

paragraphs: Continual learning must absorb new tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones. Much of its research targets this forgetting problem, but repeated training can also be too expensive for resource-limited devices. SparCL addresses both concerns by introducing sparsity throughout the continual-learning process, aiming to reduce computation while preserving accuracy.

The framework combines three mechanisms. Task-aware dynamic masking maintains a sparse network, dynamic data removal excludes less informative training examples, and dynamic gradient masking makes parameter updates sparse. The authors report that each mechanism contributes to efficiency and also helps mitigate catastrophic forgetting, making their combination relevant to both cost and retention.

Applied to existing state-of-the-art continual-learning methods, SparCL consistently improves training efficiency, with reported reductions in training FLOPs reaching a factor of 23 and accuracy gains reaching 1.7%. It also exceeds adapted sparse-training baselines in efficiency and accuracy. Evaluation on a real mobile phone further supports the practical potential of using this approach for continual learning on edge devices.
summary.tldr: SparCL combines sparse weights, selective training data, and sparse gradients to reduce continual-learning cost while improving retention and accuracy.

title: SparCL: Sparse Continual Learning on the Edge

abstract: In this work, we are dedicated to a new task, i.e., hand-object interaction image generation, which aims to conditionally generate the hand-object image under the given hand, object and their interaction status. This task is challenging and research-worthy in many potential application scenarios, such as AR/VR games and online shopping, etc. To address this problem, we propose a novel HOGAN framework, which utilizes the expressive model-aware hand-object representation and leverages its inherent topology to build the unified surface space. In this space, we explicitly consider the complex self- and mutual occlusion during interaction. During final image synthesis, we consider different characteristics of hand and object and generate the target image in a split-and-combine manner. For evaluation, we build a comprehensive protocol to access both the fidelity and structure preservation of the generated image. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets, i.e., HO3Dv3 and DexYCB, demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our framework both quantitatively and qualitatively. The code will be available at https://github.com/play-with-HOI-generation/HOIG.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the task of generating an image conditioned on a specified hand, object, and interaction state. Producing a convincing interaction requires maintaining the arrangement of both entities while handling how they hide parts of themselves and each other. The authors motivate the task through potential uses such as augmented or virtual reality games and online shopping.

Their HOGAN framework builds a unified surface space from a model-aware representation of the hand and object and its underlying topology. Within this space, it explicitly accounts for self-occlusion and mutual occlusion. The final image is synthesized through a split-and-combine process that accommodates the different characteristics of hands and objects.

The evaluation protocol measures both image fidelity and preservation of structure, reflecting that visual realism alone does not capture whether the requested interaction is maintained. Experiments on HO3Dv3 and DexYCB support the framework's effectiveness through quantitative and qualitative comparisons. The contribution combines a conditional generation task, a representation for reasoning about interacting surfaces, and an evaluation approach sensitive to their structure.
summary.tldr: HOGAN generates hand-object interaction images using a unified surface representation that explicitly handles occlusion and preserves interaction structure.

title: Hand-Object Interaction Image Generation

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) suffer from domain shift when the test dataset follows a distribution different from the training dataset. Domain generalization aims to tackle this issue by learning a model that can generalize to unseen domains. In this paper, we propose a new approach that aims to explicitly remove domain-specific features for domain generalization. Following this approach, we propose a novel framework called Learning and Removing Domain-specific features for Generalization (LRDG) that learns a domain-invariant model by tactically removing domain-specific features from the input images. Specifically, we design a classifier to effectively learn the domain-specific features for each source domain, respectively. We then develop an encoder-decoder network to map each input image into a new image space where the learned domain-specific features are removed. With the images output by the encoder-decoder network, another classifier is designed to learn the domain-invariant features to conduct image classification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A classifier can struggle when its test images come from a different distribution than its training images. Domain generalization tries to prepare for these unseen settings using the available source domains. This paper proposes addressing the problem by explicitly learning which image features are specific to each source domain and then removing those features.

The framework, called LRDG, assigns different roles to its components. First, a classifier learns domain-specific features for each source domain. An encoder-decoder network then transforms input images into a new image space where those learned features are removed. A separate classifier trains on the transformed images to learn features intended to remain useful across domains.

This design makes image transformation the bridge between identifying domain dependence and learning a more transferable classifier. The final classifier receives images processed to reduce the domain-specific information identified earlier. Extensive experiments report better performance than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings support the proposed learn-and-remove strategy empirically; they do not establish that every transformed image is free of all possible domain-specific information.
summary.tldr: LRDG learns domain-specific image features, removes them through an encoder-decoder, and trains a classifier on the resulting images to improve generalization.

title: Domain Generalization by Learning and Removing Domain-specific Features

abstract: Heterophilous Graph Neural Network (GNN) is a family of GNNs that specializes in learning graphs under heterophily, where connected nodes tend to have different labels. Most existing heterophilous models incorporate iterative non-local computations to capture node relationships. However, these approaches have limited application to large-scale graphs due to their high computational costs and challenges in adopting minibatch schemes. In this work, we study the scalability issues of heterophilous GNN and propose a scalable model, LD2, which simplifies the learning process by decoupling graph propagation and generating expressive embeddings prior to training. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that LD2 achieves optimal time complexity in training, as well as a memory footprint that remains independent of the graph scale. We conduct extensive experiments to showcase that our model is capable of lightweight minibatch training on large-scale heterophilous graphs, with up to $15\times$ speed improvement and efficient memory utilization, while maintaining comparable or better performance than the baselines.

paragraphs: In a heterophilous graph, connected nodes tend to have different labels. Graph neural networks designed for this setting often use repeated computations involving nonlocal relationships. These operations can be costly on large graphs and difficult to organize into minibatches, limiting the scale at which the models can be trained.

LD2 separates graph propagation from model training and constructs expressive node embeddings beforehand. Moving this work outside training simplifies the learning process and enables lightweight minibatch updates. The authors’ theoretical analysis establishes optimal training time complexity and a training memory footprint that does not depend on the scale of the graph.

Experiments on large heterophilous graphs report speed improvements of up to 15 times, efficient memory use, and predictive performance comparable to or better than the evaluated baselines. The results connect the architectural separation to practical scalability: training can use precomputed graph information without repeatedly performing the expensive graph operations that burden existing approaches. The stated complexity result specifically concerns training.
summary.tldr: LD2 precomputes graph embeddings to enable efficient minibatch training on heterophilous graphs, with reported speedups of up to 15 times.

title: LD2: Scalable Heterophilous Graph Neural Network with Decoupled Embeddings

abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to synthesize a small dataset whose test performance is comparable to a full dataset using the same model. State-of-the-art (SoTA) methods optimize synthetic datasets primarily by matching heuristic indicators extracted from two networks: one from real data and one from synthetic data (see Fig.1, Left), such as gradients and training trajectories. DD is essentially a compression problem that emphasizes on maximizing the preservation of information contained in the data. We argue that well-defined metrics which measure the amount of shared information between variables in information theory are necessary for success measurement, but are never considered by previous works. Thus, we introduce mutual information (MI) as the metric to quantify the shared information between the synthetic and the real datasets, and devise MIM4DD numerically maximizing the MI via a newly designed optimizable objective within a contrastive learning framework to update the synthetic dataset. Specifically, we designate the samples in different datasets who share the same labels as positive pairs, and vice versa negative pairs. Then we respectively pull and push those samples in positive and negative pairs into contrastive space via minimizing NCE loss. As a result, the targeted MI can be transformed into a lower bound represented by feature maps of samples, which is numerically feasible. Experiment results show that MIM4DD can be implemented as an add-on module to existing SoTA DD methods.

Existing approaches often match quantities such as gradients or training trajectories. This paper views the task as information compression and proposes measuring shared information between real and synthetic data using mutual information.

MIM4DD makes that objective numerically manageable through contrastive learning. The resulting feature-based objective provides a tractable lower bound on the targeted mutual information.

The contribution is therefore a complementary optimization signal grounded in shared information, rather than requiring every existing matching strategy to be replaced. The computed lower bound is the practical route used to pursue the mutual-information goal.
summary.tldr: MIM4DD uses a contrastive lower bound on mutual information to guide synthetic dataset optimization as an add-on to existing distillation methods.

title: MIM4DD: Mutual Information Maximization for Dataset Distillation

abstract: Bayesian persuasion studies the problem faced by an informed sender who strategically discloses information to influence the behavior of an uninformed receiver. Recently, a growing attention has been devoted to settings where the sender and the receiver interact sequentially, in which the receiver's decision-making problem is usually modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP). However, the literature focuses on computing optimal information-revelation policies (a.k.a. signaling schemes) under the restrictive assumption that the receiver acts myopically, selecting actions to maximize the one-step utility and disregarding future rewards. This is justified by the fact that, when the receiver is farsighted and thus considers future rewards, finding an optimal Markovian signaling scheme is NP-hard. In this paper, we show that Markovian signaling schemes do not constitute the "right" class of policies. Indeed, differently from most of the MDPs settings, we show that Markovian signaling schemes are not optimal, and general history-dependent signaling schemes should be considered. Moreover, we also show that history-dependent signaling schemes circumvent the negative complexity results affecting Markovian signaling schemes. Formally, we design an algorithm that computes an optimal and $\epsilon$-persuasive history-dependent signaling scheme in time polynomial in ${1}/{\epsilon}$ and in the instance size. The crucial challenge is that general history-dependent signaling schemes cannot be represented in polynomial space. Nevertheless, we introduce a convenient subclass of history-dependent signaling schemes, called promise-form, which are as powerful as general history-dependent ones and efficiently representable. Intuitively, promise-form signaling schemes compactly encode histories in the form of honest promises on future receiver's rewards.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender can influence another decision-maker by choosing what information to reveal. In sequential settings, a farsighted receiver considers future rewards as well as immediate ones. Computing an optimal Markovian signaling scheme in this setting is NP-hard, motivating the paper's reconsideration of the policy class itself.

The authors show that Markovian schemes can be suboptimal and that allowing dependence on interaction history can overcome the stated computational obstacle. The difficulty is representation: a general history-dependent scheme may require more than polynomial space. Their solution is a compact subclass called promise-form schemes, which encode relevant history through honest promises about the receiver's future rewards.

Promise-form schemes are as powerful as general history-dependent schemes while admitting efficient representation. Using them, the authors give an algorithm that computes an optimal, epsilon-persuasive scheme in time polynomial in the instance size and in 1/epsilon. The result combines optimality with an approximate persuasion requirement. It shows how choosing a richer policy class and a suitable compact representation can improve both achievable outcomes and computational tractability.
summary.tldr: Compact, honest promises enable efficient computation of optimal epsilon-persuasive history-dependent signaling for farsighted receivers.

title: Persuading Farsighted Receivers in MDPs: the Power of Honesty

abstract: Deep deraining networks consistently encounter substantial generalization issues when deployed in real-world applications, although they are successful in laboratory benchmarks. A prevailing perspective in deep learning encourages using highly complex data for training, with the expectation that richer image background content will facilitate overcoming the generalization problem. However, through comprehensive and systematic experimentation, we discover that this strategy does not enhance the generalization capability of these networks. On the contrary, it exacerbates the tendency of networks to overfit specific degradations. Our experiments reveal that better generalization in a deraining network can be achieved by simplifying the complexity of the training background images. This is because that the networks are ``slacking off'' during training, that is, learning the least complex elements in the image background and degradation to minimize training loss. When the background images are less complex than the rain streaks, the network will prioritize the background reconstruction, thereby suppressing overfitting the rain patterns and leading to improved generalization performance. Our research offers a valuable perspective and methodology for better understanding the generalization problem in low-level vision tasks and displays promising potential for practical application.

paragraphs: Image deraining networks can perform well on laboratory benchmarks yet struggle on real-world images. A common response is to train with richer, more complex backgrounds, expecting that greater variety will improve generalization. The authors systematically investigate this idea and find that, in their experiments, increasing background complexity instead encourages overfitting to particular rain degradations.

Their explanation is that the network tends to learn whichever elements of the background and degradation are least complex and most useful for reducing training loss. With sufficiently complex backgrounds, learning specific rain patterns becomes an attractive shortcut. When backgrounds are simpler than the rain streaks, the network instead prioritizes reconstructing the background, reducing its tendency to specialize in those rain patterns.

The experiments show that simplifying training backgrounds can improve deraining generalization. This makes the relative complexity of image content and corruption a meaningful training consideration, rather than assuming that more complicated content is always beneficial. The authors also present this explanation as a promising perspective for understanding generalization in other low-level vision tasks.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest that simpler training backgrounds can improve deraining generalization by shifting learning away from memorizing specific rain patterns.

title: Networks are Slacking Off: Understanding Generalization Problem in Image Deraining

abstract: The recent Segment Anything Model (SAM) represents a big leap in scaling up segmentation models, allowing for powerful zero-shot capabilities and flexible prompting. Despite being trained with 1.1 billion masks, SAM's mask prediction quality falls short in many cases, particularly when dealing with objects that have intricate structures. We propose HQ-SAM, equipping SAM with the ability to accurately segment any object, while maintaining SAM's original promptable design, efficiency, and zero-shot generalizability. Our careful design reuses and preserves the pre-trained model weights of SAM, while only introducing minimal additional parameters and computation. We design a learnable High-Quality Output Token, which is injected into SAM's mask decoder and is responsible for predicting the high-quality mask. Instead of only applying it on mask-decoder features, we first fuse them with early and final ViT features for improved mask details. To train our introduced learnable parameters, we compose a dataset of 44K fine-grained masks from several sources. HQ-SAM is only trained on the introduced detaset of 44k masks, which takes only 4 hours on 8 GPUs. We show the efficacy of HQ-SAM in a suite of 10 diverse segmentation datasets across different downstream tasks, where 8 out of them are evaluated in a zero-shot transfer protocol. Our code and pretrained models are at https://github.com/SysCV/SAM-HQ.

paragraphs: The Segment Anything Model supports flexible prompts and strong zero-shot segmentation, but its masks can miss fine details in objects with intricate structures. HQ-SAM aims to improve that mask quality while preserving the original model’s promptable design, efficiency, and ability to generalize to new segmentation settings.

The method preserves SAM’s pre-trained weights and adds a small number of trainable parameters. Its main addition is a learnable High-Quality Output Token inside the mask decoder, responsible for predicting the refined mask. The model also combines decoder features with early and final vision-transformer features to improve the detail available for mask prediction.

The added parameters are trained on 44,000 fine-grained masks assembled from several sources, with training reported to take four hours on eight GPUs. Evaluation spans ten segmentation datasets and different downstream tasks; eight datasets use a zero-shot transfer protocol. The results support improving detailed segmentation through targeted additions to an existing foundation model, with minimal extra parameters and computation.
summary.tldr: HQ-SAM improves detailed segmentation by adding a learned output token and fused features while preserving SAM’s pre-trained weights.

title: Segment Anything in High Quality

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in diverse domains such as image synthesis, super-resolution, and 3D molecule generation. Surprisingly, the application of diffusion models in graph learning has garnered little attention. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by exploring the use of diffusion models for unsupervised graph representation learning. Our investigation commences with the identification of anisotropic structures within graphs and the recognition of a crucial limitation in the vanilla forward diffusion process when dealing with these anisotropic structures. The original forward diffusion process continually adds isotropic Gaussian noise to the data, which may excessively dilute anisotropic signals, leading to rapid signal-to-noise conversion. This rapid conversion poses challenges for training denoising neural networks and obstructs the acquisition of semantically meaningful representations during the reverse process. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel class of models termed {\it directional diffusion models}. These models adopt data-dependent, anisotropic, and directional noises in the forward diffusion process. In order to assess the effectiveness of our proposed models, we conduct extensive experiments on 12 publicly available datasets, with a particular focus on two distinct graph representation learning tasks. The experimental results unequivocally establish the superiority of our models over state-of-the-art baselines, underscoring their effectiveness in capturing meaningful graph representations. Our research not only sheds light on the intricacies of the forward process in diffusion models but also underscores the vast potential of these models in addressing a wide spectrum of graph-related tasks. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/statsle/DDM}.

paragraphs: This paper explores diffusion models as a way to learn graph representations without supervision. Its starting point is that graphs can contain anisotropic structure: meaningful variation is not distributed equally across all directions. Standard forward diffusion adds isotropic Gaussian noise, which treats directions uniformly and may wash out these unevenly distributed signals too quickly.

When meaningful structure becomes noise rapidly, the reverse denoising process becomes harder to learn and may produce less useful representations. The proposed directional diffusion models change the forward process itself. They introduce noise that depends on the data and varies by direction, adapting the corruption process to the structure the representation learner needs to capture.

The authors evaluate the models on 12 public datasets across two graph representation learning tasks and report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. These findings support their argument that the choice of forward noise matters for learning meaningful graph features. The work identifies direction-sensitive corruption as a useful design choice for the evaluated graph-learning settings.
summary.tldr: Directional diffusion adapts noise to graph structure to improve unsupervised representation learning.

title: Directional diffusion models for graph representation learning

abstract: The question of what makes a data distribution suitable for deep learning is a fundamental open problem. Focusing on locally connected neural networks (a prevalent family of architectures that includes convolutional and recurrent neural networks as well as local self-attention models), we address this problem by adopting theoretical tools from quantum physics. Our main theoretical result states that a certain locally connected neural network is capable of accurate prediction over a data distribution if and only if the data distribution admits low quantum entanglement under certain canonical partitions of features. As a practical application of this result, we derive a preprocessing method for enhancing the suitability of a data distribution to locally connected neural networks. Experiments with widespread models over various datasets demonstrate our findings. We hope that our use of quantum entanglement will encourage further adoption of tools from physics for formally reasoning about the relation between deep learning and real-world data.

paragraphs: A neural network's architecture determines which relationships in data it can readily capture. This paper asks what makes a data distribution suitable for locally connected networks, a family including convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and local self-attention models. It brings tools from quantum physics to a question about the match between data structure and predictive architecture.

It states that accurate prediction is possible if and only if the data distribution has low quantum entanglement under specified canonical partitions of its features. Entanglement serves here as a theoretical property of the distribution across those partitions. Both the particular network and the specified partitions are part of the result's scope.

The authors turn this characterization into a preprocessing method intended to make data more suitable for locally connected networks. Experiments with widely used models on several datasets support their findings. The work therefore connects a formal necessary-and-sufficient condition to a practical intervention, while illustrating how concepts from physics can help explain relationships between learning architectures and data.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes accurate prediction by a particular locally connected network through low quantum entanglement and derives a data-preprocessing method.

title: What Makes Data Suitable for a Locally Connected Neural Network? A Necessary and Sufficient Condition Based on Quantum Entanglement.

abstract: We study the fundamental problems of Gaussian mean estimation and linear regression with Gaussian covariates in the presence of Huber contamination. Our main contribution is the design of the first sample near-optimal and almost linear-time algorithms with optimal error guarantees for both these problems. Specifically, for Gaussian robust mean estimation on $\mathbb R^d$ with contamination parameter $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_0)$ for a small absolute constant $\epsilon_0$, we give an algorithm with sample complexity $n = \tilde{O}(d/\epsilon^2)$ and almost linear runtime that approximates the target mean within $\ell_2$-error $O(\epsilon)$. This improves on prior work that achieved this error guarantee with polynomially suboptimal sample and time complexity. For robust linear regression, we give the first algorithm with sample complexity $n = \tilde{O}(d/\epsilon^2)$ and almost linear runtime that approximates the target regressor within $\ell_2$-error $O(\epsilon)$. This is the first polynomial sample and time algorithm achieving the optimal error guarantee, answering an open question in the literature. At the technical level, we develop a methodology that yields almost-linear time algorithms for multi-directional filtering that may be of broader interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies Gaussian mean estimation and linear regression with Gaussian covariates under Huber contamination. Its goal is to achieve optimal estimation error while using nearly optimal amounts of data and almost linear computation. These requirements address statistical accuracy and computational feasibility together.

For mean estimation in d dimensions and a sufficiently small contamination parameter epsilon, the algorithm uses roughly d divided by epsilon squared samples, up to logarithmic factors, and achieves Euclidean error proportional to epsilon. The authors obtain the same sample scaling and error order for robust linear regression, also with almost linear runtime.

For mean estimation, the result improves on earlier methods that achieved the error guarantee with polynomially worse sample and time requirements. For regression, the authors identify their method as the first with polynomial sample and time complexity to attain the optimal error, resolving an open question. Their technical contribution is a methodology for almost-linear-time multidirectional filtering, which they suggest may be useful beyond these two Gaussian estimation problems.
summary.tldr: New robust Gaussian estimation algorithms combine optimal error with near-optimal sample requirements and almost linear runtime.

title: Near-Optimal Algorithms for Gaussians with Huber Contamination: Mean Estimation and Linear Regression

abstract: In non-linear filtering, it is traditional to compare non-linear architectures such as neural networks to the standard linear Kalman Filter (KF). We observe that this mixes the evaluation of two separate components: the non-linear architecture, and the parameters optimization method. In particular, the non-linear model is often optimized, whereas the reference KF model is not. We argue that both should be optimized similarly, and to that end present the Optimized KF (OKF). We demonstrate that the KF may become competitive to neural models – if optimized using OKF. This implies that experimental conclusions of certain previous studies were derived from a flawed process. The advantage of OKF over the standard KF is further studied theoretically and empirically, in a variety of problems. Conveniently, OKF can replace the KF in real-world systems by merely updating the parameters.

paragraphs: When a neural filtering model outperforms a Kalman filter, the difference may reflect how the models were optimized as well as their architectures. This paper identifies a comparison problem in nonlinear filtering: neural models are often optimized, while the reference linear Kalman filter is left unoptimized. That makes it difficult to separate the value of nonlinear architecture from the value of parameter fitting.

The authors introduce the Optimized Kalman Filter, or OKF, to make the optimization treatment more comparable. Their results show that a Kalman filter may become competitive with neural models when optimized using OKF. This supports their criticism of conclusions in certain earlier studies: an observed gap under unequal optimization does not cleanly establish the advantage of the neural architecture.

The paper examines OKF’s advantage over the standard Kalman filter through both theoretical and empirical work across a variety of problems. It also highlights a practical benefit: existing systems can replace their standard filter with OKF by updating parameters. The contribution therefore concerns both fairer experimental evaluation and a potentially useful improvement to an established filtering method.
summary.tldr: Optimizing Kalman filter parameters can make the filter competitive with neural models and exposes confounded comparisons between optimization and architecture.

title: Optimization or Architecture: How to Hack Kalman Filtering

abstract: The decision tree is a flexible machine-learning model that finds its success in numerous applications. It is usually fitted in a recursively greedy manner using CART. In this paper, we study the convergence rate of CART under a regression setting. First, we prove an upper bound on the prediction error of CART under a sufficient impurity decrease (SID) condition \cite{chi2020asymptotic} -- our result is an improvement over the known result by \cite{chi2020asymptotic} under a similar assumption. We show via examples that this error bound cannot be further improved by more than a constant or a log factor. Second, we introduce a few easy-to-check sufficient conditions of the SID condition. In particular, we show that the SID condition can be satisfied by an additive model when the component functions satisfy a ``locally reverse Poincare inequality". We discuss a few familiar function classes in non-parametric estimation to demonstrate the usefulness of this conception.

paragraphs: CART fits decision trees through a sequence of greedy splits, making a locally attractive choice at each stage. This paper studies how quickly its prediction error decreases in regression. The analysis assumes a sufficient impurity decrease condition, which supplies a mathematical requirement on the improvement available through splitting.

Under that condition, the authors prove an upper bound on CART's prediction error that improves an earlier result based on a similar assumption. They also provide examples showing that the new bound cannot generally be tightened by more than a constant or logarithmic factor. This makes the result informative about both achievable guarantees and their remaining room for improvement.

The paper then makes the assumption easier to assess by deriving sufficient conditions for it. In particular, additive models can satisfy the requirement when their component functions obey a locally reverse Poincare inequality. Examples from familiar nonparametric function classes illustrate its usefulness. The contribution therefore combines a sharper conditional error bound with ways to recognize settings where that bound applies.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens CART regression error bounds under sufficient impurity decrease and provides conditions for checking when that assumption holds.

title: On the Convergence of CART under Sufficient Impurity Decrease Condition

abstract: Current machine learning models for vision are often highly specialized and limited to a single modality and task. In contrast, recent large language models exhibit a wide range of capabilities, hinting at a possibility for similarly versatile models in computer vision.In this paper, we take a step in this direction and propose a multimodal training scheme called 4M. It consists of training a single unified Transformer encoder-decoder using a masked modeling objective across a wide range of input/output modalities – including text, images, geometric, and semantic modalities, as well as neural network feature maps. 4M achieves scalability by unifying the representation space of all modalities through mapping them into discrete tokens and performing multimodal masked modeling on a small randomized subset of tokens.4M leads to models that exhibit several key capabilities: (1) they can perform a diverse set of vision tasks out of the box, (2) they excel when fine-tuned for unseen downstream tasks or new input modalities, and (3) they can function as a generative model that can be conditioned on arbitrary modalities, enabling a wide variety of expressive multimodal editing capabilities with remarkable flexibility.Through experimental analyses, we demonstrate the potential of 4M for training versatile and scalable foundation models for vision tasks, setting the stage for further exploration in multimodal learning for vision and other domains.
originalAbstract: Current machine learning models for vision are often highly specialized and limited to a single modality and task. In contrast, recent large language models exhibit a wide range of capabilities, hinting at a possibility for similarly versatile models in computer vision.In this paper, we take a step in this direction and propose a multimodal training scheme called 4M. It consists of training a single unified Transformer encoder-decoder using a masked modeling objective across a wide range of input/output modalities – including text, images, geometric, and semantic modalities, as well as neural network feature maps. 4M achieves scalability by unifying the representation space of all modalities through mapping them into discrete tokens and performing multimodal masked modeling on a small randomized subset of tokens.4M leads to models that exhibit several key capabilities: (1) they can perform a diverse set of vision tasks out of the box, (2) they excel when fine-tuned for unseen downstream tasks or new input modalities, and (3) they can function as a generative model that can be conditioned on arbitrary modalities, enabling a wide variety of expressive multimodal editing capabilities with remarkable flexibility.Through experimental analyses, we demonstrate the potential of 4M for training versatile and scalable foundation models for vision tasks, setting the stage for further exploration in multimodal learning for vision and other domains.

paragraphs: 4M investigates how a single vision model can support many tasks and kinds of information. Its training inputs and outputs span text, images, geometry, semantic information, and feature maps produced by neural networks. A unified Transformer encoder-decoder learns across these modalities through a masked modeling objective: it uses available information to predict information that has been hidden.

The central design choice is to convert all modalities into discrete tokens. This gives otherwise different kinds of data a shared representational format. Training operates on a small, randomly selected subset of tokens, providing a way to scale multimodal learning without processing every token at once.

The experiments show several forms of versatility. Trained models perform diverse vision tasks directly and adapt effectively through fine-tuning to new tasks or input modalities. They also generate outputs conditioned on different modalities, supporting flexible multimodal editing. These findings establish the potential of this training scheme for broadly capable vision models, while presenting it as a step toward that goal.
summary.tldr: 4M trains one Transformer across tokenized visual and textual modalities, enabling varied vision tasks, adaptation, and multimodal generation.

title: 4M: Massively Multimodal Masked Modeling

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is notoriously impractical to deploy due to sample inefficiency. Meta-RL directly addresses this sample inefficiency by learning to perform few-shot learning when a distribution of related tasks is available for meta-training. While many specialized meta-RL methods have been proposed, recent work suggests that end-to-end learning in conjunction with an off-the-shelf sequential model, such as a recurrent network, is a surprisingly strong baseline. However, such claims have been controversial due to limited supporting evidence, particularly in the face of prior work establishing precisely the opposite. In this paper, we conduct an empirical investigation. While we likewise find that a recurrent network can achieve strong performance, we demonstrate that the use of hypernetworks is crucial to maximizing their potential. Surprisingly, when combined with hypernetworks, the recurrent baselines that are far simpler than existing specialized methods actually achieve the strongest performance of all methods evaluated. We provide code at https://github.com/jacooba/hyper.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to teach an agent how to learn quickly, using a distribution of related tasks during meta-training. One appealing approach is to train an ordinary sequential model end to end. Whether such recurrent models are strong alternatives to specialized meta-learning methods has been disputed, with earlier findings pointing in different directions.

This paper investigates that question empirically and identifies hypernetworks as a crucial ingredient for maximizing recurrent models' performance in the study. The authors also find that recurrent networks can perform strongly, but the combination with hypernetworks provides the strongest results. The architectural combination is therefore central to their assessment of how capable these comparatively simple baselines can be.

When equipped with hypernetworks, the recurrent baselines outperform every other method evaluated, despite being much simpler than the specialized alternatives. This result strengthens the case for using them as serious comparison points in meta-RL research. Its scope remains the empirical comparison conducted in the paper, within the setting where related tasks are available for meta-training.
summary.tldr: Recurrent models combined with hypernetworks achieve the strongest performance among the meta-RL methods evaluated in this study.

title: Recurrent Hypernetworks are Surprisingly Strong in Meta-RL

abstract: Confidence calibration is central to providing accurate and interpretable uncertainty estimates, especially under safety-critical scenarios. However, we find that existing calibration algorithms often overlook the issue of proximity bias, a phenomenon where models tend to be more overconfident in low proximity data (i.e., data lying in the sparse region of the data distribution) compared to high proximity samples, and thus suffer from inconsistent miscalibration across different proximity samples. We examine the problem over $504$ pretrained ImageNet models and observe that: 1) Proximity bias exists across a wide variety of model architectures and sizes; 2) Transformer-based models are relatively more susceptible to proximity bias than CNN-based models; 3) Proximity bias persists even after performing popular calibration algorithms like temperature scaling; 4) Models tend to overfit more heavily on low proximity samples than on high proximity samples. Motivated by the empirical findings, we propose ProCal, a plug-and-play algorithm with a theoretical guarantee to adjust sample confidence based on proximity. To further quantify the effectiveness of calibration algorithms in mitigating proximity bias, we introduce proximity-informed expected calibration error (PIECE) with theoretical analysis. We show that ProCal is effective in addressing proximity bias and improving calibration on balanced, long-tail, and distribution-shift settings under four metrics over various model architectures. We believe our findings on proximity bias will guide the development of fairer and better-calibrated} models, contributing to the broader pursuit of trustworthy AI.

paragraphs: A model's confidence should communicate how reliable its predictions are. This paper identifies proximity bias: models tend to be more overconfident on examples in sparse regions of the data distribution than on examples in denser regions. Consequently, calibration quality can vary across examples even after applying a standard confidence adjustment.

The authors study 504 pretrained ImageNet models and observe this pattern across architectures and sizes. Transformer-based models are relatively more susceptible than convolutional models, and temperature scaling does not eliminate the effect. They also find that models tend to overfit more strongly on low-proximity examples, connecting the calibration problem with differences in learned behavior.

The proposed ProCal algorithm adjusts confidence using proximity and comes with a theoretical guarantee. The paper also introduces proximity-informed expected calibration error, or PIECE, to assess this issue. Across balanced, long-tail, and distribution-shift settings, the reported results show improved calibration and reduced proximity bias. The contribution makes variation across data-density regions an explicit part of confidence evaluation.
summary.tldr: ProCal adjusts confidence using data proximity to address greater overconfidence in sparse regions of the data distribution.

title: Proximity-Informed Calibration for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We present a new dataset condensation framework termed Squeeze, Recover and Relabel (SRe$^2$L) that decouples the bilevel optimization of model and synthetic data during training, to handle varying scales of datasets, model architectures and image resolutions for efficient dataset condensation. The proposed method demonstrates flexibility across diverse dataset scales and exhibits multiple advantages in terms of arbitrary resolutions of synthesized images, low training cost and memory consumption with high-resolution synthesis, and the ability to scale up to arbitrary evaluation network architectures. Extensive experiments are conducted on Tiny-ImageNet and full ImageNet-1K datasets. Under 50 IPC, our approach achieves the highest 42.5\% and 60.8\% validation accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K, outperforming all previous state-of-the-art methods by margins of 14.5\% and 32.9\%, respectively. Our approach also surpasses MTT in terms of speed by approximately 52$\times$ (ConvNet-4) and 16$\times$ (ResNet-18) faster with less memory consumption of 11.6$\times$ and 6.4$\times$ during data synthesis. Our code and condensed datasets of 50, 200 IPC with 4K recovery budget are available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/SRe2L.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation seeks to create a small synthetic dataset useful for training models. Squeeze, Recover and Relabel, or SRe²L, changes how that synthetic data and the model are optimized. It decouples their bilevel optimization, aiming to make condensation practical across dataset sizes, network architectures, and image resolutions.

The framework supports synthesized images at arbitrary resolutions and reduces training cost and memory demands for high-resolution synthesis. It also supports scaling to arbitrary evaluation architectures. These properties address several connected obstacles: a condensation method must handle large source datasets, produce suitably detailed images, and remain useful across the networks trained on its output.

At 50 images per class, experiments report validation accuracies of 42.5% on Tiny-ImageNet and 60.8% on ImageNet-1K, exceeding previous state-of-the-art results by 14.5 and 32.9 percentage points. Against MTT during synthesis, reported speedups are about 52-fold for ConvNet-4 and 16-fold for ResNet-18, with 11.6-fold and 6.4-fold lower memory consumption. These results demonstrate both predictive utility and substantial computational savings in the evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: SRe²L decouples model and synthetic-data optimization to scale dataset condensation while improving accuracy, synthesis speed, and memory use.

title: Squeeze, Recover and Relabel: Dataset Condensation at ImageNet Scale From A New Perspective

abstract: Monocular 3D object detection poses a significant challenge due to the lack of depth information in RGB images. Many existing methods strive to enhance the object depth estimation performance by allocating additional parameters for object depth estimation, utilizing extra modules or data. In contrast, we introduce a novel metric learning scheme that encourages the model to extract depth-discriminative features regardless of the visual attributes without increasing inference time and model size. Our method employs the distance-preserving function to organize the feature space manifold in relation to ground-truth object depth. The proposed $(K,B,\epsilon)$-quasi-isometric loss leverages predetermined pairwise distance restriction as guidance for adjusting the distance among object descriptors without disrupting the non-linearity of the natural feature manifold. Moreover, we introduce an auxiliary head for object-wise depth estimation, which enhances depth quality while maintaining the inference time. The broad applicability of our method is demonstrated through experiments that show improvements in overall performance when integrated into various baselines. The results show that our method consistently improves the performance of various baselines by 23.51\% and 5.78\% on average across KITTI and Waymo, respectively.

paragraphs: Detecting objects in three dimensions from one RGB image requires estimating depth without direct depth measurements. This paper aims to improve the features used for that estimate. It introduces a metric-learning scheme that encourages object representations to distinguish depth regardless of visual attributes, without increasing model size or inference time.

The training objective organizes distances between object descriptors using known object depths. Its quasi-isometric loss imposes predetermined restrictions on pairwise distances while preserving the nonlinear structure of the feature space. In practical terms, depth relationships guide how representations are arranged without requiring their underlying geometry to become linear. An auxiliary object-depth estimation head further improves depth quality while maintaining inference time.

The authors integrate the method into multiple existing detection baselines and report consistent performance improvements. The average reported gains are 23.51% on KITTI and 5.78% on Waymo. These experiments support the approach as a broadly applicable training addition to the tested detectors, with the benefit coming from more depth-informative representations rather than a larger inference model.
summary.tldr: Depth-guided metric learning improves monocular 3D detection across tested baselines without increasing model size or inference time.

title: Depth-discriminative Metric Learning for Monocular 3D Object Detection

abstract: The vulnerability of deep neural networks to imperceptible adversarial perturbations has attracted widespread attention. Inspired by the success of vision-language foundation models, previous efforts achieved zero-shot adversarial robustness by aligning adversarial visual features with text supervision. However, in practice, they are still unsatisfactory due to several issues, including heavy adaptation cost, suboptimal text supervision, and uncontrolled natural generalization capacity. In this paper, to address these issues, we propose a few-shot adversarial prompt framework where adapting input sequences with limited data makes significant adversarial robustness improvement. Specifically, we achieve this by providing adversarially correlated text supervision that is end-to-end learned from adversarial examples. We also propose a novel training objective that enhances the consistency of multi-modal features while encourages differentiated uni-modal features between natural and adversarial examples. The proposed framework gives access to learn adversarial text supervision, which provides superior cross-modal adversarial alignment and matches state-of-the-art zero-shot adversarial robustness with only 1\% training data. Code is available at: https://github.com/lionel-w2/FAP.

paragraphs: This paper aims to make vision-language models more resistant to adversarial image changes that are difficult to perceive. Earlier approaches align attacked visual features with text supervision, but the authors identify costly adaptation, inadequate text supervision, and uncontrolled generalization on natural examples as obstacles. They propose adapting prompts using limited training data.

The framework learns its text supervision directly from adversarial examples, so the text guidance is tailored to the attacked visual features. Its training objective combines two goals: making features across the visual and textual modalities more consistent, while encouraging features within an individual modality to distinguish natural examples from adversarial ones.

The reported result is stronger cross-modal adversarial alignment and robustness matching leading zero-shot adversarial methods with only 1% of the training data. The contribution is therefore a way to learn useful adversarial supervision through prompts with much less data. The result concerns the evaluated robustness setting rather than establishing resistance to every possible image perturbation.
summary.tldr: Learning adversarially informed prompts matches leading zero-shot robustness results using only 1% of the training data.

title: Few-Shot Adversarial Prompt Learning on Vision-Language Models

abstract: Recent 3D large reconstruction models (LRMs) can generate high-quality 3D content in sub-seconds by integrating multi-view diffusion models with scalable multi-view reconstructors. Current works further leverage 3D Gaussian Splatting as 3D representation for improved visual quality and rendering efficiency. However, we observe that existing Gaussian reconstruction models often suffer from multi-view inconsistency and blurred textures. We attribute this to the compromise of multi-view information propagation in favor of adopting powerful yet computationally intensive architectures (\eg, Transformers). To address this issue, we introduce MVGamba, a general and lightweight Gaussian reconstruction model featuring a multi-view Gaussian reconstructor based on the RNN-like State Space Model (SSM). Our Gaussian reconstructor propagates causal context containing multi-view information for cross-view self-refinement while generating a long sequence of Gaussians for fine-detail modeling with linear complexity.With off-the-shelf multi-view diffusion models integrated, MVGamba unifies 3D generation tasks from a single image, sparse images, or text prompts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVGamba outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in all 3D content generation scenarios with approximately only $0.1\times$ of the model size. The codes are available at \url{https://github.com/SkyworkAI/MVGamba}.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D object from multiple views requires information to remain consistent across those views. The authors observe that existing Gaussian reconstruction models can produce inconsistent views and blurred textures. They attribute this partly to architectures that sacrifice information propagation across views to accommodate computationally expensive components.

MVGamba uses a lightweight state-space model with recurrent-style processing to reconstruct a sequence of 3D Gaussians. As it generates that sequence, it propagates context containing information from multiple views, allowing cross-view refinement. Linear complexity supports long Gaussian sequences for representing fine detail. Combined with existing multi-view diffusion models, the same reconstruction framework supports generation from one image, several sparse images, or text.

Across the evaluated 3D generation scenarios, MVGamba outperforms state-of-the-art comparison methods with approximately one-tenth of the model size. The findings support sequence modeling as an effective way to combine detailed Gaussian representations with efficient information sharing across views. The reported advantage connects reconstruction quality and model compactness within a single design.
summary.tldr: MVGamba uses state-space sequence modeling for multi-view Gaussian reconstruction, outperforming tested baselines with roughly one-tenth of their model size.

title: MVGamba: Unify 3D Content Generation as State Space Sequence Modeling

abstract: Improving out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization during in-distribution (ID) adaptation is a primary goal of robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models beyond naive fine-tuning. However, despite decent OOD generalization performance from recent robust fine-tuning methods, confidence calibration for reliable model output has not been fully addressed. This work proposes a robust fine-tuning method that improves both OOD accuracy and confidence calibration simultaneously in vision language models. Firstly, we show that both OOD classification and OOD calibration errors have a shared upper bound consisting of two terms of ID data: 1) ID calibration error and 2) the smallest singular value of the ID input covariance matrix. Based on this insight, we design a novel framework that conducts fine-tuning with a constrained multimodal contrastive loss enforcing a larger smallest singular value, which is further guided by the self-distillation of a moving-averaged model to achieve calibrated prediction as well. Starting from empirical evidence supporting our theoretical statements, we provide extensive experimental results on ImageNet distribution shift benchmarks that demonstrate the effectiveness of our theorem and its practical implementation.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a vision-language model on one distribution should ideally preserve performance when inputs change. Accuracy alone does not establish reliability, however: confidence should also reflect how often predictions are correct. This paper addresses out-of-distribution accuracy and confidence calibration together during adaptation.

The authors derive a shared upper bound for out-of-distribution classification and calibration errors. It involves two quantities from the training distribution: calibration error and the smallest singular value of the input covariance matrix. This connects behavior under distribution shift to both confidence quality and the structure of in-distribution inputs.

The proposed method uses a constrained multimodal contrastive loss that encourages a larger smallest singular value. Self-distillation from a moving-averaged model provides additional guidance toward calibrated predictions. Experiments on ImageNet distribution-shift benchmarks support the theoretical statements and the practical method. The contribution is a linked treatment of two reliability concerns, using one analytical perspective to motivate training changes that improve both reported accuracy and calibration.
summary.tldr: The paper connects shifted-distribution accuracy and calibration through a shared bound and uses it to guide robust fine-tuning.

title: Towards Calibrated Robust Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language Models

abstract: The rapid progress in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC), especially with diffusion models, has significantly advanced development of high-quality video generation. However, current video diffusion models exhibit demanding computational requirements and high peak memory usage, especially for generating longer and higher-resolution videos. These limitations greatly hinder the practical application of video diffusion models on standard hardware platforms. To tackle this issue, we present a novel, training-free framework named Streamlined Inference, which leverages the temporal and spatial properties of video diffusion models. Our approach integrates three core components: Feature Slicer, Operator Grouping, and Step Rehash. Specifically, Feature Slicer effectively partitions input features into sub-features and Operator Grouping processes each sub-feature with a group of consecutive operators, resulting in significant memory reduction without sacrificing the quality or speed. Step Rehash further exploits the similarity between adjacent steps in diffusion, and accelerates inference through skipping unnecessary steps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces peak memory and computational overhead, making it feasible to generate high-quality videos on a single consumer GPU (e.g., reducing peak memory of Animatediff from 42GB to 11GB, featuring faster inference on 2080Ti).

paragraphs: Streamlined Inference targets the high computation and peak memory needed to generate videos with diffusion models. These demands become particularly restrictive for longer or higher-resolution outputs. The proposed framework changes how inference is executed without requiring training, using spatial and temporal properties already present in video diffusion models.

Two components work together to reduce memory. Feature Slicer divides input features into smaller pieces, and Operator Grouping processes each piece through a sequence of consecutive operators. The authors report that this reduces memory without sacrificing quality or speed. A third component, Step Rehash, uses similarities between neighboring diffusion steps to skip unnecessary steps and further accelerate generation.

Experiments show reductions in both peak memory and computational overhead, making high-quality video generation feasible on a single consumer GPU in the evaluated settings. One example reduces AnimateDiff's peak memory from 42 GB to 11 GB and achieves faster inference on a 2080 Ti. The contribution shows how reorganizing execution and exploiting repeated computation can improve deployment practicality.
summary.tldr: Streamlined Inference reduces video-diffusion memory and computation through feature partitioning, grouped operations, and selective step skipping without training.

title: Fast and Memory-Efficient Video Diffusion Using Streamlined Inference

abstract: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) have become integral to various software workflows. Such languages offer domain-specific optimizations and abstractions that improve code readability and maintainability. However, leveraging these languages requires developers to rewrite existing code using the specific DSL's API. While large language models (LLMs) have shown some success in automatic code transpilation, none of them provide any functional correctness guarantees on the rewritten code. Another approach for automating this task is verified lifting, which relies on program synthesis to find programs in the target language that are functionally equivalent to the source language program. While several verified lifting tools have been developed for various application domains, they are specialized for specific source-target languages or require significant expertise in domain knowledge to make the search efficient. In this paper, leveraging recent advances in LLMs, we propose an LLM-based approach (LLMLift) to building verified lifting tools. We use the LLM's capabilities to reason about programs to translate a given program into its corresponding equivalent in the target language. Additionally, we use LLMs to generate proofs for functional equivalence. We develop lifting-based compilers for four DSLs targeting different application domains. Our approach not only outperforms previous symbolic-based tools in number of benchmarks transpiled and transpilation time, but also requires significantly less effort to build.

paragraphs: Domain-specific languages can make specialized software clearer and more efficient, but adopting them often requires rewriting existing programs. Language models can help translate code, yet their translations alone do not guarantee that behavior is preserved. Verified lifting addresses this problem by seeking target programs that are functionally equivalent to the source.

LLMLift uses language models both to translate programs and to generate proofs of functional equivalence. The approach combines their program-reasoning capabilities with the objective of verified lifting. It aims to reduce the specialization and domain expertise required by earlier synthesis-based tools, whose search procedures can be difficult to build for new language pairs.

The authors develop lifting-based compilers for four domain-specific languages across different application areas. Their approach translates more benchmark programs and takes less transpilation time than previous symbolic tools, while requiring substantially less construction effort. The contribution is therefore both a translation approach and a method for building verified translators: generating equivalence proofs is part of the workflow for establishing that rewritten code preserves the original computation.
summary.tldr: LLMLift uses language models to translate programs and generate equivalence proofs, improving verified lifting across four domain-specific languages.

title: Verified Code Transpilation with LLMs

abstract: Macroscopic observables of a system are of keen interest in real applications such as the design of novel materials. Current methods rely on microscopic trajectory simulations, where the forces on all microscopic coordinates need to be computed or measured. However, this can be computationally prohibitive for realistic systems. In this paper, we propose a method to learn macroscopic dynamics requiring only force computations on a subset of the microscopic coordinates. Our method relies on a sparsity assumption: the force on each microscopic coordinate relies only on a small number of other coordinates. The main idea of our approach is to map the training procedure on the macroscopic coordinates back to the microscopic coordinates, on which partial force computations can be used as stochastic estimation to update model parameters. We provide a theoretical justification of this under suitable conditions. We demonstrate the accuracy, force computation efficiency, and robustness of our method on learning macroscopic closure models from a variety of microscopic systems, including those modeled by partial differential equations or molecular dynamics simulations.
