It asks which parts of the training corpus contribute to the bias observed in an already learned embedding.

The authors develop a technique that reveals how changes to the training corpus would affect the resulting embedding bias. This connects a property of the learned representation back to particular source documents. That connection can identify document subsets whose removal would most reduce bias, making the analysis relevant to decisions about the training data itself.

The methodology is demonstrated on Wikipedia and New York Times corpora, where the authors report high accuracy. Its main contribution is therefore a way to trace and assess the origins of embedding bias, complementing efforts that modify representations after training. The stated findings support accurate attribution in the examined corpora, rather than claiming that document removal eliminates every form of stereotypical behavior.
summary.tldr: A corpus-perturbation analysis traces word-embedding bias to training documents and identifies document subsets whose removal would most reduce it.

title: Understanding the Origins of Bias in Word Embeddings

abstract: We present a predictor-corrector framework, called PicCoLO, that can transform a first-order model-free reinforcement or imitation learning algorithm into a new hybrid method that leverages predictive models to accelerate policy learning. The new “PicCoLOed” algorithm optimizes a policy by recursively repeating two steps: In the Prediction Step, the learner uses a model to predict the unseen future gradient and then applies the predicted estimate to update the policy; in the Correction Step, the learner runs the updated policy in the environment, receives the true gradient, and then corrects the policy using the gradient error. Unlike previous algorithms, PicCoLO corrects for the mistakes of using imperfect predicted gradients and hence does not suffer from model bias. The development of PicCoLO is made possible by a novel reduction from predictable online learning to adversarial online learning, which provides a systematic way to modify existing first-order algorithms to achieve the optimal regret with respect to predictable information. We show, in both theory and simulation, that the convergence rate of several first-order model-free algorithms can be improved by PicCoLO.

paragraphs: PicCoLO is a framework for accelerating policy learning by adding predictive models to existing first-order model-free reinforcement or imitation learning algorithms. It uses a model to anticipate useful updates while retaining feedback from interaction with the environment. The method repeatedly separates learning into a prediction step and a correction step.

During prediction, the model estimates a future gradient that has not yet been observed, and the learner updates its policy using that estimate. It then runs the updated policy in the environment, receives the true gradient, and corrects using the prediction error. The authors explain that this correction removes the model bias arising from imperfect predicted gradients.

The theoretical construction reduces predictable online learning to adversarial online learning. This supplies a systematic way to adapt first-order algorithms and achieve optimal regret relative to the available predictable information. Theory and simulations show improved convergence rates for several model-free algorithms. The contribution is thus a reusable mechanism for obtaining benefits from predictions while explicitly correcting their mistakes.
summary.tldr: PicCoLO accelerates policy learning with predicted gradients and corrects their errors using environmental feedback to avoid model bias.

title: Predictor-Corrector Policy Optimization

abstract: Boosting is a technique that boosts a weak and inaccurate machine learning algorithm into a strong accurate learning algorithm. The AdaBoost algorithm by Freund and Schapire (for which they were awarded the G{ö}del prize in 2003) is one of the widely used boosting algorithms, with many applications in theory and practice. Suppose we have a gamma-weak learner for a Boolean concept class C that takes time R(C), then the time complexity of AdaBoost scales as VC(C)poly(R(C), 1/gamma), where VC(C) is the VC-dimension of C. In this paper, we show how quantum techniques can improve the time complexity of classical AdaBoost. To this end, suppose we have a gamma-weak quantum learning algorithm for a Boolean concept class C that takes time Q(C), we introduce a quantum boosting algorithm whose complexity scales as sqrt{VC(C)}poly(Q(C),1/gamma); thereby achieving quadratic quantum improvement over classical AdaBoost in terms of VC(C).

paragraphs: Boosting turns a weak learner into a more accurate learning algorithm. This paper asks how quantum computation can improve the time needed for that transformation. It compares the dependence of classical AdaBoost and a proposed quantum boosting algorithm on the VC dimension, which measures the capacity of the Boolean concept class being learned.

For a classical weak learner taking time R(C), the stated AdaBoost complexity scales linearly with VC(C), multiplied by a polynomial in R(C) and the inverse weak-learning advantage. Assuming access to a quantum weak learner taking time Q(C), the proposed algorithm replaces that linear VC-dimension dependence with a square-root dependence.

The resulting improvement is quadratic in the VC-dimension factor. The full runtime still includes a polynomial dependence on quantum weak-learner cost and inverse learning advantage, so the comparison isolates a particular source of computational savings. The contribution is a conditional theoretical speedup for boosting when the required quantum weak learner is available.
summary.tldr: Given a quantum weak learner, quantum boosting achieves a quadratic improvement over AdaBoost in its dependence on VC dimension.

title: Quantum Boosting

abstract: Embedding layers are commonly used to map discrete symbols into continuous embedding vectors that reflect their semantic meanings. Despite their effectiveness, the number of parameters in an embedding layer increases linearly with the number of symbols and poses a critical challenge on memory and storage constraints. In this work, we propose a generic and end-to-end learnable compression framework termed differentiable product quantization (DPQ). We present two instantiations of DPQ that leverage different approximation techniques to enable differentiability in end-to-end learning. Our method can readily serve as a drop-in alternative for any existing embedding layer. Empirically, DPQ offers significant compression ratios (14-238X) at negligible or no performance cost on 10 datasets across three different language tasks.

paragraphs: Embedding layers assign continuous vectors to discrete symbols so that a model can represent their meanings numerically. Their storage cost grows linearly with the number of symbols. Consequently, even an effective embedding layer can become a major obstacle when a system has limited memory or storage capacity.

The paper introduces differentiable product quantization, or DPQ, as a general framework for compressing embeddings while learning them end-to-end. It presents two versions that use different approximation techniques to make the compression compatible with differentiable training. The framework is designed to replace an existing embedding layer directly, making compression part of the model’s learning process.

Across ten datasets covering three language tasks, DPQ achieves compression ratios ranging from 14 to 238 times with negligible or no observed performance loss. These results indicate that substantial embedding compression can coexist with useful task performance in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is an adaptable compression framework whose representations can be optimized together with the rest of the model.
summary.tldr: DPQ makes embedding compression trainable end-to-end, achieving 14–238-fold compression with negligible or no performance cost in the reported evaluations.

title: Differentiable Product Quantization for End-to-End Embedding Compression

abstract: Out-of-training-distribution (OOD) scenarios are a common challenge of learning agents at deployment, typically leading to arbitrary deductions and poorly-informed decisions. In principle, detection of and adaptation to OOD scenes can mitigate their adverse effects. In this paper, we highlight the limitations of current approaches to novel driving scenes and propose an epistemic uncertainty-aware planning method, called \emph{robust imitative planning} (RIP). Our method can detect and recover from some distribution shifts, reducing the overconfident and catastrophic extrapolations in OOD scenes. If the model’s uncertainty is too great to suggest a safe course of action, the model can instead query the expert driver for feedback, enabling sample-efficient online adaptation, a variant of our method we term \emph{adaptive robust imitative planning} (AdaRIP). Our methods outperform current state-of-the-art approaches in the nuScenes \emph{prediction} challenge, but since no benchmark evaluating OOD detection and adaption currently exists to assess \emph{control}, we introduce an autonomous car novel-scene benchmark, \texttt{CARNOVEL}, to evaluate the robustness of driving agents to a suite of tasks with distribution shifts, where our methods outperform all the baselines.

paragraphs: A driving agent can encounter scenes that differ from its training experience, making confident predictions unreliable. This paper studies whether agents can recognize those situations, recover from them, and learn from additional feedback. Its central idea is to make planning sensitive to epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with what the model has learned.

The proposed robust imitative planning method, RIP, uses this uncertainty to detect and recover from some distribution shifts. The authors report that it reduces overconfident, catastrophic extrapolations in unfamiliar scenes. When uncertainty is too high to suggest a safe action, an adaptive variant, AdaRIP, can ask an expert driver for feedback. That feedback supports sample-efficient adaptation during deployment.

The methods outperform the compared state-of-the-art approaches on the nuScenes prediction challenge. To assess control under distribution shifts, the authors also introduce CARNOVEL, a benchmark of novel driving scenes, where their methods outperform all evaluated baselines. These results support uncertainty-aware planning and expert-assisted adaptation in the tested settings; the recovery claim remains limited to some distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware driving methods recover from some distribution shifts and use expert feedback to adapt when the model cannot suggest a safe action.

title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Identify, Recover From, and Adapt to Distribution Shifts?

abstract: It is well known that (stochastic) gradient descent has an implicit bias towards flat minima. In deep neural network training, this mechanism serves to screen out minima. However, the precise effect that this has on the trained network is not yet fully understood. In this paper, we characterize the flat minima in linear neural networks trained with a quadratic loss. First, we show that linear ResNets with zero initialization necessarily converge to the flattest of all minima. We then prove that these minima correspond to nearly balanced networks whereby the gain from the input to any intermediate representation does not change drastically from one layer to the next. Finally, we show that consecutive layers in flat minima solutions are coupled. That is, one of the left singular vectors of each weight matrix, equals one of the right singular vectors of the next matrix. This forms a distinct path from input to output, that, as we show, is dedicated to the signal that experiences the largest gain end-to-end. Experiments indicate that these properties are characteristic of both linear and nonlinear models trained in practice.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what the preference of gradient descent for flat minima means for a trained network’s internal structure. Its theoretical setting is linear neural networks trained with quadratic loss. Within that setting, the authors show that linear residual networks initialized at zero necessarily converge to the flattest minima.

Those minima correspond to nearly balanced networks: amplification from the input to intermediate representations does not change sharply between successive layers. The authors also prove a coupling between neighboring weight matrices through matching singular-vector directions. These alignments create a distinct path through the network associated with the signal receiving the greatest overall amplification.

The findings give structural meaning to flatness by connecting the shape of the loss landscape with how signals propagate through layers. Experiments indicate that the identified properties also characterize linear and nonlinear models trained in practice. The nonlinear evidence is empirical, while the formal characterization and zero-initialization convergence result are established in the stated linear-network setting.
summary.tldr: Flat minima in linear networks exhibit balanced amplification and aligned layer directions, with related properties observed empirically in nonlinear models.

title: Unique Properties of Flat Minima in Deep Networks

abstract: Regularizing the optimal transport (OT) problem has proven crucial for OT theory to impact the field of machine learning. For instance, it is known that regularizing OT problems with entropy leads to faster computations and better differentiation using the Sinkhorn algorithm, as well as better sample complexity bounds than classic OT. In this work we depart from this practical perspective and propose a new interpretation of regularization as a robust mechanism, and show using Fenchel duality that any convex regularization of OT can be interpreted as ground cost adversarial. This incidentally gives access to a robust dissimilarity measure on the ground space, which can in turn be used in other applications. We propose algorithms to compute this robust cost, and illustrate the interest of this approach empirically.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions using a ground cost that specifies how costly it is to move mass between points. Regularization has helped make these problems practical for machine learning. Entropy regularization, for example, supports faster computation and differentiation through the Sinkhorn algorithm, along with improved sample-complexity bounds.

This paper develops a different interpretation of regularization: robustness to adversarial choices of the ground cost. Using Fenchel duality, the authors show that any convex regularization of optimal transport admits this ground-cost-adversarial interpretation. The convexity qualification defines the scope of the stated result. The contribution gives an alternative mathematical meaning to modifying the transport objective.

The interpretation also yields a robust dissimilarity measure on the underlying space of points. The authors propose algorithms for computing this robust cost and illustrate the approach empirically. That makes the result more than a reinterpretation of an existing calculation: it provides a cost measure that can be used in other applications. The work links regularized distribution comparison with robustness in the pointwise costs that comparison uses.
summary.tldr: Convex regularization of optimal transport can be interpreted as adversarial modification of the ground cost, yielding a computable robust dissimilarity.

title: Regularized Optimal Transport is Ground Cost Adversarial

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) achieves significant empirical successes. However, MARL suffers from the curse of many agents. In this paper, we exploit the symmetry of agents in MARL. In the most generic form, we study a mean-field MARL problem. Such a mean-field MARL is defined on mean-field states, which are distributions that are supported on continuous space. Based on the mean embedding of the distributions, we propose MF-FQI algorithm, which solves the mean-field MARL and establishes a non-asymptotic analysis for MF-FQI algorithm. We highlight that MF-FQI algorithm enjoys a “blessing of many agents” property in the sense that a larger number of observed agents improves the performance of MF-FQI algorithm.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows. This paper addresses that challenge by exploiting symmetry among agents. It studies a mean-field formulation, where a state describes a distribution over a continuous space, shifting the learning problem toward the collective population representation.

The proposed MF-FQI algorithm represents these distributions through their mean embeddings and uses that representation to solve the mean-field reinforcement learning problem. This is the key connection between the population-level formulation and a learning algorithm: distributions themselves become the objects on which the method operates. The paper also provides a non-asymptotic analysis, addressing performance without relying only on an infinite-data limit.

A highlighted finding is that observing more agents improves MF-FQI's performance in this setting. The authors describe this as a beneficial effect of having many agents, reversing the usual concern that additional agents only make learning harder. The result concerns the symmetric mean-field problem studied here; its significance is that population size can supply useful information to an algorithm designed around distributions.
summary.tldr: MF-FQI uses distribution embeddings to learn in mean-field multi-agent systems, with performance improving as more agents are observed.

title: Breaking the Curse of Many Agents: Provable Mean Embedding Q-Iteration for Mean-Field Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a convolution-free approach to video classification built exclusively on self-attention over space and time. Our method, named “TimeSformer,” adapts the standard Transformer architecture to video by enabling spatiotemporal feature learning directly from a sequence of frame-level patches. Our experimental study compares different self-attention schemes and suggests that “divided attention,” where temporal attention and spatial attention are separately applied within each block, leads to the best video classification accuracy among the design choices considered. Despite the radically new design, TimeSformer achieves state-of-the-art results on several action recognition benchmarks, including the best reported accuracy on Kinetics-400 and Kinetics-600. Finally, compared to 3D convolutional networks, our model is faster to train, it can achieve dramatically higher test efficiency (at a small drop in accuracy), and it can also be applied to much longer video clips (over one minute long). Code and models are available at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/TimeSformer.

paragraphs: Video classification requires combining information within individual frames with information about how scenes change over time. TimeSformer addresses both using self-attention, without convolutional operations. It adapts the Transformer architecture to sequences of patches extracted from video frames, allowing the model to learn spatial and temporal relationships directly from those patch sequences.

The authors compare several ways to organize attention. Their experiments favor divided attention, which applies temporal attention and spatial attention separately inside each block. This result identifies the strongest option among the designs they tested. TimeSformer achieves leading results on several action-recognition benchmarks, including the best reported accuracies on Kinetics-400 and Kinetics-600.

Compared with 3D convolutional networks, the model trains faster and can deliver much greater test-time efficiency with a small accuracy reduction. It can also process clips longer than one minute. Together, these findings establish self-attention as an effective basis for video classification, while making clear that the largest reported inference-efficiency gains involve an accuracy trade-off.
summary.tldr: TimeSformer uses spatial and temporal self-attention to classify videos accurately, with favorable training speed and inference-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Is Space-Time Attention All You Need for Video Understanding?

abstract: We consider a linear autoencoder in which the latent variables are quantized, or corrupted by noise, and the constraint is Schur-concave in the set of latent variances. Although finding the optimal encoder/decoder pair for this setup is a nonconvex optimization problem, we show that decomposing the source into its principal components is optimal. If the constraint is strictly Schur-concave and the empirical covariance matrix has only simple eigenvalues, then any optimal encoder/decoder must decompose the source in this way. As one application, we consider a strictly Schur-concave constraint that estimates the number of bits needed to represent the latent variables under fixed-rate encoding, a setup that we call \emph{Principal Bit Analysis (PBA)}. This yields a practical, general-purpose, fixed-rate compressor that outperforms existing algorithms. As a second application, we show that a prototypical autoencoder-based variable-rate compressor is guaranteed to decompose the source into its principal components.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear autoencoders whose latent variables are quantized or affected by noise. It imposes a constraint with a mathematical property called Schur-concavity on the collection of latent variances. Although jointly choosing the best encoder and decoder is a nonconvex optimization problem, the authors show that decomposing the input into principal components is optimal in this setting.

A stronger conclusion requires stronger assumptions. If the constraint is strictly Schur-concave and the empirical covariance matrix has distinct eigenvalues, every optimal encoder-decoder pair must perform that principal-component decomposition. This distinguishes showing that a familiar construction achieves an optimum from showing that all optimal solutions must have the same decomposition structure.

For compression, the authors choose a strictly Schur-concave constraint estimating the bits needed to encode latent variables at a fixed rate. The resulting Principal Bit Analysis method yields a practical general-purpose compressor reported to outperform existing algorithms. A second application establishes that a prototypical variable-rate autoencoder compressor is guaranteed to decompose its source into principal components.
summary.tldr: Principal-component decomposition is optimal for the studied constrained linear autoencoders, yielding a practical fixed-rate compression method.

title: Principal Bit Analysis: Autoencoding with Schur-Concave Loss

abstract: Deep neural networks have shown the ability to extract universal feature representations from data such as images and text that have been useful for a variety of learning tasks. However, the fruits of representation learning have yet to be fully-realized in federated settings. Although data in federated settings is often non-i.i.d. across clients, the success of centralized deep learning suggests that data often shares a global {\em feature representation}, while the statistical heterogeneity across clients or tasks is concentrated in the {\em labels}. Based on this intuition, we propose a novel federated learning framework and algorithm for learning a shared data representation across clients and unique local heads for each client. Our algorithm harnesses the distributed computational power across clients to perform many local-updates with respect to the low-dimensional local parameters for every update of the representation. We prove that this method obtains linear convergence to the ground-truth representation with near-optimal sample complexity in a linear setting, demonstrating that it can efficiently reduce the problem dimension for each client. Further, we provide extensive experimental results demonstrating the improvement of our method over alternative personalized federated learning approaches in heterogeneous settings.

paragraphs: Federated clients often have different data distributions, making a single shared predictor an imperfect fit. This paper starts from the intuition that clients may still share useful features even when their labeling relationships differ. It proposes learning a common representation together with a separate prediction head for each client, combining shared learning with local personalization.

The algorithm performs many local updates of the low-dimensional client parameters for each update of the shared representation. This uses computation across clients to adapt their individual heads while coordinating the common features. The design places client-specific variation in a smaller parameter space, allowing the shared representation to reduce the dimension of each client’s learning problem.

In a linear setting, the authors prove linear convergence to the true representation with near-optimal sample complexity. Experiments also show improvements over alternative personalized federated approaches in heterogeneous settings. The theoretical result gives a precise guarantee for the linear case, while the experimental findings support the broader usefulness of sharing representations and personalizing prediction heads.
summary.tldr: Sharing a representation while learning client-specific prediction heads improves personalized federated learning, with convergence guarantees in a linear setting.

title: Exploiting Shared Representations for Personalized Federated Learning

abstract: Predictor combination is the problem of improving a task predictor using predictors of other tasks when the forms of individual predictors are unknown. Previous work approached this problem by nonparametrically assessing predictor relationships based on their joint evaluations on a shared sample. This limits their application to cases where all predictors are defined on the same task category, e.g. all predictors estimate attributes of shoes. We present a new predictor combination algorithm that overcomes this limitation. Our algorithm aligns the heterogeneous domains of different predictors in a shared latent space to facilitate comparisons of predictors independently of the domains on which they are originally defined. We facilitate this by a new data alignment scheme that matches data distributions across task categories. Based on visual attribute ranking experiments on datasets that span diverse task categories (e.g. shoes and animals), we demonstrate that our approach often significantly improves the performances of the initial predictors.

Its empirical wording matters: improvements occur often in the reported experiments, rather than being asserted for every predictor combination.
summary.tldr: Aligning different task domains in a shared latent space lets predictor combination improve visual attribute ranking across diverse categories.

title: Improving Predictors via Combination Across Diverse Task Categories

abstract: While single-agent policy optimization in a fixed environment has attracted a lot of research attention recently in the reinforcement learning community, much less is known theoretically when there are multiple agents playing in a potentially competitive environment. We take steps forward by proposing and analyzing new fictitious play policy optimization algorithms for two-player zero-sum Markov games with structured but unknown transitions. We consider two classes of transition structures: factored independent transition and single-controller transition. For both scenarios, we prove tight $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bounds after $T$ steps in a two-agent competitive game scenario. The regret of each player is measured against a potentially adversarial opponent who can choose a single best policy in hindsight after observing the full policy sequence. Our algorithms feature a combination of Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)-type optimism and fictitious play under the scope of simultaneous policy optimization in a non-stationary environment. When both players adopt the proposed algorithms, their overall optimality gap is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$.

These ingredients support simultaneous policy optimization while the environment experienced by each player changes with the other's behavior. The analysis measures each player's regret against an opponent allowed to choose a single best policy in hindsight after seeing the full policy sequence.

For both transition structures, the authors prove tight regret bounds growing as the square root of the number of steps, up to logarithmic factors. When both players use the algorithms, the overall optimality gap has the same stated scaling. These results provide theoretical control of learning in the two structured competitive settings. The transition assumptions are central to the scope of the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Fictitious play with optimistic policy optimization achieves tight square-root regret bounds in two classes of zero-sum Markov games.

title: Provably Efficient Fictitious Play Policy Optimization for Zero-Sum Markov Games with Structured Transitions

abstract: Recently directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure learning is formulated as a constrained continuous optimization problem with continuous acyclicity constraints and was solved iteratively through subproblem optimization. To further improve efficiency, we propose a novel learning framework to model and learn the weighted adjacency matrices in the DAG space directly. Specifically, we first show that the set of weighted adjacency matrices of DAGs are equivalent to the set of weighted gradients of graph potential functions, and one may perform structure learning by searching in this equivalent set of DAGs. To instantiate this idea, we propose a new algorithm, DAG-NoCurl, which solves the optimization problem efficiently with a two-step procedure: $1)$ first we find an initial non-acyclic solution to the optimization problem, and $2)$ then we employ the Hodge decomposition of graphs and learn an acyclic graph by projecting the non-acyclic graph to the gradient of a potential function. Experimental studies on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method provides comparable accuracy but better efficiency than baseline DAG structure learning methods on both linear and generalized structural equation models, often by more than one order of magnitude.

The algorithm uses this result in two stages. It first obtains an initial solution that may contain cycles. It then uses a graph Hodge decomposition and a projection toward the gradient of a potential function to learn an acyclic structure.

Benchmark experiments cover both linear and generalized structural equation models. The authors report accuracy comparable to baseline structure-learning methods with better efficiency, often exceeding a tenfold improvement. The contribution connects a mathematical representation of acyclicity to a practical two-step procedure, reducing the computational burden observed in those comparisons.
summary.tldr: DAG-NoCurl uses graph potentials and a two-step projection procedure to learn acyclic structures with comparable accuracy and substantially better reported efficiency.

title: DAGs with No Curl: An Efficient DAG Structure Learning Approach

abstract: Model extraction attacks attempt to replicate a target machine learning model by querying its inference API. State-of-the-art attacks are learning-based and construct replicas by supervised training on the target model’s predictions, but an emerging class of attacks exploit algebraic properties to obtain high-fidelity replicas using orders of magnitude fewer queries. So far, these algebraic attacks have been limited to neural networks with few hidden layers and ReLU activations. In this paper we present algebraic and hybrid algebraic/learning-based attacks on large-scale natural language models. We consider a grey-box setting, targeting models with a pre-trained (public) encoder followed by a single (private) classification layer. Our key findings are that (i) with a frozen encoder, high-fidelity extraction is possible with a small number of in-distribution queries, making extraction attacks indistinguishable from legitimate use; (ii) when the encoder is fine-tuned, a hybrid learning-based/algebraic attack improves over the learning-based state-of-the-art without requiring additional queries.

This paper extends algebraic and combined algebraic-and-learning approaches to large natural language models in a specific grey-box setting.

The target consists of a publicly available pretrained encoder followed by one private classification layer. When the encoder remains frozen, the authors find that a high-fidelity replica can be obtained with a small number of queries drawn from the normal input distribution. Because these queries resemble ordinary use, the reported attack does not depend on conspicuously unusual inputs.

When the encoder has been fine-tuned, the authors combine algebraic techniques with learning-based extraction. This hybrid improves over the learning-based state of the art without increasing the number of queries. Together, the findings show how knowledge of a public encoder can materially change extraction possibilities, with different approaches suited to frozen and fine-tuned encoders.
summary.tldr: Public encoder knowledge enables efficient extraction of language classifiers, with algebraic attacks for frozen encoders and hybrid attacks for fine-tuned ones.

title: Grey-box Extraction of Natural Language Models

abstract: This paper presents a new approach for assembling graph neural networks based on framelet transforms. The latter provides a multi-scale representation for graph-structured data. We decompose an input graph into low-pass and high-pass frequencies coefficients for network training, which then defines a framelet-based graph convolution. The framelet decomposition naturally induces a graph pooling strategy by aggregating the graph feature into low-pass and high-pass spectra, which considers both the feature values and geometry of the graph data and conserves the total information. The graph neural networks with the proposed framelet convolution and pooling achieve state-of-the-art performance in many node and graph prediction tasks. Moreover, we propose shrinkage as a new activation for the framelet convolution, which thresholds high-frequency information at different scales. Compared to ReLU, shrinkage activation improves model performance on denoising and signal compression: noises in both node and structure can be significantly reduced by accurately cutting off the high-pass coefficients from framelet decomposition, and the signal can be compressed to less than half its original size with well-preserved prediction performance.

paragraphs: This paper builds graph neural networks around framelet transforms, which represent graph data at multiple scales. The transform separates the input into low-pass and high-pass coefficients. These components provide the basis for a graph convolution that can work with different frequency content rather than treating the graph representation as a single undivided signal.

The same decomposition also supplies a pooling strategy. It aggregates graph features into low-pass and high-pass spectra while accounting for both feature values and graph geometry, and the paper states that this conserves total information. Networks using the proposed convolution and pooling achieve state-of-the-art results on many node- and graph-prediction tasks.

The authors additionally replace ReLU with shrinkage, an activation that thresholds high-frequency coefficients at different scales. Compared with ReLU, it improves denoising and signal compression: the reported results reduce noise in both nodes and graph structure, and compress signals below half their original size while largely preserving prediction performance. The decomposition thus supports prediction, noise removal, and compression within one framework.
summary.tldr: Framelet-based graph networks use multiscale frequency representations to improve prediction, denoising, and compression.

title: How Framelets Enhance Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In active visual tracking, it is notoriously difficult when distracting objects appear, as distractors often mislead the tracker by occluding the target or bringing a confusing appearance. To address this issue, we propose a mixed cooperative-competitive multi-agent game, where a target and multiple distractors form a collaborative team to play against a tracker and make it fail to follow. Through learning in our game, diverse distracting behaviors of the distractors naturally emerge, thereby exposing the tracker’s weakness, which helps enhance the distraction-robustness of the tracker. For effective learning, we then present a bunch of practical methods, including a reward function for distractors, a cross-modal teacher-student learning strategy, and a recurrent attention mechanism for the tracker. The experimental results show that our tracker performs desired distraction-robust active visual tracking and can be well generalized to unseen environments. We also show that the multi-agent game can be used to adversarially test the robustness of trackers.

paragraphs: An active visual tracker must keep following its target even when other objects obscure it or look confusingly similar. This paper trains a tracker through a multi-agent game designed to create such difficulties. The target and several distractors cooperate against the tracker, trying to make it lose the object it is meant to follow.

As the competing agents learn, different distracting behaviors emerge and expose weaknesses in the tracker. The authors support this training process with a reward function for distractors, a cross-modal teacher-student strategy, and a recurrent attention mechanism for the tracker. Together, these methods help turn the adversarial interactions into a learning process that improves resistance to distraction.

Experiments show successful distraction-robust tracking and generalization to unseen environments. The same game also serves as a way to test tracker robustness by generating challenging interactions. The contribution therefore gives learned distractors two roles: they provide difficult training experiences and help reveal where a tracker can still be misled during evaluation.
summary.tldr: A game with cooperating distractors trains and tests visual trackers against learned behaviors that make targets difficult to follow.

title: Towards Distraction-Robust Active Visual Tracking

abstract: This work addresses meta-learning (ML) by considering deep networks with stochastic local winner-takes-all (LWTA) activations. This type of network units results in sparse representations from each model layer, as the units are organized into blocks where only one unit generates a non-zero output. The main operating principle of the introduced units rely on stochastic principles, as the network performs posterior sampling over competing units to select the winner. Therefore, the proposed networks are explicitly designed to extract input data representations of sparse stochastic nature, as opposed to the currently standard deterministic representation paradigm. Our approach produces state-of-the-art predictive accuracy on few-shot image classification and regression experiments, as well as reduced predictive error on an active learning setting; these improvements come with an immensely reduced computational cost. Code is available at: https://github.com/Kkalais/StochLWTA-ML

paragraphs: This paper explores a network architecture for meta-learning in which units compete locally to produce an activation. The units are arranged into blocks, and only one unit in each block contributes a nonzero output. As a result, each layer produces a sparse representation rather than activating all of its competing units.

The winning unit is chosen stochastically through posterior sampling. Randomness is therefore part of how the network builds its representations, alongside the sparsity imposed by local competition. The proposed design makes this sparse, stochastic representation mechanism a central component of the model used for learning across tasks.

The authors report state-of-the-art predictive accuracy in their few-shot image classification and regression experiments, as well as lower prediction error in an active learning setting. They also report a very large reduction in computational cost. These findings indicate that, in the evaluated tasks, stochastic local competition can support strong predictions while reducing computation. The contribution combines an architectural change with empirical evidence across several forms of learning from limited information.
summary.tldr: Networks with stochastic local winner-takes-all units achieve strong reported meta-learning results while substantially reducing computational cost.

title: Stochastic Deep Networks with Linear Competing Units for Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning

abstract: Strategic classification studies learning in settings where self-interested users can strategically modify their features to obtain favorable predictive outcomes. A key working assumption, however, is that “favorable” always means “positive”; this may be appropriate in some applications (e.g., loan approval), but reduces to a fairly narrow view of what user interests can be. In this work we argue for a broader perspective on what accounts for strategic user behavior, and propose and study a flexible model of generalized strategic classification. Our generalized model subsumes most current models but includes other novel settings; among these, we identify and target one intriguing sub-class of problems in which the interests of users and the system are aligned. This setting reveals a surprising fact: that standard max-margin losses are ill-suited for strategic inputs. Returning to our fully generalized model, we propose a novel max-margin framework for strategic learning that is practical and effective, and which we analyze theoretically. We conclude with a set of experiments that empirically demonstrate the utility of our approach.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies prediction when people can change their features to obtain outcomes they prefer. Many existing models assume everyone wants a positive prediction, as might occur with loan approval. This paper argues that this assumption captures only a limited range of user interests and develops a more flexible account of strategic behavior.

The proposed generalized model includes most current models while allowing additional settings. The authors focus especially on cases where users and the predictive system have aligned interests. Even there, they find that standard maximum-margin losses are poorly suited to strategic inputs. Shared goals therefore do not by themselves make a conventional training objective appropriate.

Returning to the broader model, the paper introduces a maximum-margin framework designed for strategic learning and provides theoretical analysis. Experiments demonstrate its practical utility. The contribution combines a broader description of what users want with a learning approach that accounts for their ability to respond to predictions, making the interaction between incentives and training objectives explicit.
summary.tldr: A broader model of user incentives motivates a strategic maximum-margin framework, including cases where users and the system share goals.

title: Generalized Strategic Classification and the Case of Aligned Incentives

abstract: Time series alignment methods call for highly expressive, differentiable and invertible warping functions which preserve temporal topology, i.e diffeomorphisms. Diffeomorphic warping functions can be generated from the integration of velocity fields governed by an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Gradient-based optimization frameworks containing diffeomorphic transformations require to calculate derivatives to the differential equation’s solution with respect to the model parameters, i.e. sensitivity analysis. Unfortunately, deep learning frameworks typically lack automatic-differentiation-compatible sensitivity analysis methods; and implicit functions, such as the solution of ODE, require particular care. Current solutions appeal to adjoint sensitivity methods, ad-hoc numerical solvers or ResNet’s Eulerian discretization. In this work, we present a closed-form expression for the ODE solution and its gradient under continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) velocity functions. We present a highly optimized implementation of the results on CPU and GPU. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments on several datasets to validate the generalization ability of our model to unseen data for time-series joint alignment. Results show significant improvements both in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: Aligning time series requires adjusting when events occur while preserving their temporal ordering. The paper focuses on smooth, invertible warping functions that provide this kind of transformation. Such warps can be generated by integrating a velocity field, but training a model containing them also requires derivatives of the resulting transformation with respect to its parameters.

Those derivatives are difficult to handle because the transformation is defined through the solution of a differential equation. The authors derive closed-form expressions for both the solution and its gradient when the velocity field is continuous and piecewise affine. This gives a direct mathematical treatment for that specified class of velocity functions.

The paper also provides optimized CPU and GPU implementations. Experiments on several datasets evaluate joint time-series alignment and the model's ability to generalize to unseen data, reporting significant improvements in efficiency and accuracy. The contribution links the mathematical form of the warp to its trainability: choosing a suitable velocity-field family makes both transformation and parameter sensitivity available in closed form.
summary.tldr: Closed-form time-warp solutions and gradients for continuous piecewise-affine velocity fields improve time-series alignment efficiency and accuracy.

title: Closed-Form Diffeomorphic Transformations for Time Series Alignment

abstract: Estimating optimal transport (OT) maps (a.k.a. Monge maps) between two measures P and Q is a problem fraught with computational and statistical challenges. A promising approach lies in using the dual potential functions obtained when solving an entropy-regularized OT problem between samples P_n and Q_n, which can be used to recover an approximately optimal map. The negentropy penalization in that scheme introduces, however, an estimation bias that grows with the regularization strength. A well-known remedy to debias such estimates, which has gained wide popularity among practitioners of regularized OT, is to center them, by subtracting auxiliary problems involving P_n and itself, as well as Q_n and itself. We do prove that, under favorable conditions on P and Q, debiasing can yield better approximations to the Monge map. However, and perhaps surprisingly, we present a few cases in which debiasing is provably detrimental in a statistical sense, notably when the regularization strength is large or the number of samples is small. These claims are validated experimentally on synthetic and real datasets, and should reopen the debate on whether debiasing is needed when using entropic OT.

paragraphs: Optimal transport maps describe how to move one probability distribution into another. Estimating them from samples is computationally and statistically challenging. Entropy regularization offers a useful route to approximate maps, but it introduces bias that increases with regularization strength. A common response is to center the estimates using auxiliary transport problems that compare each sampled distribution with itself.

This paper examines whether that correction actually improves the resulting map. The authors prove that it can produce better approximations under favorable conditions on the two distributions. They also construct cases where applying the correction is statistically harmful, including settings involving strong regularization or small sample sizes.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support both sides of the theoretical analysis. The practical implication is that reducing regularization bias through centering does not automatically improve map estimation overall. The benefit depends on the distributions and estimation setting. The paper therefore challenges routine use of this correction while preserving a positive result for cases where its stated conditions are favorable.
summary.tldr: Centering regularized transport maps can help under favorable conditions but can also provably worsen statistical estimation.

title: Debiaser Beware: Pitfalls of Centering Regularized Transport Maps

abstract: Content-addressable memory (CAM) networks, so-called because stored items can be recalled by partial or corrupted versions of the items, exhibit near-perfect recall of a small number of information-dense patterns below capacity and a ’memory cliff’ beyond, such that inserting a single additional pattern results in catastrophic loss of all stored patterns. We propose a novel CAM architecture, Memory Scaffold with Heteroassociation (MESH), that factorizes the problems of internal attractor dynamics and association with external content to generate a CAM continuum without a memory cliff: Small numbers of patterns are stored with complete information recovery matching standard CAMs, while inserting more patterns still results in partial recall of every pattern, with a graceful trade-off between pattern number and pattern richness. Motivated by the architecture of the Entorhinal-Hippocampal memory circuit in the brain, MESH is a tripartite architecture with pairwise interactions that uses a predetermined set of internally stabilized states together with heteroassociation between the internal states and arbitrary external patterns. We show analytically and experimentally that for any number of stored patterns, MESH nearly saturates the total information bound (given by the number of synapses) for CAM networks, outperforming all existing CAM models.

paragraphs: Content-addressable memory retrieves a stored pattern from an incomplete or corrupted version of it. Conventional networks can recover a small collection of rich patterns almost perfectly, then suffer a sharp collapse when their storage capacity is exceeded. This paper introduces MESH, an architecture designed to replace that sudden failure with a gradual trade-off between how many patterns are stored and how much detail remains recoverable.

MESH separates the internal dynamics that stabilize memory states from the associations connecting those states to external content. Its three-part architecture uses pairwise interactions, a predetermined collection of stabilized internal states, and associations to arbitrary external patterns. The design is motivated by the brain’s entorhinal–hippocampal memory circuit.

With few patterns, MESH recovers complete information at the level of standard content-addressable memories. As more patterns are inserted, it retains partial recall of every pattern. The authors report analytical and experimental evidence that it nearly reaches the information bound set by the number of synapses for any number of stored patterns, outperforming existing CAM models.
summary.tldr: MESH separates stable internal memory states from stored content, allowing recall to degrade gradually as more patterns are added.

title: Content Addressable Memory Without Catastrophic Forgetting by Heteroassociation with a Fixed Scaffold

abstract: Differentially private (DP) optimization is the standard paradigm to learn large neural networks that are accurate and privacy-preserving. The computational cost for DP deep learning, however, is notoriously heavy due to the per-sample gradient clipping. Existing DP implementations are 2$\sim$1000$\times$ more costly in time and space complexity than the standard (non-private) training. In this work, we develop a novel Book-Keeping (BK) technique that implements existing DP optimizers (thus achieving the same accuracy), with a substantial improvement on the computational cost. Specifically, BK enables DP training on large models and high dimensional data to be roughly as fast and memory-saving as the standard training, whereas previous DP algorithms can be inefficient or incapable of training due to memory error. The computational advantage of BK is supported by the complexity analysis as well as extensive experiments on vision and language tasks. Our implementation achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy with very small extra cost: on GPT2 and at almost the same memory cost ($<$1% overhead), BK has 1.03$\times$ the time complexity of the standard training (0.83$\times$ training speed in practice), and 0.61$\times$ the time complexity of the most efficient DP implementation (1.36$\times$ training speed in practice). We open-source the codebase for the BK algorithm at https://github.com/awslabs/fast-differential-privacy.

Its aim is to bring their computational demands close to ordinary, non-private training. summary.tldr: Book-Keeping implements existing differentially private optimisers with substantially lower time and memory costs while preserving accuracy.

title: Differentially Private Optimization on Large Model at Small Cost

abstract: Transformer-based detection and segmentation methods use a list of learned detection queries to retrieve information from the transformer network and learn to predict the location and category of one specific object from each query. We empirically find that random convex combinations of the learned queries are still good for the corresponding models. We then propose to learn a convex combination with dynamic coefficients based on the high-level semantics of the image. The generated dynamic queries, named as modulated queries, better capture the prior of object locations and categories in the different images. Equipped with our modulated queries, a wide range of DETR-based models achieve consistent and superior performance across multiple tasks (object detection, instance segmentation, panoptic segmentation) and on different benchmarks (MS COCO, CityScapes, YoutubeVIS).

paragraphs: Transformer-based detection and segmentation models use learned queries to retrieve information and predict individual objects' locations and categories. This paper asks whether those queries can be combined to make them better suited to a particular image. The authors first observe empirically that even random convex combinations of learned queries continue to work well in the corresponding models.

Building on that observation, they learn combination weights that depend on the image's high-level semantic information. A convex combination mixes the existing queries with nonnegative weights that sum to one. The resulting modulated queries adapt that mixture to each image, allowing them to better capture image-specific expectations about object categories and locations.

The authors add these queries to a range of DETR-based models and report consistent performance improvements. Evaluation spans object detection, instance segmentation, and panoptic segmentation, using MS COCO, CityScapes, and YoutubeVIS. The results support dynamic query construction as a broadly applicable modification within the tested model family, connecting a simple empirical observation about query mixtures to an image-conditioned mechanism.
summary.tldr: Image-conditioned mixtures of learned queries improve DETR-based models across detection and segmentation tasks.

title: Learning Dynamic Query Combinations for Transformer-based Object Detection and Segmentation

abstract: Understanding how the dynamics in biological and artificial neural networks implement the computations required for a task is a salient open question in machine learning and neuroscience. In particular, computations requiring complex memory storage and retrieval pose a significant challenge for these networks to implement or learn. Recently, a family of models described by neural ordinary differential equations (nODEs) has emerged as powerful dynamical neural network models capable of capturing complex dynamics. Here, we extend nODEs by endowing them with adaptive timescales using gating interactions. We refer to these as gated neural ODEs (gnODEs). Using a task that requires memory of continuous quantities, we demonstrate the inductive bias of the gnODEs to learn (approximate) continuous attractors. We further show how reduced-dimensional gnODEs retain their modeling power while greatly improving interpretability, even allowing explicit visualization of the structure of learned attractors. We introduce a novel measure of expressivity which probes the capacity of a neural network to generate complex trajectories. Using this measure, we explore how the phase-space dimension of the nODEs and the complexity of the function modeling the flow field contribute to expressivity. We see that a more complex function for modeling the flow field allows a lower-dimensional nODE to capture a given target dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of gating in nODEs on several real-world tasks.

summary.tldr: Gating gives neural ODEs adaptive timescales, supporting continuous memory and interpretable low-dimensional dynamics.

title: Trainability, Expressivity and Interpretability in Gated Neural ODEs

abstract: $k$-Clustering in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (e.g., $k$-median and $k$-means) is a fundamental machine learning problem. While near-linear time approximation algorithms were known in the classical setting for a dataset with cardinality $n$, it remains open to find sublinear-time quantum algorithms. We give quantum algorithms that find coresets for $k$-clustering in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nk}d^{3/2})$ query complexity. Our coreset reduces the input size from $n$ to $\mathrm{poly}(k\epsilon^{-1}d)$, so that existing $\alpha$-approximation algorithms for clustering can run on top of it and yield $(1 + \epsilon)\alpha$-approximation. This eventually yields a quadratic speedup for various $k$-clustering approximation algorithms. We complement our algorithm with a nearly matching lower bound, that any quantum algorithm must make $\Omega(\sqrt{nk})$ queries in order to achieve even $O(1)$-approximation for $k$-clustering.

paragraphs: Clustering methods such as k-means and k-median must organize large collections of points into k groups. This paper develops quantum algorithms that first compress the clustering input into a coreset. The coreset preserves enough information for existing approximation algorithms to operate on a much smaller representation of the original dataset.

For n points in d dimensions, the construction uses approximately sqrt(nk) times d to the three-halves queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its output size is polynomial in k, inverse approximation tolerance, and d. Running an alpha-approximation algorithm on this coreset yields a (1 + epsilon) times alpha approximation to the original clustering problem.

The construction gives quadratic speedups for various clustering approximation algorithms. The authors also prove a lower bound: even a constant-factor approximation requires at least order sqrt(nk) quantum queries. This nearly matches the construction's dependence on n and k, supporting its near-optimality in query complexity while leaving the stated dimensional and logarithmic factors visible.
summary.tldr: Quantum coreset construction accelerates clustering approximation algorithms with nearly optimal dependence on dataset size and cluster count in query complexity.

title: Near-Optimal Quantum Coreset Construction Algorithms for Clustering

abstract: In the realm of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), two exciting research directions have recently emerged: Subgraph GNNs and Graph Transformers. In this paper, we propose an architecture that integrates both approaches, dubbed Subgraphormer, which combines the enhanced expressive power, message-passing mechanisms, and aggregation schemes from Subgraph GNNs with attention and positional encodings, arguably the most important components in Graph Transformers. Our method is based on an intriguing new connection we reveal between Subgraph GNNs and product graphs, suggesting that Subgraph GNNs can be formulated as Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) operating on a product of the graph with itself. We use this formulation to design our architecture: first, we devise an attention mechanism based on the connectivity of the product graph. Following this, we propose a novel and efficient positional encoding scheme for Subgraph GNNs, which we derive as a positional encoding for the product graph. Our experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements over both Subgraph GNNs and Graph Transformers on a wide range of datasets.

paragraphs: Subgraph neural networks and graph transformers offer different ingredients for learning from graph structure. Subgraph methods provide expressive message passing and aggregation, while transformers contribute attention and positional information. Subgraphormer brings these ingredients together through a mathematical connection that gives the combined architecture a common structural basis.

The authors show that subgraph GNNs can be formulated as message-passing networks operating on a product of a graph with itself. They use this formulation to design attention around the connectivity of the product graph. They also derive an efficient positional encoding for subgraph GNNs by treating it as a positional encoding problem on that same product graph.

This construction matters because the attention mechanism and positional information both arise from the structure used to express subgraph computation. The architecture consequently links the two research directions through a shared formulation. Experiments report significant performance improvements over both subgraph GNNs and graph transformers across a wide range of datasets, supporting the usefulness of the integrated design in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Subgraphormer uses graph products to combine subgraph message passing with structurally grounded attention and positional encodings.

title: Subgraphormer: Unifying Subgraph GNNs and Graph Transformers via Graph Products

abstract: In this work, we give a new technique for analyzing individualized privacy accounting via the following simple observation: if an algorithm is one-sided add-DP, then its subsampled variant satisfies two-sided DP. From this, we obtain several improved algorithms for private combinatorial optimization problems, including decomposable submodular maximization and set cover. Our error guarantees are asymptotically tight and our algorithm satisfies pure-DP while previously known algorithms (Gupta et al., 2010; Chaturvedi et al., 2021) are approximate-DP. We also show an application of our technique beyond combinatorial optimization by giving a pure-DP algorithm for the shifting heavy hitter problem in a stream; previously, only an approximate-DP algorithm was known (Kaplan et al., 2021; Cohen & Lyu, 2023).

paragraphs: Private optimization seeks useful solutions while limiting what an algorithm reveals about individual contributions to its input. This paper introduces a technique for tracking those privacy effects through subsampling. Its central observation is conditional: an algorithm satisfying one-sided add differential privacy has a subsampled variant satisfying two-sided differential privacy.

The authors use that conversion to improve algorithms for combinatorial optimization, including decomposable submodular maximization and set cover. Here too, the authors provide a pure-private algorithm where previously only an approximate-private one was known. Across these applications, the shared contribution is a reusable privacy-analysis step: prove the appropriate one-sided property, then use subsampling to obtain the two-sided guarantee.
summary.tldr: A subsampling-based privacy conversion yields pure-private algorithms for several optimization and streaming problems.

title: Individualized Privacy Accounting via Subsampling with Applications in Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Large language models based on the Transformer architecture have demonstrated impressive capabilities to learn in context. However, existing theoretical studies on how this phenomenon arises are limited to the dynamics of a single layer of attention trained on linear regression tasks. In this paper, we study the optimization of a Transformer consisting of a fully connected layer followed by a linear attention layer. The MLP acts as a common nonlinear representation or feature map, greatly enhancing the power of in-context learning. We prove in the mean-field and two-timescale limit that the infinite-dimensional loss landscape for the distribution of parameters, while highly nonconvex, becomes quite benign. We also analyze the second-order stability of mean-field dynamics and show that Wasserstein gradient flow almost always avoids saddle points. Furthermore, we establish novel methods for obtaining concrete improvement rates both away from and near critical points. This represents the first saddle point analysis of mean-field dynamics in general and the techniques are of independent interest.

paragraphs: Theoretical studies of in-context learning had largely examined a single attention layer on linear regression tasks. This paper adds a learned nonlinear feature map, bringing the analyzed model closer to a mechanism that can reuse representations across tasks. The architecture consists of a fully connected layer followed by linear attention.

The guarantees concern the specified limiting model and dynamics, rather than establishing identical behavior for every finite Transformer or language-model training setup.
summary.tldr: A mean-field analysis shows favorable optimization dynamics for Transformers that learn nonlinear features for in-context learning.

title: Transformers Learn Nonlinear Features In Context: Nonconvex Mean-field Dynamics on the Attention Landscape

abstract: To interact with humans and act in the world, agents need to understand the range of language that people use and relate it to the visual world. While current agents can learn to execute simple language instructions, we aim to build agents that leverage diverse language—language like "this button turns on the TV" or "I put the bowls away"—that conveys general knowledge, describes the state of the world, provides interactive feedback, and more. Our key idea is that agents should interpret such diverse language as a signal that helps them predict the future: what they will observe, how the world will behave, and which situations will be rewarded. This perspective unifies language understanding with future prediction as a powerful self-supervised learning objective. We instantiate this in Dynalang, an agent that learns a multimodal world model to predict future text and image representations, and learns to act from imagined model rollouts. While current methods that learn language-conditioned policies degrade in performance with more diverse types of language, we show that Dynalang learns to leverage environment descriptions, game rules, and instructions to excel on tasks ranging from game-playing to navigating photorealistic home scans. Finally, we show that our method enables additional capabilities due to learning a generative model: Dynalang can be pretrained on text-only data, enabling learning from offline datasets, and generate language grounded in an environment.

paragraphs: Language received by an agent can describe the world, explain a rule, report an action, or provide feedback. Treating all of it only as instructions misses these other functions. The paper proposes using diverse language as evidence for predicting future observations, environmental behavior, and situations associated with rewards.

Dynalang implements this idea through a multimodal world model that predicts future text and image representations. The agent learns to act using imagined rollouts from that model. Language understanding and future prediction therefore share a self-supervised learning objective, allowing different kinds of linguistic information to contribute to the model used for action learning.

They contrast this with language-conditioned policy methods whose performance degrades as language becomes more diverse. The generative formulation also enables text-only pretraining from offline data and language generation grounded in an environment, extending its use beyond immediate instruction following.
summary.tldr: Dynalang learns to use diverse language for predicting the world and trains its actions through imagined model rollouts.

title: Learning to Model the World With Language

abstract: With the increasingly powerful performances and enormous scales of pretrained models, promoting parameter efficiency in fine-tuning has become a crucial need for effective and efficient adaptation to various downstream tasks. One representative line of fine-tuning methods is Orthogonal Fine-tuning (OFT), which rigorously preserves the angular distances within the parameter space to preserve the pretrained knowledge. Despite the empirical effectiveness, OFT still suffers low parameter efficiency at $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ and limited capability of downstream adaptation. Inspired by Givens rotation, in this paper, we proposed quasi-Givens Orthogonal Fine-Tuning (qGOFT) to address the problems. We first use $\mathcal{O}(d)$ Givens rotations to accomplish arbitrary orthogonal transformation in $SO(d)$ with provable equivalence, reducing parameter complexity from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(d)$. Then we introduce flexible norm and relative angular adjustments under soft orthogonality regularization to enhance the adaptation capability of downstream semantic deviations. Extensive experiments on various tasks and pretrained models validate the effectiveness of our methods.

paragraphs: Orthogonal fine-tuning adapts pretrained models while preserving angular relationships in parameter space, aiming to retain pretrained knowledge. This paper identifies two drawbacks: quadratic parameter complexity in dimension d and limited flexibility for adapting to downstream tasks. The proposed quasi-Givens Orthogonal Fine-Tuning method, qGOFT, addresses both issues.

The authors first use a construction based on Givens rotations and establish a provable equivalence for the orthogonal transformation they describe. They report reducing parameter complexity from O(d²) to O(d). This makes the transformation substantially more parameter-efficient within their formulation, addressing the cost of adapting very large pretrained models.

The method then softens strict orthogonality through regularization, permitting adjustments to norms and relative angles. These extra degrees of freedom are intended to accommodate semantic differences in downstream tasks while retaining an orthogonality-based constraint. Experiments across multiple tasks and pretrained models validate the methods' effectiveness. The overall contribution combines a compact rotation-based parameterization with controlled flexibility for adaptation.
summary.tldr: qGOFT combines a parameter-efficient Givens-rotation construction with soft orthogonality constraints to make pretrained-model adaptation more flexible.

title: Parameter Efficient Quasi-Orthogonal Fine-Tuning via Givens Rotation

abstract: Ensemble of deep neural networks has achieved great success in hedging against single-model failure under distribution shift. However, existing techniques suffer from producing redundant models, limiting predictive diversity and yielding compromised generalization performance. Existing ensemble pruning methods can only guarantee predictive diversity for in-distribution data, which may not transfer well to out-of-distribution (OoD) data. To address this gap, we propose a principled optimization framework for ensemble pruning under distribution shifts. Since the annotations of test data are not available, we explore relationships between prediction distributions of the models, encapsulated in a topology graph. By incorporating this topology into a combinatorial optimization framework, complementary models with high predictive diversity are selected with theoretical guarantees. Our approach is model-agnostic and can be applied on top of a broad spectrum of off-the-shelf ensembling methods for improved generalization performance. Experiments on common benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach in both multi- and single-source OoD generalization. The source codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/joffery/TEP.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks can protect against failures of individual models when data distributions change. However, an ensemble may contain models that make redundant predictions. Selecting diverse models on familiar data alone does not ensure that their predictions will remain complementary on unfamiliar data.

This paper builds an ensemble-pruning framework specifically for distribution shifts. Because test annotations are unavailable, it examines relationships among models' prediction distributions and represents those relationships as a topology graph. A combinatorial optimization procedure uses this graph to select complementary models with high predictive diversity, supported by theoretical guarantees.

The method is model-agnostic and can be applied to a broad range of existing ensembling approaches. Experiments on common benchmarks report superior out-of-distribution generalization in both single-source and multiple-source settings. The findings support treating the relationships between predictions as a useful selection signal under shift, extending ensemble pruning beyond diversity measured only on the original training distribution.
summary.tldr: Graph-based ensemble pruning selects complementary models and improves generalization under distribution shift in benchmark experiments.

title: Ensemble Pruning for Out-of-distribution Generalization

abstract: Neural image classifiers are known to undergo severe performance degradation when exposed to inputs that are sampled from environmental conditions that differ from their training data. Given the recent progress in Text-to-Image (T2I) generation, a natural question is how modern T2I generators can be used to simulate arbitrary interventions over such environmental factors in order to augment training data and improve the robustness of downstream classifiers. We experiment across a diverse collection of benchmarks in single domain generalization (SDG) and reducing reliance on spurious features (RRSF), ablating across key dimensions of T2I generation, including interventional prompting strategies, conditioning mechanisms, and post-hoc filtering, showing that modern T2I generators like Stable Diffusion can indeed be used to implement a powerful interventional data augmentation (IDA) mechanism, outperforming previously state-of-the-art data augmentation techniques regardless of how each dimension is configured.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can lose accuracy when deployment conditions differ from those represented in training. This paper investigates using text-to-image generators to vary environmental factors in synthetic training images. The objective is to improve robustness by exposing classifiers to deliberate changes in conditions that might otherwise undermine their predictions.

The authors study interventional data augmentation across benchmarks for single-domain generalization and reduced reliance on spurious features. They vary three parts of the generation process: how interventions are described in prompts, how generation is conditioned, and how generated images are filtered afterward. These comparisons examine whether the benefit depends on particular choices within the augmentation pipeline.

Across the evaluated benchmarks and configurations, modern generators such as Stable Diffusion outperform the compared state-of-the-art augmentation techniques. The reported advantage persists across the tested settings of each generation dimension. The findings support generated images as a practical means of varying environmental conditions for classifier training, extending their usefulness from image production to the robustness of downstream predictions.
summary.tldr: Text-to-image generation improves classifier robustness by augmenting training data with deliberate variations in environmental conditions.

title: Not Just Pretty Pictures: Toward Interventional Data Augmentation Using Text-to-Image Generators

abstract: Code auditing is the process of reviewing code with the aim of identifying bugs. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for this task without requiring compilation, while also supporting user-friendly customization. However, auditing a code repository with LLMs poses significant challenges: limited context windows and hallucinations can degrade the quality of bug reports, and analyzing large-scale repositories incurs substantial time and token costs, hindering efficiency and scalability. This work introduces an LLM-based agent, RepoAudit, designed to perform autonomous repository-level code auditing. Equipped with agent memory, RepoAudit explores the codebase on demand by analyzing data-flow facts along feasible program paths within individual functions. It further incorporates a validator module to mitigate hallucinations by verifying data-flow facts and checking the satisfiability of path conditions associated with potential bugs, thereby reducing false positives. RepoAudit detects 40 true bugs across 15 real-world benchmark projects with a precision of 78.43%, requiring on average only 0.44 hours and $2.54 per project. Also, it detects 185 new bugs in high-profile projects, among which 174 have been confirmed or fixed. We have open-sourced RepoAudit at https://github.com/PurCL/RepoAudit.
