title: RepoAudit: An Autonomous LLM-Agent for Repository-Level Code Auditing

abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning aims to learn a unified policy capable of solving multiple tasks using only pre-collected task-mixed datasets, without requiring any online interaction with the environment. However, it faces significant challenges in effectively sharing knowledge across tasks. Inspired by the efficient knowledge abstraction observed in human learning, we propose Goal-Oriented Skill Abstraction (GO-Skill), a novel approach designed to extract and utilize reusable skills to enhance knowledge transfer and task performance. Our approach uncovers reusable skills through a goal-oriented skill extraction process and leverages vector quantization to construct a discrete skill library. To mitigate class imbalances between broadly applicable and task-specific skills, we introduce a skill enhancement phase to refine the extracted skills. Furthermore, we integrate these skills using hierarchical policy learning, enabling the construction of a high-level policy that dynamically orchestrates discrete skills to accomplish specific tasks. Extensive experiments on diverse robotic manipulation tasks within the MetaWorld benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of GO-Skill.

paragraphs: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning seeks one policy that can solve several tasks using previously collected experience. Because the learner cannot interact with the environment during learning, it must extract useful structure from a dataset mixing different tasks. GO-Skill addresses the difficulty of sharing knowledge across those tasks by organizing experience into reusable skills.

The method first extracts skills through a goal-oriented process and uses vector quantization to build a discrete skill library. A skill enhancement stage then addresses imbalances between skills that apply broadly and skills specific to particular tasks. This refinement targets a tension in shared learning: widely useful behavior and specialized behavior both need adequate representation.

Finally, hierarchical policy learning builds a higher-level policy that selects and coordinates the discrete skills for a requested task. Experiments on varied robotic manipulation tasks in MetaWorld demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and versatility. The results support reusable skill abstraction as a way to transfer knowledge within offline multi-task learning while preserving the ability to handle distinct task requirements.
summary.tldr: GO-Skill turns mixed offline experience into a reusable discrete skill library coordinated by a higher-level policy.

title: Goal-Oriented Skill Abstraction for Offline Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of novel view synthesis from unposed images in a single feed-forward. Our framework capitalizes on fast speed, scalability, and high-quality 3D reconstruction and view synthesis capabilities of 3DGS, where we further extend it to offer a practical solution that relaxes common assumptions such as dense image views, accurate camera poses, and substantial image overlaps. We achieve this through identifying and addressing unique challenges arising from the use of pixel-aligned 3DGS: misaligned 3D Gaussians across different views induce noisy or sparse gradients that destabilize training and hinder convergence, especially when above assumptions are not met. To mitigate this, we employ pre-trained monocular depth estimation and visual correspondence models to achieve coarse alignments of 3D Gaussians. We then introduce lightweight, learnable modules to refine depth and pose estimates from the coarse alignments, improving the quality of 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Furthermore, the refined estimates are leveraged to estimate geometry confidence scores, which assess the reliability of 3D Gaussian centers and condition the prediction of Gaussian parameters accordingly. Extensive evaluations on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate that PF3plat sets a new state-of-the-art across all benchmarks, supported by comprehensive ablation studies validating our design choices. We will make the code and weights publicly available.

paragraphs: PF3plat reconstructs a scene and synthesizes new views from images without supplied camera poses, using a single feed-forward pass. Misaligned Gaussians produce noisy or sparse training gradients, which can destabilize learning. The refined geometry also produces confidence scores that indicate how reliable Gaussian centers are and guide the prediction of Gaussian parameters.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets, with ablations supporting the design choices. The approach matters because it connects initial geometric alignment, learned refinement, and confidence-aware prediction within one pipeline. This gives the reconstruction process a way to account for uncertainty in its geometry while operating under less restrictive input conditions.
summary.tldr: PF3plat combines coarse alignment, learned geometry refinement, and confidence-aware Gaussian prediction to synthesize views from unposed images.

title: PF3plat: Pose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis

abstract: While showing sophisticated reasoning abilities, large language models (LLMs) still struggle with long-horizon decision-making tasks due to deficient exploration and long-term credit assignment, especially in sparse-reward scenarios. Inspired by the divide-and-conquer principle, we propose an innovative framework GLIDER (Grounding Language Models as EffIcient Decision-Making Agents via Offline HiErarchical Reinforcement Learning) that introduces a parameter-efficient and generally applicable hierarchy to LLM policies. We develop a scheme where the low-level controller is supervised with abstract, step-by-step plans that are learned and instructed by the high-level policy. This design decomposes complicated problems into a series of coherent chain-of-thought reasoning sub-tasks, providing flexible temporal abstraction to significantly enhance exploration and learning for long-horizon tasks. Furthermore, GLIDER facilitates fast online adaptation to non-stationary environments owing to the strong transferability of its task-agnostic low-level skills. Experiments on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld benchmarks show that GLIDER achieves consistent performance gains, along with enhanced generalization capabilities.

paragraphs: Language models can reason through complicated questions yet struggle when success requires a long sequence of decisions. Sparse rewards make this harder: useful feedback arrives infrequently, leaving the agent with little guidance about exploration or which earlier actions contributed to success. GLIDER addresses this problem by organizing a language-model policy into a hierarchy.

A high-level policy learns abstract, step-by-step plans and uses them to supervise a low-level controller. This separates an extended task into coherent reasoning subtasks and allows decisions to operate over flexible spans of time. The hierarchy is designed to be parameter-efficient and generally applicable, making structured planning part of how the agent learns to act.

Experiments on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld report consistent performance improvements and better generalization. These results support hierarchical decomposition as a way to improve long-horizon learning while reusing lower-level capabilities across tasks and changing conditions.
summary.tldr: GLIDER combines high-level planning with reusable low-level skills to improve language-model agents on long-horizon tasks and changing environments.

title: Divide and Conquer: Grounding LLMs as Efficient Decision-Making Agents via Offline Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel 3D registration paradigm, Generative Point Cloud Registration, which bridges advanced 2D generative models with 3D matching tasks to enhance registration performance. Our key idea is to generate cross-view consistent image pairs that are well-aligned with the source and target point clouds, enabling geometric-color feature fusion to facilitate robust matching. To ensure high-quality matching, the generated image pair should feature both 2D-3D geometric consistency and cross-view texture consistency. To achieve this, we introduce Match-ControlNet, a matching-specific, controllable 2D generative model. Specifically, it leverages the depth-conditioned generation capability of ControlNet to produce images that are geometrically aligned with depth maps derived from point clouds, ensuring 2D-3D geometric consistency. Additionally, by incorporating a coupled conditional denoising scheme and coupled prompt guidance, Match-ControlNet further promotes cross-view feature interaction, guiding texture consistency generation. Our generative 3D registration paradigm is general and could be seamlessly integrated into various registration methods to enhance their performance. Extensive experiments on 3DMatch and ScanNet datasets verify the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns two sets of three-dimensional points by finding corresponding structure. This paper adds generated images to that process, allowing matching to combine geometric information with color features. The key is to generate an image for each point cloud whose geometry fits that cloud and whose texture remains consistent with the other view.

Match-ControlNet supplies these paired images. It uses depth maps derived from the point clouds to condition image generation, aligning the images with the underlying three-dimensional geometry. A coupled denoising procedure and coupled prompt guidance connect the two generation processes, encouraging cross-view feature interaction and consistent textures rather than independently producing unrelated appearances.

These two forms of consistency make the generated imagery useful for matching: geometric alignment ties image features to points, while texture consistency helps connect the views. Experiments on 3DMatch and ScanNet support the approach’s effectiveness. The authors present it as a general registration paradigm that could be integrated into various registration methods to enhance their performance.
summary.tldr: Match-ControlNet generates geometrically aligned, texture-consistent image pairs to enrich point cloud registration with complementary color features.

title: Generative Point Cloud Registration

abstract: In this paper, we present $Morse$, a simple dual-sampling framework for accelerating diffusion models losslessly. The key insight of Morse is to reformulate the iterative generation (from noise to data) process via taking advantage of fast jump sampling and adaptive residual feedback strategies. Specifically, Morse involves two models called $Dash$ and $Dot$ that interact with each other. The Dash model is just the pre-trained diffusion model of any type, but operates in a jump sampling regime, creating sufficient space for sampling efficiency improvement. The Dot model is significantly faster than the Dash model, which is learnt to generate residual feedback conditioned on the observations at the current jump sampling point on the trajectory of the Dash model, lifting the noise estimate to easily match the next-step estimate of the Dash model without jump sampling. By chaining the outputs of the Dash and Dot models run in a time-interleaved fashion, Morse exhibits the merit of flexibly attaining desired image generation performance while improving overall runtime efficiency. With our proposed weight sharing strategy between the Dash and Dot models, Morse is efficient for training and inference. Our method shows a lossless speedup of 1.78$\times$ to 3.31$\times$ on average over a wide range of sampling step budgets relative to 9 baseline diffusion models on 6 image generation tasks. Furthermore, we show that our method can be also generalized to improve the Latent Consistency Model (LCM-SDXL, which is already accelerated with consistency distillation technique) tailored for few-step text-to-image synthesis. The code and models are available at https://github.com/deep-optimization/Morse.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate data through repeated updates from noise, making sampling speed an important computational concern. Morse accelerates that process with two cooperating models. Dash is the pretrained diffusion model operating with jumps along the sampling trajectory, while Dot is a substantially faster model that provides corrective feedback.

Dot learns residual corrections conditioned on observations at Dash’s current jump point. Those corrections bring the noise estimate toward the next-step estimate that Dash would produce without jumping. By interleaving their outputs, Morse combines larger sampling jumps with cheaper intermediate refinement. A weight-sharing strategy further improves training and inference efficiency.

They also show improvements for LCM-SDXL, which already uses consistency distillation for few-step synthesis. The results indicate that learned residual feedback can accelerate both conventional diffusion sampling and an already accelerated model.
summary.tldr: Morse interleaves diffusion-model jumps with a faster corrective model, achieving reported lossless speedups across multiple image-generation tasks.

title: Morse: Dual-Sampling for Lossless Acceleration of Diffusion Models

abstract: Video Question-Answering (VideoQA) remains challenging in achieving advanced cognitive reasoning due to the uncontrollable and opaque reasoning processes in existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). To address this issue, we propose a novel Language-centric Tree Reasoning (LTR) framework that targets on enhancing the reasoning ability of models. In detail, it recursively divides the original question into logically manageable parts and conquers them piece by piece, enhancing the reasoning capabilities and interpretability of existing MLLMs. Specifically, in the first stage, the LTR focuses on language to recursively generate a language-centric logical tree, which gradually breaks down the complex cognitive question into simple perceptual ones and plans the reasoning path through a RAG-based few-shot approach. In the second stage, with the aid of video content, the LTR performs bottom-up logical reasoning within the tree to derive the final answer along with the traceable reasoning path. Experiments across 11 VideoQA benchmarks demonstrate that our LTR framework significantly improves both accuracy and interpretability compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs. To our knowledge, this is the first work to implement a language-centric logical tree to guide MLLM reasoning in VideoQA, paving the way for language-centric video understanding from perception to cognition.

paragraphs: Answering a complex question about a video can require several connected observations and reasoning steps. Existing multimodal language models can make that process difficult to inspect or control. Language-centric Tree Reasoning, or LTR, introduces an explicit question decomposition that organizes the route from simple observations to a final answer.

The first stage works through language, recursively breaking the original question into a logical tree of simpler questions. A retrieval-augmented few-shot approach helps plan that tree until complex cognitive questions have been reduced to perceptual ones. The second stage uses video content to answer and combine these components, reasoning upward through the tree toward the original question.

The output includes both the answer and a traceable reasoning path. Across 11 VideoQA benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements in accuracy and interpretability compared with state-of-the-art multimodal language models. The framework’s contribution is making decomposition and evidence-based recombination explicit, giving existing models a structured way to connect what they perceive in a video with the reasoning a question requires.
summary.tldr: LTR improves video question answering by decomposing questions into a logical tree and resolving it from video evidence.

title: Divide and Conquer: Exploring Language-centric Tree Reasoning for Video Question-Answering

abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods are effective reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, particularly for continuous problems. While they optimize stochastic (hyper)policies via action- or parameter-space exploration, real-world applications often require deterministic policies. Existing PG convergence guarantees to deterministic policies assume a fixed stochasticity in the (hyper)policy, tuned according to the desired final suboptimality, whereas practitioners commonly use a dynamic stochasticity level. This work provides the theoretical foundations for this practice. We introduce PES, a phase-based method that reduces stochasticity via a deterministic schedule while running PG subroutines with fixed stochasticity in each phase. Under gradient domination assumptions, PES achieves last-iterate convergence to the optimal deterministic policy with a sample complexity of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-5})$. Additionally, we analyze the common practice, termed SL-PG, of jointly learning stochasticity (via an appropriate parameterization) and (hyper)policy parameters. We show that SL-PG also ensures last-iterate convergence with a rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3})$, but to the optimal stochastic (hyper)policy only, requiring stronger assumptions compared to PES.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods explore by introducing randomness into actions or policy parameters, yet deployment often calls for a deterministic policy. Existing convergence guarantees typically keep this randomness fixed at a level chosen for the desired final accuracy. This paper analyzes approaches that change stochasticity during training, as practitioners commonly do.

The first method, PES, divides learning into phases. Each phase runs policy gradient with fixed stochasticity, and a deterministic schedule reduces that stochasticity between phases. Under gradient domination assumptions, the authors prove convergence of the final iterate to an optimal deterministic policy. The paper also studies SL-PG, which jointly learns policy parameters and stochasticity through an appropriate parameterization. Under stronger assumptions, it achieves last-iterate convergence at a rate of approximately epsilon to the power minus three. Its guarantee concerns an optimal stochastic policy or hyperpolicy, however. The two results establish different trade-offs: PES targets deterministic optimality, while the stronger-assumption SL-PG analysis guarantees stochastic optimality.
summary.tldr: The paper proves distinct convergence guarantees for scheduled stochasticity reduction and jointly learned stochasticity in policy gradient methods.

title: Convergence Analysis of Policy Gradient Methods with Dynamic Stochasticity

abstract: We investigate an emerging setup in which a small, on-device language model (LM) with access to local data collaborates with a frontier, cloud-hosted LM to solve real-world tasks involving financial, medical, and scientific reasoning over long documents. Can a local-remote collaboration reduce cloud inference costs while preserving quality? First, we consider a naïve collaboration protocol, coined MINION, where the local and remote models simply chat back and forth. Because only the local model ingests the full context, this protocol reduces cloud costs by 30.4x, but recovers only 87% of the performance of the frontier model. We identify two key limitations of this protocol: the local model struggles to (1) follow the remote model’s multi-step instructions and (2) reason over long contexts. Motivated by these observations, we propose MINIONS, a protocol in which the remote model decomposes the task into easier subtasks over shorter chunks of the document, that are executed locally in parallel. MINIONS reduces costs by 5.7$\times$ on average while recovering 97.9% of the remote-only performance. Our analysis reveals several key design choices that influence the trade-off between cost and performance in local-remote systems.

title: Cost-efficient Collaboration between On-device and Cloud Language Models

abstract: Structure-Based Drug Design (SBDD) is crucial for identifying bioactive molecules. Recent deep generative models are faced with challenges in geometric structure modeling. A major bottleneck lies in the twisted probability path of multi-modalities—continuous 3D positions and discrete 2D topologies—which jointly determine molecular geometries. By establishing the fact that noise schedules decide the Variational Lower Bound (VLB) for the twisted probability path, we propose VLB-Optimal Scheduling (VOS) strategy in this under-explored area, which optimizes VLB as a path integral for SBDD. Our model effectively enhances molecular geometries and interaction modeling, achieving state-of-the-art PoseBusters passing rate of 95.9% on CrossDock, more than 10% improvement upon strong baselines, while maintaining high affinities and robust intramolecular validity evaluated on held-out test set. Code is available at https://github.com/AlgoMole/MolCRAFT.

paragraphs: Generating molecules for a protein target requires coordinating continuous three-dimensional positions with discrete molecular topology. These two forms of information jointly determine molecular geometry, but their probability paths can be difficult to coordinate during generation. This paper identifies the noise schedules governing those paths as an important design choice.

The authors establish that the schedules determine the variational lower bound associated with this coupled probability path. They then introduce VLB-Optimal Scheduling, which optimizes that bound as an integral along the path. The method makes the evolution of the different modalities part of the optimization, with the goal of improving both molecular geometry and interaction modeling.

On CrossDock, the model achieves a reported state-of-the-art PoseBusters passing rate of 95.9%, improving by more than 10% over strong baselines. The authors also report maintained high affinities and robust intramolecular validity on a held-out test set. These findings connect a change in generative scheduling to better geometric outcomes while retaining other evaluated qualities relevant to structure-based molecular design.
summary.tldr: VLB-Optimal Scheduling coordinates molecular generation modalities and achieves a 95.9% PoseBusters passing rate on CrossDock.

title: Piloting Structure-Based Drug Design via Modality-Specific Optimal Schedule

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values is essential for their safe deployment and widespread adoption. Current LLM safety benchmarks often focus solely on the refusal of individual problematic queries, which overlooks the importance of the context where the query occurs and may cause undesired refusal of queries under safe contexts that diminish user experience. Addressing this gap, we introduce CASE-Bench, a Context-Aware SafEty Benchmark that integrates context into safety assessments of LLMs. CASE-Bench assigns distinct, formally described contexts to categorized queries based on Contextual Integrity theory. Additionally, in contrast to previous studies which mainly rely on majority voting from just a few annotators, we recruited a sufficient number of annotators necessary to ensure the detection of statistically significant differences among the experimental conditions based on power analysis. Our extensive analysis using CASE-Bench on various open-source and commercial LLMs reveals a substantial and significant influence of context on human judgments ($p<$0.0001 from a z-test), underscoring the necessity of context in safety evaluations. We also identify notable mismatches between human judgments and LLM responses, particularly in commercial models within safe contexts. Code and data used in the paper are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CASEBench-D5DB.

paragraphs: A request can receive different safety judgments depending on the circumstances in which it appears. CASE-Bench addresses safety evaluations that focus on whether a model refuses isolated problematic queries. Such evaluations can overlook situations in which responding would be acceptable, making unnecessary refusals difficult to distinguish from appropriate caution.

The benchmark pairs categorized queries with distinct, formally described contexts grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. It also uses power analysis to determine the number of human annotators needed to detect statistically significant differences between experimental conditions. This makes the evaluation sensitive both to the surrounding circumstances and to whether observed differences in human judgments have statistical support.

Tests involving open-source and commercial models find a substantial influence of context on human judgments, with a z-test reporting p < 0.0001. The authors also find mismatches between those judgments and model responses, particularly for commercial models in safe contexts. These findings support evaluating context-sensitive decisions alongside refusal behavior when assessing model safety.
summary.tldr: CASE-Bench shows that context substantially affects human safety judgments and exposes mismatches with language-model responses.

title: CASE-Bench: Context-Aware SafEty Benchmark for Large Language Models

abstract: A key challenge in personalized healthcare is identifying optimal intervention sequences to guide temporal systems toward target outcomes, a novel problem we formalize as counterfactual target achievement. In addressing this problem, directly adopting counterfactual estimation methods face compounding errors due to the unobservability of counterfactuals. To overcome this, we propose Variational Counterfactual Intervention Planning (VCIP), which reformulates the problem by modeling the conditional likelihood of achieving target outcomes, implemented through variational inference. By leveraging the g-formula to bridge the gap between interventional and observational log-likelihoods, VCIP enables reliable training from observational data. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that VCIP significantly outperforms existing methods in target achievement accuracy.

paragraphs: Planning a sequence of interventions requires deciding how to guide a changing system toward a desired outcome. This paper formalizes that problem as counterfactual target achievement, motivated by personalized healthcare. It highlights a difficulty with directly using counterfactual prediction methods: errors can compound across a sequence because the alternative outcomes being considered are not observed.

Variational Counterfactual Intervention Planning, or VCIP, changes the modeling objective to the conditional likelihood of reaching the target outcome. It implements this formulation through variational inference. The method also uses the g-formula to connect interventional and observational log-likelihoods, providing the basis for training the planner from observational data.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significantly higher target-achievement accuracy than existing methods. The result supports organizing the learning problem around whether an intervention sequence reaches its goal. This focus is directly aligned with the planning task described in the paper: the desired output is a sequence that guides the system toward a target, and the reported evaluation measures success at achieving that target.
summary.tldr: VCIP learns intervention plans from observational data by modeling the likelihood of reaching a target outcome through variational inference.

title: Variational Counterfactual Intervention Planning to Achieve Target Outcomes

abstract: Recent progress in imitation learning has been enabled by policy architectures that scale to complex visuomotor tasks, multimodal distributions, and large datasets. However, these methods often rely on learning from large amount of expert demonstrations. To address these shortcomings, we propose Latent Diffusion Planning (LDP), a modular approach consisting of a planner which can leverage action-free demonstrations, and an inverse dynamics model which can leverage suboptimal data, that both operate over a learned latent space. First, we learn a compact latent space through a variational autoencoder, enabling effective forecasting of future states in image-based domains. Then, we train a planner and an inverse dynamics model with diffusion objectives. By separating planning from action prediction, LDP can benefit from the denser supervision signals of suboptimal and action-free data. On simulated visual robotic manipulation tasks, LDP outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning approaches, as they cannot leverage such additional data.

paragraphs: Latent Diffusion Planning addresses imitation learning’s dependence on large collections of expert demonstrations. It divides the task into planning future states and predicting the actions needed to move between states. This separation lets the two components learn from different kinds of data, including demonstrations without action labels and behavior that is not optimal.

The system first learns a compact representation of image observations using a variational autoencoder. A planner then forecasts future states in this latent space, while an inverse dynamics model predicts actions. Both components are trained with diffusion objectives. The planner can use action-free demonstrations, and the inverse dynamics model can benefit from suboptimal data.

This modular design extracts supervision from data that the compared imitation-learning approaches cannot exploit. In simulated visual robot-manipulation tasks, LDP outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives under that data advantage. The result supports separating planning from action prediction when additional observations or imperfect behavior are available, expanding the useful training material beyond complete expert demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Latent Diffusion Planning separates planning from action prediction so imitation learning can use action-free demonstrations and suboptimal data.

title: Latent Diffusion Planning for Imitation Learning

abstract: Substantial quantity and high quality are the golden rules of making a good training dataset with sample privacy protection equally important. Generating synthetic samples that resemble high-quality private data while ensuring Differential Privacy (DP), a formal privacy guarantee, promises scalability and practicality. However, existing methods relying on pre-trained models for data synthesis often struggle in data-deficient scenarios, suffering from limited sample size, inevitable generation noise and existing pre-trained model bias. To address these challenges, we propose a novel contrAstive private data Synthesis via Weighted multiple Pre-trained generative models framework, named as WASP. WASP utilizes limited private samples for more accurate private data distribution estimation via a Top-Q voting mechanism, and leverages low-quality synthetic samples for contrastive generation via collaboration among dynamically weighted multiple pre-trained models. Extensive experiments on 6 well-developed datasets with 6 open-source and 3 closed-source PLMs demonstrate the superiority of WASP in improving model performance over diverse downstream tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/LindaLydia/WASP.

paragraphs: WASP addresses synthetic training-data generation when only a small amount of private data is available. The goal is to produce useful samples resembling that private data within a differential-privacy setting. Limited examples make this difficult because the generator must contend with an uncertain picture of the desired data, generation noise, and biases already present in pretrained models.

The framework combines two mechanisms. A Top-Q voting procedure uses the available private samples to estimate their distribution more accurately. A contrastive generation process then uses low-quality synthetic samples as informative material, while multiple pretrained generative models collaborate with dynamically adjusted weights. This makes both model diversity and unsuccessful synthetic examples part of the generation strategy.

The authors evaluate WASP on six datasets using six open-source and three closed-source pretrained models. They report improved model performance across varied downstream tasks. These findings support the usefulness of combining private-data estimation with weighted multi-model generation, particularly for the data-deficient setting that motivates the method.
summary.tldr: WASP combines private-data voting, contrastive generation, and dynamically weighted pretrained models to improve synthetic training data when private examples are scarce.

title: Contrastive Private Data Synthesis via Weighted Multi-PLM Fusion

abstract: We introduce MedXpertQA, a highly challenging and comprehensive benchmark to evaluate expert-level medical knowledge and advanced reasoning. MedXpertQA includes 4,460 questions spanning 17 specialties and 11 body systems. It includes two subsets, Text for text evaluation and MM for multimodal evaluation. Notably, MM introduces expert-level exam questions with diverse images and rich clinical information, including patient records and examination results, setting it apart from traditional medical multimodal benchmarks with simple QA pairs generated from image captions. MedXpertQA applies rigorous filtering and augmentation to address the insufficient difficulty of existing benchmarks like MedQA, and incorporates specialty board questions to improve clinical relevance and comprehensiveness. We perform data synthesis to mitigate data leakage risk and conduct multiple rounds of expert reviews to ensure accuracy and reliability. We evaluate 18 leading models on MedXpertQA. Moreover, medicine is deeply connected to real-world decision-making, providing a rich and representative setting for assessing reasoning abilities beyond mathematics and code. To this end, we develop a reasoning-oriented subset to facilitate the assessment of o1-like models.

paragraphs: MedXpertQA is a benchmark designed to test demanding medical knowledge and advanced reasoning. It contains 4,460 questions covering 17 specialties and 11 body systems, organized into text-only and multimodal subsets. Its purpose is to provide a more challenging and clinically relevant evaluation than existing benchmarks whose questions may be insufficiently difficult.

The multimodal subset combines expert-level exam questions with varied images and substantial clinical context, including patient records and examination results. This gives the evaluation richer material than simple question-answer pairs derived from image captions. The construction process also uses filtering, augmentation, specialty board questions, data synthesis to reduce leakage risk, and repeated expert review.

The authors evaluate 18 leading models and create a reasoning-oriented subset for assessing models with capabilities like those targeted by o1. Their broader motivation is that medicine provides a setting for reasoning connected to real-world decisions, extending evaluation beyond mathematics and programming. The contribution is the benchmark and its evaluation design; the supplied abstract does not identify a winning model.
summary.tldr: MedXpertQA provides 4,460 expert-level medical questions, including rich multimodal cases, to evaluate knowledge and advanced reasoning.

title: MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding

abstract: High-stakes decision making involves reasoning under uncertainty about the future. In this work, we train language models to make predictions on open-ended forecasting questions. To scale up training data, we synthesize novel forecasting questions from global events reported in daily news. While directly training on this data leads to performance drops, carefully curating questions creates a valuable training resource. We use the resulting dataset, OpenForesight, to post-train Qwen3 thinking models. To prevent leakage of future information during training and evaluation, we use an offline news corpus, both for data generation and retrieval in our forecasting system. Guided by a small validation set, we show the benefits of retrieval, and an improved reward function for reinforcement learning (RL). Once we obtain our final forecasting system, we perform held-out testing between May to August 2025. Our specialized model, OpenForecaster-8B, matches much larger proprietary models, with our training improving the accuracy, calibration, and consistency of predictions. We find calibration improvements from forecasting training generalize across popular benchmarks. We will open-source our models, code, and data to make LLM based forecasting research broadly accessible.

paragraphs: This paper trains language models to answer open-ended questions about future events. To obtain training examples at scale, the authors generate forecasting questions from daily global news. A central finding is that directly using the generated data hurts performance, whereas carefully selecting questions produces the useful OpenForesight training dataset.

The authors use this dataset to post-train Qwen3 thinking models. Both question generation and information retrieval rely on an offline news collection to prevent future information from leaking into training or evaluation. In held-out testing, OpenForecaster-8B matches much larger proprietary models. The reported training gains cover accuracy, calibration, and consistency: predictions improve, confidence better reflects correctness, and answers become more consistent. Calibration gains also transfer across popular benchmarks. The results support a recipe in which careful question selection, controlled information access, and forecasting-specific training jointly improve performance.
summary.tldr: Curated news-derived questions and forecasting-specific training produce an 8B model that matches much larger proprietary forecasters in held-out testing.

title: Curating the Future: A Scalable Recipe for Training Open-Ended Forecasters

abstract: Supervised Causal Learning has shown promise in causal discovery, yet it often struggles with generalization across diverse interventional settings, particularly when intervention targets are unknown. To address this, we propose TICL (Test-time Interventional Causal Learning), a novel method that synergizes Test-Time Training with Joint Causal Inference (JCI). Specifically, we design a self-augmentation strategy to generate instance-specific training data at test time, effectively avoiding distribution shifts. Furthermore, by integrating JCI, we developed a PC-inspired two-phase supervised learning scheme, which effectively leverages self-augmented data while ensuring theoretical identifiability. Extensive experiments on bnlearn benchmarks demonstrate TICL’s superiority in multiple aspects of causal discovery and intervention target detection.

Specifically, we design a self-augmentation strategy to generate instance-specific training data at test time, effectively avoiding distribution shifts. Furthermore, by integrating JCI, we developed a PC-inspired two-phase supervised learning scheme, which effectively leverages self-augmented data while ensuring theoretical identifiability. paragraphs: TICL studies causal discovery from interventional data, including settings where the variables targeted by interventions are unknown. Supervised causal learners can struggle to generalize when the intervention setting changes. The method responds by adapting its learning process to the specific instance encountered at test time.

A self-augmentation strategy generates instance-specific training data during testing, addressing the distribution mismatch that motivates the work. TICL combines this adaptation with Joint Causal Inference in a two-phase supervised learning scheme inspired by the PC algorithm. The design uses the augmented data to learn causal structure while providing a theoretical identifiability result.

The contribution brings together adaptation to the current dataset and a causal-inference formulation for reasoning about interventions. Experiments on bnlearn benchmarks report superior performance across multiple aspects of causal discovery and intervention-target detection. These are related but distinct outputs: recovering causal relationships concerns how variables influence one another, while target detection concerns which variables were directly affected by interventions. The reported results support learning both within the proposed framework.
summary.tldr: TICL combines test-time self-augmentation with Joint Causal Inference to learn causal structure and identify intervention targets.

title: Test-Time Learning of Causal Structure from Interventional Data

abstract: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

paragraphs: Soil microorganisms help determine how organic matter and carbon move through soil systems. Process-based models need parameters describing microbial activity, but these are difficult to infer from observations. This paper connects DNA-derived functional traits to those parameters, addressing the difficult relationship between microbial genomes and the processes the organisms drive.

The hybrid framework uses a neural network to predict biokinetic parameters for a process-based organic matter turnover model. Genomic traits inferred from metagenomic sequencing provide the inputs. summary.tldr: A constrained neural network maps microbial genomic traits to soil-model parameters, improving reported predictions even with small datasets.

title: Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems

abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) motility assessment via bowel sounds (BS) offers a non-invasive alternative to resource-intensive clinical standards. However, the diagnostic utility of BS is often compromised by its spectral overlap with non-stationary speech interference. While generative models have advanced signal restoration, traditional Gaussian-based diffusion frameworks struggle with the impulsive, heavy-tailed nature of real-world clinical noise. In this paper, we propose a novel Cauchy-driven Diffusion Bridge framework to isolate high-fidelity bowel sounds from complex interference. Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We introduce ClinBS, a large-scale clinical dataset (over 25 hours) containing rare pathological transients verified by experts; (2) We mathematically formulate a Cauchy bridge driver, deriving closed-form expressions for the score and density to better model heavy-tailed perturbations; and (3) We implement an efficient sampling procedure via Gaussian scale-mixture reparameterization. Extensive experiments show our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming baselines by 13.4%–49.8% across core metrics and elevating abnormal BS recognition accuracy to 88.01%. These results demonstrate the system’s potential for robust clinical GI monitoring and diagnosis.

paragraphs: Bowel sounds offer a non-invasive way to assess gastrointestinal movement, but speech interference can overlap with their frequencies. Clinical noise can also contain abrupt, unusually large disturbances that Gaussian-based diffusion methods struggle to model. This paper develops a Cauchy-driven diffusion bridge to recover bowel sounds from such interference.

The authors introduce ClinBS, a clinical dataset containing more than 25 hours of recordings and expert-verified rare pathological transients. Their mathematical formulation uses a Cauchy driver to better represent heavy-tailed noise and derives closed-form density and score expressions. An efficient sampling procedure represents the noise through a Gaussian scale mixture, making the proposed restoration process practical to execute.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results, with improvements of 13.4%–49.8% over baselines across the core metrics and abnormal bowel-sound recognition accuracy reaching 88.01%. These findings connect better noise modeling with both signal restoration and recognition of abnormal sounds. They support the system's potential for gastrointestinal monitoring and diagnosis, as stated by the authors.
summary.tldr: A Cauchy-driven diffusion bridge restores bowel sounds amid heavy-tailed interference and improves abnormal-sound recognition.

title: Listening Through the Noise: Cauchy-Driven Diffusion Bridges for Robust Gastrointestinal Auscultation and Clinical Benchmarking

abstract: How can we distinguish whether a peer review was written by a human or generated by an AI model? We argue that, in this setting, authorship should not be attributed solely from the textual features of a review, but also from the ideas, judgments, and claims it expresses. To this end, we propose Sem-Detect, an authorship detection method for peer reviews that operationalizes this principle by combining textual features with claim-level semantic analysis. Sem-Detect compares a target review against multiple AI-generated reviews of the same paper, leveraging the observation that different AI models tend to converge on similar points, while human reviewers introduce more unique and diverse ones. As a result, Sem-Detect is able to distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from authentic human-written ones, including those that have been refined using an LLM but still reflect human judgment. Across a dataset of over 20,000 peer reviews from ICLR and NeurIPS conferences, Sem-Detect improves over the strongest prior detector by 36.5% in TPR@1% FPR in the binary setting. More importantly, in the three-class scenario, we empirically show that LLM refinement preserves the semantic signals of human reviews, which remain distinct from the patterns exhibited by fully AI-generated text; as a result, fewer than 3.5% of LLM-refined human reviews are misclassified as AI-generated.

paragraphs: Detecting AI-written peer reviews becomes more complicated when human reviewers use a language model to refine their prose. Sem-Detect examines the ideas and judgments in a review alongside textual features. Its aim is to distinguish fully generated reviews from reviews that still express human judgment despite language-model editing.

The method compares a target review with multiple AI-generated reviews of the same paper. It builds on the observation that different AI models tend to raise similar points, whereas human reviewers contribute more varied and distinctive claims. Claim-level semantic analysis therefore adds evidence about the review's intellectual content beyond its writing style.

In a three-class evaluation, fewer than 3.5% of LLM-refined human reviews are classified as AI-generated. The results provide empirical evidence that human semantic signals can survive language-model refinement and remain useful for detection.
summary.tldr: Sem-Detect combines writing features with claim-level comparisons to distinguish AI-generated reviews from human reviews, including LLM-refined ones.

title: Sem-Detect: Semantic Level Detection of AI Generated Peer-Reviews

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) spend substantial test-time compute on long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, but what characterizes an effective CoT remains unclear. While prior work reports gains from lengthening CoTs and increasing review via appended wait tokens, recent studies suggest that shorter thinking can outperform longer traces. We therefore conduct a systematic evaluation across ten LRMs on math and scientific reasoning. Contrary to the “longer-is-better” narrative, we find that both naively using longer CoTs and more review behaviors are associated with lower accuracy. As CoT unfolds step by step, token-level metrics can conflate verbosity with process quality. We introduce a graph view of CoT to extract structure and identify a single statistic—the Failed-Step Fraction (FSF), the fraction of steps in abandoned branches—that consistently outpredicts length and review ratio for correctness across models. To probe causality, we design two interventions. First, we rank candidate CoTs by each metric at test time, where FSF yields the largest pass@1 gains; second, we edit CoTs to remove failed branches, which significantly improves accuracy, indicating that failed branches bias subsequent reasoning. Taken together, these results characterize effective CoTs as those that fail less and support structure-aware test-time scaling over indiscriminately generating long CoTs.

As CoT unfolds step by step, token-level metrics can conflate verbosity with process quality. First, we rank candidate CoTs by each metric at test time, where FSF yields the largest pass@1 gains; second, we edit CoTs to remove failed branches, which significantly improves accuracy, indicating that failed branches bias subsequent reasoning. paragraphs: Long reasoning traces consume substantial computation, but length alone may say little about whether the reasoning is productive. This paper evaluates ten reasoning models on mathematical and scientific tasks. It finds that naively longer traces and more review behavior are associated with lower accuracy in the studied settings.

The authors represent reasoning as a graph and measure the Failed-Step Fraction: the share of steps belonging to branches that are later abandoned. This statistic predicts correctness more consistently than trace length or review ratio across models. It distinguishes structural failure within the reasoning process from the amount of text produced.

Two interventions probe whether this structure is practically useful. Ranking candidate traces by Failed-Step Fraction produces the largest gains in first-answer success among the compared metrics. Editing traces to remove failed branches also significantly improves accuracy, supporting the interpretation that abandoned paths can bias later reasoning. These results favor structure-aware allocation of reasoning computation. They do not establish that shorter reasoning is always better; the initial length finding is an association.
summary.tldr: The fraction of reasoning spent on abandoned branches predicts correctness better than length or review frequency and guides interventions that improve accuracy.

abstract: The rapidly increasing realism of AI-generated media has intensified the spread of deceptive content and undermined public trust. Existing research largely treats this challenge along two separate axes: media authenticity, which assesses whether content is real or machine-generated, and content veracity, which evaluates semantic consistency and factual correctness. This separation overlooks how real-world deception jointly exploits both dimensions. In this work, we present FakeWorld 1.0, an omni-modal benchmark that unifies media authenticity and content veracity within a single evaluation framework. Along the media axis, FakeWorld spans text, audio, image, and video synthesis. Along the content axis, it systematically instantiates cross-modal semantic inconsistencies and factual errors. These two axes are jointly embedded in realistic web-based and streaming-style presentation scenarios, reflecting how multimodal deception is composed, contextualized, and delivered in practice. FakeWorld further provides explainable annotations in the form of per-instance rationales, enabling transparent and evidence-based analysis. Under a unified evaluation protocol, experiments on both open- and closed-source multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reveal fundamental capability limits and demonstrate FakeWorld’s effectiveness in exposing high-fidelity, mixed-source deception. Beyond the benchmark, we introduce OmniChecker, an agentic framwork that performs joint, explainable detection across both axes and produces evidence-backed diagnostic reports. We position FakeWorld 1.0 as a realistic stress test and a practical foundation for advancing scalable, explainable detection of fake multimodal content.

Its evaluation covers media authenticity alongside factual correctness and consistency between different types of content.

It pairs this coverage with factual errors and semantic mismatches across modalities, presenting examples in web-based and streaming-style settings. These settings preserve the surrounding context in which deception is encountered. Each example also includes an explanatory rationale, supporting analysis of why a particular item should be judged deceptive.

Tests of open- and closed-source multimodal language models reveal capability limits in detecting realistic deception that combines different sources and media types. The paper also introduces OmniChecker, an agentic framework that jointly assesses both dimensions and produces diagnostic reports backed by evidence. Together, the benchmark and framework make explanations part of evaluating deception, rather than reducing the task to a single unexplained label.

title: FakeWorld 1.0: An Omni-modal Benchmark for Fake Media and Content

abstract: Speculative Decodin promises to accelerate Large Language Model inference, yet its efficacy often degrades in production-grade scenarios. Existing evaluations typically overlook the compute-bound nature of high-concurrency regimes, where verification compute becomes the dominant bottleneck. Consequently, prior methods face a dilemma: static trees incur massive verification waste, while dynamic trees suffer from cumulative misjudgments and kernel incompatibility. To bridge this gap, we introduce ECHO, a high concurrency-oriented framework integrated into SGLang that reformulates speculative execution as a budgeted scheduling problem. Crucially, ECHO employs sparse confidence gating to manage the batch as a unified super-tree, elastically pivoting budget between depth and width to co-optimize the trade-off between reducing global verification steps and maximizing per-step efficiency. Extensive evaluations across diverse model scales—particularly the industrial-grade Qwen3-235B—demonstrate that ECHO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both low-load and high-load scenarios, achieving up to 5.35$\times$ walltime speedup and delivering over 20% relative speedup gain against the strongest baselines.

paragraphs: ECHO addresses speculative decoding when many language-model requests run concurrently. In this setting, checking speculative candidates can become the main computational bottleneck. The paper argues that fixed candidate trees waste verification work, while dynamically constructed trees can accumulate poor decisions and encounter incompatibilities with computational kernels.

Integrated into SGLang, ECHO treats speculative execution as a scheduling problem with a limited budget. It combines the batch into a unified candidate tree and uses sparse confidence gating to allocate that budget. Allocation can shift between deeper speculation and wider branching, balancing fewer overall verification steps against the efficiency of each step.

Evaluations cover different model scales, including Qwen3-235B, and both low-load and high-load serving conditions. ECHO consistently outperforms the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines, with up to 5.35-fold walltime speedup and more than 20% relative speedup gain against the strongest baselines. These findings support allocating speculation jointly across a batch when verification cost constrains serving throughput, rather than evaluating speculative choices only in isolation.
summary.tldr: ECHO dynamically budgets speculative decoding across a batch to reduce verification waste and improve serving speed under concurrent workloads.

title: ECHO: Elastic Speculative Decoding with Sparse Gating for High-Concurrency Scenarios

abstract: Textual Gradient-style optimizers (TextGrad) enable gradient-like feedback propagation through compound AI systems. However, they do not work well for deep chains. The root cause of this limitation stems from the Semantic Entanglement problem in these extended workflows. In standard textual backpropagation, feedback signals mix local critiques with upstream contexts, leading to Attribution Ambiguity. To address this challenge, we propose TextResNet, a framework that reformulates the optimization process to achieve precise signal routing via four key innovations. Firstly, in the forward pass, it enforces Additive Semantic Deltas to preserve an Identity Highway for gradient flow. Secondly, in the backward pass, it introduces Semantic Gradient Decomposition via a Semantic Projector to disentangle feedback into causally independent subspaces. Thirdly, it implements Causal Routing, which routes projected signals to their specific components. Finally, it performs Density-Aware Optimization Scheduling to leverage the disentangled signals to dynamically allocate resources to key system bottlenecks. Our results show that TextResNet not only achieves superior performance compared to TextGrad, but also exhibits remarkable stability for agentic tasks in compound AI systems where baselines collapse. Code is available at https://github.com/JeanDiable/TextResNet.

paragraphs: Compound AI systems can improve their components using textual critiques passed backward through a workflow. In deep chains, however, local criticism becomes mixed with context from other stages. The paper calls this semantic entanglement: feedback becomes difficult to attribute to the component that should actually change.

TextResNet restructures both forward computation and backward feedback. Forward steps express changes as additive semantic deltas, preserving an identity path through the workflow. During the backward pass, a semantic projector decomposes feedback into causally independent subspaces. Causal routing sends the resulting signals to their specific components, giving the optimization process more targeted instructions.

The framework also schedules optimization according to signal density, dynamically assigning resources to key bottlenecks. The authors report better performance than TextGrad and strong stability on agentic tasks where baseline systems collapse. The result connects reliable optimization of long workflows to clearer attribution: components receive feedback aimed at their own contribution, and optimization effort follows the identified bottlenecks.
summary.tldr: TextResNet decomposes and routes textual feedback to improve optimization performance and stability in deep compound AI workflows.

title: TextResNet: Decoupling and Routing Optimization Signals in Compound AI Systems via Deep Residual Tuning

abstract: Elucidating molecular structures from spectra is a foundational problem in chemical and materials characterization, yet remains challenging due to spectral ambiguity and the vast molecular space. Although recent diffusion-based generators show strong promise for spectra-conditioned elucidation, existing methods struggle to learn robust spectra-structure relationships from limited paired data when relying solely on global spectral representation. Moreover, the repeated full sampling inference strategy incurs substantial computation overhead. To address these limitations, we propose MAST, a Motif-Augmented diffusion framework with Search Tree, for joint 2D-3D spectroscopic molecular structure elucidation. MAST introduces explicit, interpretable motif priors as intermediate evidences throughout denoising, reducing conditional ambiguity and facilitating spectra-conditioned optimization. We further cast diffusion sampling as reward-guided tree search to prioritize high-reward denoising trajectories, yielding a compact set of spectra-consistent candidates under limited budgets. On the QM9S multi-spectra benchmark, MAST achieves 94.89% exact recovery and improves 3D fidelity, while preserving high chemical validity and stability. Code is available at https://github.com/Jia040223/MAST.

paragraphs: MAST tackles the reconstruction of molecular structures from spectra, where ambiguous measurements and a vast space of possible molecules make inference difficult. The paper identifies two problems with existing diffusion approaches: global spectral representations can be difficult to learn from limited paired data, and repeatedly performing full sampling runs is computationally costly.

The framework introduces explicit molecular motif priors as interpretable intermediate evidence throughout denoising. These structural clues reduce ambiguity and help guide optimization toward molecules consistent with the spectra. MAST also turns sampling into reward-guided tree search, prioritizing promising denoising trajectories to produce a compact set of candidates within a limited computational budget.

MAST jointly addresses two-dimensional molecular structure and three-dimensional geometry. On the QM9S multi-spectra benchmark, it achieves 94.89% exact recovery and improves 3D fidelity while preserving high chemical validity and stability. The findings support combining intermediate structural evidence with selective search: the model receives more informative guidance, and inference concentrates computation on promising candidate-generation paths.
summary.tldr: MAST combines interpretable motif guidance with reward-guided diffusion search to recover molecular structures from spectra efficiently.

title: MAST: Motif-Augmented Diffusion with Search Tree for Spectroscopic Molecular Structure Elucidation

abstract: Compositional generalization is essential for reaching unseen goals under novel contextual variations in offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL), where a generalist goal-reaching agent must be learned from limited data. Most prior approaches pursue this via trajectory stitching over temporally contiguous segments, which limits composing behaviors across varying contexts. To overcome this limitation, we formalize analogy transduction as synthesizing new plans by composing task-endogenous analogies with given contexts and propose a novel analogy representation tailored for it. Grounded in our theory, this analogy representation captures what changes under optimal task execution, remains invariant to contextual variations, and is sufficient for optimal goal reaching. We further contend that generalization to unseen analogy-context pairs is a practical obstacle in analogy transduction, and introduce a new approach for offline GCRL that enables analogy transduction beyond seen pairs to unseen combinations. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on OGBench manipulation environments, substantially outperforming prior methods that do not perform analogy transduction.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn goal-reaching behavior from a fixed collection of experience. Reaching unfamiliar goals in changed contexts requires recombining what that experience teaches. Existing approaches often stitch together temporally contiguous trajectory segments, which can restrict their ability to compose behavior across different contexts.

This paper formalizes analogy transduction: constructing a new plan by combining a task-related analogy with a given context. Its proposed representation captures the changes associated with optimal task execution while remaining invariant to contextual differences. Within the authors’ theoretical framework, that representation is sufficient for optimal goal reaching, providing a basis for transferring task changes across contexts.

The method also addresses the practical difficulty of combining analogies and contexts that were never observed together. Experiments in OGBench manipulation environments show substantial gains over prior methods that do not perform analogy transduction. The results support learning transferable descriptions of task change as a route to composing new behavior from limited offline data, beyond the combinations directly represented in training experience.
summary.tldr: The method combines context-invariant task analogies with new contexts to improve offline goal-reaching generalization.

title: Compositional Transduction with Latent Analogies for Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Score-based diffusion models have emerged as prominent deep generative models; however, their application to tabular data remains challenging because their backbones assume fully specified inputs, whereas real-world tabular data often contain missing values. We propose AugMask, a plug-and-play training framework that adapts missing-unaware backbones to incomplete data via stochastic regularization. AugMask 1) completes inputs via conditional stochastic augmentation using lightweight auxiliary models and 2) masks the loss, using augmented missing entries for conditioning while restricting supervision to observed coordinates. We connect AugMask to a Rao-Blackwellized objective and show that marginalizing missing entries yields a variance-weighted sensitivity penalty, promoting invariance of observed-coordinate reconstruction with respect to uncertain missing entries. Across diverse datasets and missingness regimes, AugMask enables standard diffusion-based tabular generators to match or outperform specialized missing-aware baselines in both sample fidelity and downstream utility. The code will be released.

paragraphs: Diffusion models for tables often expect every field in every training example to contain a value. Real datasets frequently violate that expectation. AugMask addresses this mismatch through a training framework that lets existing diffusion architectures learn from incomplete tables without requiring a backbone specifically designed to handle missing entries.

The framework uses lightweight auxiliary models to sample plausible values for missing fields, conditional on the available information. These sampled values complete the input and provide context, but the training loss supervises only fields that were actually observed. This distinction matters: an invented completion can help the model interpret a row without being treated as a known correct target.

The theoretical analysis connects this procedure to an objective that averages over missing values. That averaging introduces a penalty discouraging reconstructed observed fields from being overly sensitive to uncertain completions. Across the reported datasets and missingness settings, standard generators trained with AugMask match or exceed specialized alternatives in generated-data fidelity and downstream usefulness. The findings support stochastic completion and selective supervision as a practical combination for incomplete tables.
summary.tldr: AugMask trains standard tabular diffusion models on incomplete data by sampling missing inputs while supervising only observed values.

title: AugMask: Training Diffusion Models on Incomplete Tabular Data via Stochastic Augmentation and Masking

abstract: Training large language models for code generation often involves selecting data from verifiable multi-solution pools, where each problem admits multiple correct implementations. Conventional studies on data selection suggest that complex selection strategies, such as diversity maximization or difficulty ranking, should outperform naive random sampling. In this work, we systematically evaluate within-problem solution selection strategies across different representation spaces, including continuous embeddings, discrete tokens, and syntactic structures, using various base language models. Instead, simple random sampling achieves consistently competitive performance across all models, exhibiting greater cross-model stability than complex methods. We interpret these results through the lens of implicit knowledge consensus: verified solution pools may contain representative algorithmic patterns that random sampling can preserve. Our findings suggest that practitioners should treat random sampling as a low-cost default for verifiable code-generation fine-tuning and move to complex selectors when hard-tail or constraint-focused coverage is the target.

paragraphs: Code-generation training can draw from collections containing several verified correct implementations for each problem. Choosing which solutions to include introduces another design decision. This paper tests whether sophisticated selection methods, such as prioritizing diversity or difficulty, improve on randomly choosing solutions within each problem’s verified pool.

The comparison spans multiple base language models and selection methods based on continuous embeddings, token sequences, and syntactic structure. Random sampling remains consistently competitive across the models and shows greater stability across models than the more complex strategies. The result challenges the expectation that additional selection machinery will reliably produce better training data in this setting.

The authors interpret this through implicit knowledge consensus: verified solution pools may already contain representative algorithmic patterns that random selection preserves. This is a proposed explanation for the empirical finding. Their practical recommendation is to use random sampling as an inexpensive default, turning to specialized selectors when the objective specifically requires coverage of difficult cases or particular constraints.
summary.tldr: Randomly selecting verified code solutions is consistently competitive and more stable across models than the complex selectors studied.

title: Random Selection Reveals Implicit Knowledge Consensus in Code Generation

abstract: Effective DNA modeling demands the integration of complex patterns such as local motifs, long-range dependencies, and periodic signals. Yet, architectures like CNNs, Transformers, and SSMs are hindered by static or time-domain-exclusive designs, which limit their representational flexibility. To address this, we introduce the Synergistic Plasticity Unit (SPU), a scalable architecture that achieves multi-level plasticity through three synergistic layers. Specifically, SPU integrates a Locus Plasticity Layer (LPL) to capture fine-grained local motifs via token-specific convolution operations, while utilizing a Domain Plasticity Layer (DPL) to form multi-domain global features by concurrently modeling sequential (time) and spectral (frequency) patterns. Furthermore, it incorporates a Saliency Plasticity Layer (SPL) to optimize information flow through dual-axis saliency scoring. Supported by theoretical analysis, extensive empirical validation, and in-depth biological interpretation, this unified design enables SPU to achieve state-of-the-art performance with quasi-linear complexity, establishing a robust and principled paradigm for DNA modeling.

paragraphs: DNA sequences contain several kinds of structure at once: short local motifs, relationships between distant positions, and recurring patterns. The paper introduces the Synergistic Plasticity Unit, or SPU, to represent these patterns together. Its motivation is that static processing rules or an exclusive focus on sequence order can restrict how flexibly existing architectures capture DNA structure.

SPU combines three layers with distinct responsibilities. The Locus Plasticity Layer uses convolution operations tailored to individual tokens to capture local motifs. The Domain Plasticity Layer models sequence patterns alongside frequency patterns, bringing long-range and periodic information into global features. The Saliency Plasticity Layer then uses importance scores along two axes to regulate information flow through the model.

The contribution is the coordination of these mechanisms within one scalable architecture. The authors support the design with theoretical analysis, empirical evaluation, and biological interpretation, and report state-of-the-art performance with quasi-linear computational complexity. These findings suggest that adapting local processing, global representations, and information selection together can improve DNA modeling while keeping computational growth manageable.
summary.tldr: SPU combines adaptive local processing, sequence and frequency modeling, and saliency scoring to improve DNA modeling with quasi-linear complexity.

title: Adaptive DNA Sequence Modeling via Synergistic Plasticity Units

abstract: We introduce Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics (EPND), a geometric-mechanics framework that casts evolution-operator learning as Lie-group flows for long-horizon dynamical modeling. Unlike conventional operator-learning approaches that treat temporal propagation as an unconstrained black-box map, EPND places geometric mechanics at the core of its architecture, playing a role of the mathematical engine. This foundation enables a principled treatment of curvature, symmetry, and conservation, with the learned evolution expressed in geometric terms. Building on this foundation, we develop the Euler–Poincaré Parallel Scan, a parallel algorithm that leverages the associative algebra of Lie-group compositions to overcome the inefficiencies of sequential computation. By unifying geometric structure with scalable computation, EPND achieves high accuracy, strong stability, and significant parallel acceleration in modeling long-horizon dynamics in versatile scientific simulations.

paragraphs: Scientific simulation requires models to predict how a system evolves, often over long periods. Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics approaches this by learning evolution through Lie-group flows, a geometric description of structured transformations. Geometry becomes part of the model's architecture, shaping how it represents temporal change.

This formulation provides a principled way to handle curvature, symmetry, and conservation when learning an evolution operator. The intended advantage is that temporal propagation follows an explicitly geometric framework instead of being represented solely as an unconstrained input-output map. That connects the learned dynamics to mathematical structure relevant to scientific systems.

The paper also introduces an Euler–Poincaré Parallel Scan to make this formulation computationally scalable. It uses the associativity of Lie-group compositions, allowing transformations to be grouped for parallel computation rather than processed entirely in sequence. The authors report high accuracy, strong stability, and substantial parallel acceleration across scientific simulations of long-horizon dynamics. The contribution brings together a structured model of evolution and an algorithm that exploits the same structure to accelerate computation.
summary.tldr: Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics combines geometric evolution models with parallel computation for accurate, stable long-horizon simulation.

title: Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics: A Geometric-Mechanics Framework for Scientific Simulation

abstract: Adversarial examples pose serious threats to deep neural networks, exposing fundamental vulnerabilities in model robustness. However, most existing adversarial attacks directly manipulate dense and redundant feature representations, often leading to overfitting on surrogate models and poor black-box transferability. Recent SVD-based attack attempts to exploit low-rank feature subspaces, yet its reliance on single-layer optimization and single-gradient pathway neglects structural redundancy in feature representations and hierarchical heterogeneity across layers. To address these limitations, we propose LRS-Attack, a low-rank and sparse decomposition attack that explicitly models robust hierarchical subspaces in latent feature spaces. Specifically, the low-rank component captures dominant semantic directions, while the sparse component captures localized and discriminative patterns. To efficiently extract low-rank structure while preserving subspace fidelity, we develop a warm-started alternating low-rank approximation algorithm. Moreover, we introduce a hierarchical mixture of robust experts that leverages depth-dependent feature characteristics and guides gradient optimization toward more transferable adversarial directions. Extensive experiments on ImageNet show that LRS-Attack consistently improves black-box transferability over state-of-the-art methods across diverse CNN/ViT architectures and defense settings. Code is available at https://github.com/AdvML-Group/LRS-Attack.
