paragraphs: An adversarial example developed against one model may fail against another if its construction depends too strongly on the first model’s particular features. This paper attributes part of that transfer problem to optimizing dense, redundant representations. LRS-Attack instead organizes internal features into low-rank and sparse components across multiple network depths.

The low-rank component represents dominant semantic directions, while the sparse component represents localized, discriminative patterns. A warm-started alternating approximation algorithm extracts the low-rank structure efficiently while preserving its fidelity. The method also combines robust experts across layers, using differences in features at different depths to guide optimization toward adversarial directions that transfer more effectively.

ImageNet experiments report consistently improved black-box transferability over state-of-the-art methods across the evaluated convolutional networks, vision transformers, and defense settings. The result supports using both feature decomposition and information from multiple layers when studying transferable vulnerabilities. It also addresses two restrictions identified in earlier SVD-based attacks: relying on a single layer and following a single gradient pathway.
summary.tldr: LRS-Attack combines low-rank and sparse features across layers to improve adversarial transfer between the evaluated vision models.

title: Low-Rank and Sparsity Are All You Need: Exploring Robust Hierarchical Latent Subspaces for Transferable Adversarial Attack

abstract: Programmatic policies are often reported to generalize better than neural policies in reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks. We revisit some of these claims and show that much of the observed gap arises from uncontrolled experimental factors rather than intrinsic representational reasons. Re-evaluating three core benchmarks used in influential papers—TORCS, Karel, and Parking—we find that neural policies, when trained with a few modifications, such as sparse observations and cautious intrinsic reward functions, can match or exceed the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of programmatic policies. We argue that a representation enables OOD generalization if (i) the policy space it induces includes a generalizing policy and (ii) the search algorithm can find it. The neural and programmatic policies in prior work are comparable in OOD generalization because the domain-specific languages used induce policy spaces similar to those of neural networks, and our modifications help the gradient search find generalizing solutions. By disentangling representational factors from experimental confounds, we advance our understanding of what makes a representation succeed or fail at OOD generalization.

summary.tldr: Reevaluating three benchmarks shows that training choices explain much of programmatic policies’ reported generalization advantage over neural policies.

title: Revisiting OOD Generalization in Programmatic RL

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) achieve excellent accuracy when trained on large Density Functional Theory (DFT) data. To be useful in practice, they must often be adapted to target chemistries using small and expensive task-specific datasets. However, MLIPs transfer inconsistently across domains, with representations that often loose accessible composition and structure information. To address this, we present TriForces, a model-agnostic three-stream framework that separates composition and structure information, combined with self-supervised learning to preserve transferable representations. TriForces improves performance on MatBench and QM9 over baselines without needing DFT labels and enables efficient similar structure retrieval through its learned latent space. On OMat24, in limited-data training regime, TriForces reduces energy MAE by 57% at 20K samples only and improves force MAE across sample sizes. We release pretrained TriForces variants across multiple MLIP architectures with code at https:/github.com/Ramlaoui/triforces.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can be accurate when trained on large collections of density-functional-theory calculations, yet adapting them to new chemistry often requires scarce, expensive data. This paper connects inconsistent transfer to representations that lose readily accessible information about composition and structure. TriForces aims to preserve that information during representation learning.

The framework uses three streams, separating composition and structural information while incorporating self-supervised learning. It is designed to work with multiple underlying interatomic-potential architectures. Its learned representation also supports retrieving similar structures, so the representation is useful beyond the immediate prediction task.

TriForces improves performance over baselines on MatBench and QM9 without requiring DFT labels for those reported improvements. On OMat24 under limited-data training, it reduces energy mean absolute error by 57% at 20,000 samples and improves force error across sample sizes. The authors release pretrained variants for several architectures. These findings support explicitly preserving chemical composition and structural information as a route to more transferable atomistic representations.
summary.tldr: TriForces preserves composition and structure in atomistic representations, improving transfer and limited-data energy and force prediction.

title: TriForces: Augmenting Atomistic GNNs for Transferable Representations

abstract: Bayesian filtering is a well-known problem that aims to estimate plausible states of a dynamical system from observations. Among existing approaches to solve this problem, particle filters are theoretically exact for non-linear dynamics and observations, but suffer from poor scalability in high dimensions. In this work, we show that diffusion-based emulators of dynamical systems can be used to implement, without additional training, an optimal variant of particle filters that has remained largely unexplored due to implementation challenges with classical numerical solvers. Experiments on nonlinear chaotic systems, including atmospheric dynamics, demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully scales particle filtering to high-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: Bayesian filtering estimates plausible hidden states of a changing system from observations. Particle filters represent that uncertainty using candidate states and can handle nonlinear dynamics and observations. Although theoretically exact, they are difficult to scale to high-dimensional systems. This paper studies how generative models of system dynamics can help overcome that computational obstacle.

The authors show that diffusion-based emulators can implement an optimal variant of particle filtering without additional training. That variant has received limited practical attention because implementing it with classical numerical solvers is challenging. The contribution is to use the capabilities of an existing generative emulator to make this filtering procedure accessible.

Experiments on nonlinear chaotic systems, including atmospheric dynamics, demonstrate successful particle filtering in high-dimensional settings. Here, training-free means the filtering approach requires no extra training of the emulator; the method still relies on a diffusion-based dynamical model. The results show a useful role for such emulators beyond simulating trajectories: they can also enable more effective inference about system states from observations.
summary.tldr: Existing diffusion-based dynamical emulators enable an optimal particle-filter variant without further training, with successful high-dimensional demonstrations.

title: Training-Free Bayesian Filtering with Generative Emulators

abstract: As language model (LM) agents become increasingly capable and adopted in real-world applications, there is a growing need for scalable evaluation frameworks beyond costly, manually designed benchmarks. We propose information-theoretic evaluation based on empowerment, an information-theoretic measure of an agent’s influence on future states through its actions. To handle the unique challenges of text-based environments, we introduce EELMA (Estimating Empowerment of Language Model Agents), an algorithm for approximating effective empowerment from multi-turn text interactions. We demonstrate EELMA on textual games and realistic web and tool-use environments, showing that empowerment strongly correlates with average task performance. We further analyze how empowerment varies across models, environment complexity, and agent configurations, and show that high-empowerment states and actions often mark pivotal moments for general capabilities. These results establish empowerment as a goal-agnostic metric that complements task-success measures for LM-agent evaluation. Code available: https://github.com/Jinyeop3110/EELMA

paragraphs: This paper evaluates language-model agents through empowerment, an information-theoretic measure of how much their actions can influence future states. The motivation is to supplement manually designed task benchmarks, which can be costly to construct. Empowerment focuses on an agent’s influence within an environment without requiring a particular task goal.

The proposed EELMA algorithm approximates effective empowerment from multi-turn text interactions. It addresses the difficulties of applying this measure in text-based settings and is demonstrated in textual games as well as realistic web and tool-use environments. The authors also examine how the resulting estimates vary with the model, environmental complexity, and agent configuration.

Across these evaluations, empowerment strongly correlates with average task performance. States and actions with high empowerment also often identify pivotal moments for general capabilities. These are empirical relationships: the paper presents empowerment as a complementary evaluation signal, not a replacement for measuring task success. It offers another way to assess an agent’s capacity to affect what happens next.
summary.tldr: EELMA estimates how strongly agents can influence future states, providing a goal-agnostic metric correlated with average task performance.

title: Estimating the Empowerment of Language Model Agents

abstract: We study a widely used Bayesian optimization method, Gaussian process Thompson sampling (GP-TS), under the assumption that the objective function is a sample path from a GP. Compared with the GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) with established high-probability and expected regret bounds, most analyses of GP-TS have been limited to expected regret. Moreover, whether the recent analyses of GP-UCB for the lenient regret and the improved cumulative regret upper bound can be applied to GP-TS remains unclear. To fill these gaps, this paper shows several regret bounds: (i) a regret lower bound for GP-TS, which implies that GP-TS suffers from a polynomial dependence on $1/\delta$ with probability $\delta$, (ii) an upper bound of the second moment of cumulative regret, which directly suggests an improved regret upper bound on $\delta$, (iii) expected lenient regret upper bounds, and (iv) an improved cumulative regret upper bound on the time horizon $T$. Along the way, we provide several useful lemmas, including a relaxation of the necessary condition from recent analysis to obtain improved regret upper bounds on $T$.

paragraphs: The paper studies Gaussian process Thompson sampling, a widely used Bayesian optimization method, assuming the objective function is a sample path from a Gaussian process. It examines regret: the performance lost through choices that fall short of the optimum. Earlier analyses of this method mostly addressed expected regret, leaving questions about guarantees beyond the average.

A central result is a regret lower bound showing that, with probability δ, the method suffers regret with polynomial dependence on 1/δ. This establishes a constraint on how favorable guarantees can become as the permitted failure probability decreases. The authors also bound the second moment of cumulative regret, which accounts for squared regret and directly suggests an improved upper bound in terms of δ.

The paper additionally establishes expected lenient regret upper bounds and improves a cumulative regret upper bound in its dependence on the number of optimization steps, T. These results address whether types of guarantees recently developed for Gaussian process upper confidence bound methods can also be established for Thompson sampling.

Supporting lemmas relax a condition used in recent analysis to obtain improved bounds in T. Together, the findings sharpen the theoretical picture of Thompson sampling under the stated Gaussian process assumption, covering both achievable guarantees and constraints on those guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under a Gaussian process assumption, the paper establishes new regret bounds for Thompson sampling, improving guarantees while identifying limits on their dependence on failure probability.

title: On Regret Bounds of Thompson Sampling for Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Optimizing maintenance strategies for large-scale infrastructure is a critical sequential decision-making problem. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a theoretical framework for such problems, practical deployment necessitates offline constrained RL—learning policies solely from static historical datasets under rigid budgetary limits without dangerous on-policy exploration. However, current research is hindered by benchmarks that fail to capture the confluence of distributional shift and hard constraints typical of real-world assets. We introduce InfraRL, a high-fidelity benchmark that uses bridge maintenance as a rigorous testbed for general infrastructure asset management challenges. Constructed from the U.S. National Bridge Inventory, InfraRL defines a rigorous offline task for optimizing maintenance strategies under hard budgetary constraints. We benchmark a diverse suite of baselines, ranging from industry-standard heuristics to single-agent, multi-agent, planning-based, and constrained offline RL methods. Through a comprehensive evaluation protocol, we analyze performance across structural utility, constraint adherence, and behavioral fidelity, revealing critical trade-offs between safety and long-term efficiency. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/BriSky-2021/InfraRL.

paragraphs: Infrastructure maintenance requires a sequence of decisions whose effects accumulate over time, all within limited budgets. Learning by trying potentially dangerous actions on real assets is unsuitable for this setting. InfraRL therefore focuses on offline constrained reinforcement learning: policies must learn from fixed historical data while respecting hard spending limits.

The benchmark uses bridge maintenance as a testbed for broader infrastructure asset management and is constructed from the U.S. National Bridge Inventory. Its task combines budget constraints with distributional shift, a pairing the authors identify as insufficiently represented in existing benchmarks. This creates a setting for examining whether learned maintenance strategies remain useful under both challenges together.

The evaluation includes industry heuristics alongside single-agent, multi-agent, planning-based, and constrained offline reinforcement learning methods. It measures structural utility, adherence to constraints, and behavioral fidelity, revealing trade-offs between safety and long-term efficiency. The contribution is a benchmark and evaluation protocol for exposing those trade-offs, rather than a claim that one maintenance policy resolves them. It provides a common basis for comparing methods on competing practical requirements.
summary.tldr: InfraRL benchmarks offline bridge-maintenance decisions under hard budgets, exposing trade-offs between structural utility, constraint adherence, and long-term efficiency.

title: InfraRL: A Benchmark for Constrained Resource Allocation in Large-Scale Infrastructure Asset Management

abstract: Unified hyperspectral image (HSI) restoration aims to recover diverse degradations within a single model. However, current methods often rely on impractical explicit priors or opaque black-box representations that overfit to training distributions, hampering generalization to unseen scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose Degradation-Aware Metric Prompting (DAMP), a novel framework that characterizes multi-dimensional degradations through interpretable spatial-spectral metrics. These metrics serve as Degradation Prompts (DP), enabling the model to capture shared characteristics across tasks and adapt to unknown corruptions. Central to our framework is the Degradation-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (DAMoE), where Spatial-Spectral Adaptive Modules (SSAMs) serve as experts that utilize learnable fusion coefficients to specialize in distinct degradation degrees. By using DP as a gating router, DAMoE dynamically activates specialized experts tailored to the specific degradation profile. Extensive experiments on natural and remote sensing HSI datasets demonstrate that DAMP achieves state-of-the-art performance and exhibits exceptional zero-shot generalization on unseen restoration tasks. Code is publicly available at DAMP.

paragraphs: A unified hyperspectral restoration model must handle different forms of image corruption within one system. The paper argues that explicit prior requirements can be impractical, while opaque learned representations can overfit the training distribution. DAMP addresses this by describing corruption through interpretable measurements of its spatial and spectral characteristics.

These measurements become degradation prompts that guide restoration. They characterize shared properties across tasks, giving the model a way to respond to unfamiliar corruption. A degradation-adaptive mixture of experts uses the prompts to route processing toward specialized modules. Those modules combine spatial and spectral processing through learnable fusion coefficients, allowing different experts to specialize in different degrees of degradation.

Experiments on natural and remote sensing hyperspectral imagery report state-of-the-art restoration performance and strong zero-shot generalization to unseen restoration tasks. The result supports using an interpretable corruption profile to select suitable processing within a single model. The approach’s practical significance is the connection between describing what has gone wrong in an image and choosing which restoration expertise to activate.
summary.tldr: DAMP uses interpretable spatial-spectral corruption measurements to route hyperspectral images through specialized restoration experts.

title: Degradation-Aware Metric Prompting for Hyperspectral Image Restoration

abstract: Calibration aligns a model’s predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Calibration asks whether a model’s reported probabilities agree with how often outcomes actually occur. In a mixture-of-experts model, predictions depend on both the experts and the mechanism that routes inputs among them. This paper studies whether calibrating individual experts is enough to calibrate the combined model when the data distribution changes.

The answer depends on routing. For hard-routed models, expert calibration is sufficient to ensure overall calibration under a broad class of distribution shifts. For soft-routed models, where expert predictions are combined, that condition is insufficient. The distinction shows why improving individual predictors does not automatically settle the reliability of probabilities produced by every mixture architecture.

To address the aggregate model directly, the authors propose adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors in the routed combination under distribution shift. Experiments across model classes, prediction tasks, and shifts show a better tradeoff between accuracy and calibration, both on average and on difficult subsets. The findings connect probability reliability to how expert outputs are routed and combined.
summary.tldr: Expert calibration suffices for hard-routed mixtures under a broad class of shifts, while soft routing motivates calibration of the aggregate prediction.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) that continue improving at test-time budgets far beyond their training budgets can solve harder problems by leveraging additional inference compute: we refer to this property as extrapolation. Standard on-policy RL operates on fixed problem distributions and training budgets, giving rise to a distribution shift between train and test that limits the resulting model’s extrapolation capabilities. To address this, we introduce RC, an iterative decoding algorithm replacing standard autoregressive decoding that enables models to extrapolate to lengths an order of magnitude longer than those seen during training. RC exploits the asymmetry between summarization and generation capabilities present in LLMs to construct a decoding process that improves consistently over iterations. Its effectiveness can be further increased through training, which amplifies the model’s ability to perform summary-conditioned reasoning while avoiding the challenges of long-horizon RL. Empirically, training a 4B instruction-following model with RC using a 16k-token training budget improves performance on HMMT 2025 from 40% to 70% when evaluated with a 512k-token test budget, substantially surpassing comparably sized LLMs.

paragraphs: Giving a reasoning model more inference time is useful only if its answers continue to improve. This paper calls that ability extrapolation and examines why fixed-budget reinforcement learning can limit it. When evaluation allows much longer reasoning than training, the model faces a shift in both its operating budget and the reasoning process it must sustain.

Reasoning Cache replaces standard autoregressive decoding with an iterative procedure that uses summaries to condition subsequent reasoning. It exploits an asymmetry between models’ summarization and generation capabilities to support continued improvement across iterations. Training can further strengthen this summary-conditioned reasoning while avoiding the challenges of directly performing reinforcement learning over very long horizons.

In the reported experiment, a 4B instruction-following model is trained with a 16k-token budget and evaluated with up to 512k tokens. Its HMMT 2025 performance improves from 40% to 70%, substantially exceeding comparably sized models. The result demonstrates that the proposed decoding and training approach can make a much larger inference budget productive, rather than requiring training to span that entire reasoning horizon.
summary.tldr: Reasoning Cache uses iterative summary-conditioned reasoning to turn short-budget training into effective reasoning over much larger test-time budgets.

title: Reasoning Cache: Continual Improvement Over Long Horizons via Short-Horizon RL

abstract: Attention sinks—tokens that receive disproportionate attention mass—are assumed to be functionally important in autoregressive language models, but their role in diffusion transformers remains unclear. We present a causal analysis in text-to-image diffusion, dynamically identifying dominant attention recipients per timestep and suppressing them via paired, training-free interventions on the score and value paths. Across 553 GenEval prompts on Stable Diffusion 3 (with SDXL corroboration), removing these sinks does not degrade text-image alignment (CLIP-T) or preference proxies (ImageReward, HPS-v2) at $k{=}1$; only under stronger interventions ($k\!\geq\!10$) does HPS-v2 exhibit a metric-dependent boundary, while CLIP-T remains robust throughout. The perceptual shifts induced by suppression are nonetheless sink-specific—$\sim\!6\times$ larger than equal-budget random masking—revealing an empirical dissociation between trajectory-level perturbation and semantic alignment in diffusion transformers. [Code available at https://github.com/wfz666/ICML26-attention-sink.]

paragraphs: Attention sinks are tokens that attract an unusually large share of a model’s attention. This paper investigates what those tokens actually do in text-to-image diffusion transformers. Rather than inferring importance from attention patterns alone, the authors intervene during generation to see how suppressing the dominant recipients changes the resulting images.

The method identifies sinks separately at each generation timestep and applies paired interventions to the attention score and value paths without training the model. Tests cover 553 GenEval prompts with Stable Diffusion 3, with corroborating evidence from SDXL. At intervention strength k = 1, suppression does not degrade measured text-image alignment or the reported preference proxies.

The images nevertheless change: perceptual shifts are roughly six times larger than those caused by random masking with the same intervention budget. Stronger interventions, at k ≥ 10, expose a boundary in HPS-v2, while CLIP-T remains robust. The finding separates influence over the generation trajectory from measured semantic alignment: a token can substantially affect appearance without being essential to prompt alignment under the tested interventions.
summary.tldr: Suppressing attention sinks changes generated images substantially while preserving measured prompt alignment across the tested intervention strengths.

title: Attention Sinks in Diffusion Transformers: A Causal Analysis

abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions from observed data. While recent generative approaches have shown promise in treating SR as machine translation or multimodal learning tasks using NN methods, they suffer from uncontrollable generation process and training-evaluation misalignment. The training objectives (average cross-entropy loss on a token level across the distribution of historical data) differ from the evaluation metric (fitting error for every test data / complexity), necessitating extensive heuristic post-processing. On the other hand, direct optimization methods suffer from an exponential slowdown as the dimensionality increases, non-differentiability and local optima traps. We propose MOD-SR, unifying multimodal distribution learning during training with direct optimization at inference time. This is achieved by modeling the task as $p(x_0 \mid \mathcal{D}, y^*)$ and employing gradient-guided diffusion in embedding space, enhanced by contrastive learning and representation alignment. Furthermore, we introduce DFEX, a fixed-depth tree relaxation method that ensures differentiability for effective gradient guidance during inference. Experiments demonstrate that MOD-SR achieves superior performance on diverse benchmarks through a unified framework integrating distribution learning and optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/KROX777/MOD-SR.

While recent generative approaches have shown promise in treating SR as machine translation or multimodal learning tasks using NN methods, they suffer from uncontrollable generation process and training-evaluation misalignment. The training objectives (average cross-entropy loss on a token level across the distribution of historical data) differ from the evaluation metric (fitting error for every test data / complexity), necessitating extensive heuristic post-processing. On the other hand, direct optimization methods suffer from an exponential slowdown as the dimensionality increases, non-differentiability and local optima traps. We propose MOD-SR, unifying multimodal distribution learning during training with direct optimization at inference time. This is achieved by modeling the task as $p(x_0 \mid \mathcal{D}, y^*)$ and employing gradient-guided diffusion in embedding space, enhanced by contrastive learning and representation alignment. Furthermore, we introduce DFEX, a fixed-depth tree relaxation method that ensures differentiability for effective gradient guidance during inference. Experiments demonstrate that MOD-SR achieves superior performance on diverse benchmarks through a unified framework integrating distribution learning and optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/KROX777/MOD-SR.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for interpretable mathematical expressions that explain observed data. Generative methods learn patterns in expressions, but their token-level training objectives differ from evaluation criteria such as fit to a particular dataset and expression complexity. Direct optimization addresses the test problem more immediately, yet faces difficulties including nondifferentiable expressions, local optima, and rapidly increasing cost with dimensionality.

MOD-SR combines distribution learning during training with direct optimization during inference. It generates expressions through gradient-guided diffusion in an embedding space, supported by contrastive learning and representation alignment. This gives the generation process guidance tied to the inference problem while retaining the patterns learned from training data.

The framework also introduces DFEX, a fixed-depth relaxation of expression trees that makes gradient guidance possible through differentiability. Experiments report superior performance across diverse benchmarks. The contribution is the integration of learned expression generation and optimization in one framework, addressing their mismatch through a representation that can receive gradients. The reported results support this combination without establishing that every optimization difficulty is eliminated.
summary.tldr: MOD-SR combines learned expression generation with gradient-guided inference to better connect symbolic regression training with test-time optimization.

title: MOD-SR: Unifying Multimodal Learning and Direct Optimization with Gradient-Guided Diffusion Model for Symbolic Regression

abstract: Driven by the imperative to leverage privacy-sensitive data scattered across decentralized devices, federated fine-tuning has emerged as a vital paradigm for adapting large language models without compromising data privacy. Yet, its practical efficacy is bottlenecked by severe client resource heterogeneity. Existing truncation-based methods typically couple the transmitted rank with the trainable rank, which (i) under-utilizes bandwidth on communication-rich but compute-limited clients and (ii) exacerbates truncation-induced gradient drift. To address this, we propose FedHera, a resource-decoupled framework that explicitly differentiates information reception from gradient optimization. FedHera employs a spectrum-preserving allocation strategy to maximize the transfer of global knowledge (via high-rank singular values) within bandwidth limits, irrespective of training constraints. Furthermore, we introduce a prefix-gating mechanism that utilizes the downloaded high-capacity basis as a frozen reference to guide local updates, thereby minimizing the optimization gap caused by aggressive truncation. Extensive experiments under different heterogeneous settings show that FedHera improves stability and accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning adapts language models using data held across decentralized devices. Those devices can have very different computing and communication resources. Existing truncation-based approaches often tie the amount of model information a device receives to the amount it can train. This wastes available bandwidth on devices that communicate well but have limited computing capacity, and can distort local gradients.

FedHera separates receiving information from optimizing parameters. Its allocation strategy preserves spectral information and transfers as much global knowledge as bandwidth allows, independently of the device’s training constraints. A client can therefore receive a richer representation than the portion it can afford to update.

A prefix-gating mechanism uses that downloaded, higher-capacity basis as a frozen reference for local learning. This reference guides updates and reduces the optimization gap introduced by aggressive truncation. Experiments across different resource-heterogeneity settings report improved stability and accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support treating communication capacity and trainable capacity as separate design choices.
summary.tldr: FedHera separates downloaded model capacity from locally trainable capacity to improve federated fine-tuning under unequal device resources.

title: FedHera: Towards Drift-Resilient Federated Fine-tuning with Heterogeneous Resources

abstract: Despite the advancing reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), many reasoning evaluations are increasingly compromised by data contamination, which induces unreliable contaminated reasoning on leaked inputs. While this phenomenon is widely observed, its underlying mechanism remains poorly understood, hindering the ability to distinguish generalization from memorization and to develop effective solutions. In this work, we first identify a distinctive signal of contaminated reasoning, namely the mutual information decay between representations and gradients. Our mechanistic analysis reveals that contaminated models exhibit pronounced eigenspectrum concentration in their representations, leading to a low-dimensional computation regime. Under leaked inputs, this mechanism weakens the linear coupling between representations and gradients, manifested as a structural decay of the singular values in the whitened space. We show that this narrowing geometry mathematically implies a reduction in mutual information, and further demonstrate the practical utility of our analysis by successfully restoring the reasoning behavior of contaminated models, achieving up to an 11.03% absolute improvement in average consistency with the base model over the strongest baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiakuan929/ContamReasoning.

paragraphs: When evaluation problems have leaked into training, a language model’s apparent reasoning can reflect contamination rather than generalization. This paper studies what changes inside contaminated models. It identifies a signal involving mutual information between internal representations and gradients: the statistical connection between what the model represents and how its training objective responds becomes weaker.

The proposed explanation is geometric. Contaminated models concentrate their representations into fewer dominant directions, producing a lower-dimensional computation regime. On leaked inputs, this concentration weakens the linear relationship between representations and gradients. The authors analyze this relationship in a whitened space and show mathematically how the resulting narrowing implies reduced mutual information.

The paper also uses this analysis to restore reasoning behavior in contaminated models. It reports up to an 11.03% absolute improvement in average consistency with the base model over the strongest baseline. That result connects the geometric diagnosis to a practical intervention, with success measured by restored agreement with the base model’s behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper links contaminated reasoning to increasingly concentrated internal representations and uses that analysis to help restore base-model reasoning behavior.

title: A Narrowing Geometry in Contaminated Reasoning

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) augments large language models with external knowledge, which in turn exposes their retrieval corpora to data poisoning risks. However, existing poisoning attacks exhibit limited effectiveness against RAG equipped with a reranker to enhance retrieval quality. Remarkably, this defensive capability requires no adversarial training: a reranker fine-tuned solely on benign, in-domain corpora can effectively filter malicious content. Towards realistic RAG red-teaming, we conclude practical prompt design principles that reveal reranker blind spots. Building on these insights, we introduce the Prompt-Perturbation Poisoning Attack ($\mathbf{P}^3 \mathbf{A}$). $\mathbf{P}^3 \mathbf{A}$ first employs rule-based prompt engineering to craft initial poisoned texts. It then injects subtle character-level perturbations into these texts, which promotes their ranking by the reranker while maintaining their adversarial effectiveness. These perturbations introduce only about 1% textual change, ensuring the poisoned texts remain natural and readable. Extensive experiments show that $\mathbf{P}^3 \mathbf{A}$ achieves strong attack effectiveness and transferability, even when constrained to poisoning a single document. Code is available at https://github.com/YyyxKun/P3A.

paragraphs: This paper studies poisoning risks in retrieval-augmented generation systems that use a reranker. A reranker improves the ordering of retrieved material before it reaches the language model. The authors find that a reranker trained only on benign, in-domain data can already filter malicious content effectively, making existing poisoning attacks less successful without explicit adversarial training.

The proposed Prompt-Perturbation Poisoning Attack investigates where that protection breaks down. It starts with poisoned texts created through rule-based prompt design and then introduces subtle character-level changes. Those changes aim to improve the texts’ reranker positions while preserving their adversarial effect. The abstract reports changes to about 1% of the text, with the resulting documents remaining natural and readable.

Experiments report strong attack effectiveness and transferability, including when the attacker can poison only one document. The findings establish a qualified security picture: benign reranker training supplies useful protection, but the tested attack can exploit weaknesses in that filtering stage. Evaluating poisoning against a complete retrieval pipeline therefore requires accounting for how malicious material interacts with reranking.
summary.tldr: Rerankers filter many poisoned documents, but P3A shows that small textual perturbations can preserve attacks while improving their ranking.

title: Reranker Helps, but Not Enough: Towards Strong Poisoning Attacks Against Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Dynamic Data selection aims to accelerate training by prioritizing informative samples during online training. However, existing methods typically rely on task-specific handcrafted metrics or static/snapshot-based criteria to estimate sample importance, limiting scalability across learning paradigms and making it difficult to capture the evolving utility of data throughout training. To address this challenge, we propose Data Agent, an end-to-end dynamic data selection framework that formulates data selection as a training-aware sequential decision-making problem. The agent learns a sample-wise selection policy that co-evolves with model optimization, guided by a composite reward that integrates loss-based difficulty and confidence-based uncertainty signals. The reward signals capture complementary objectives of optimization impact and information gain, together with a tuning-free adaptive weighting mechanism that balances these signals over training. Extensive experiments across a wide range of datasets and architectures demonstrate that Data Agent consistently accelerates training while preserving or improving performance, e.g., reducing costs by over 50% on ImageNet-1k and MMLU with lossless performance. Moreover, its dataset-agnostic formulation and modular reward make it plug-and-play across tasks and scenarios, e.g., robustness to noisy datasets, highlighting its potential in real-world scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/Jackbrocp/Data-Agent.

paragraphs: A training example’s usefulness can change as a model learns. Data Agent treats the choice of training samples as a sequence of decisions that should adapt alongside model optimization. This addresses the weakness of selection rules based on fixed importance scores, occasional snapshots, or metrics handcrafted for a particular task.

The agent learns a policy for selecting individual samples using a reward that combines two signals: difficulty measured through loss and uncertainty measured through confidence. These signals represent complementary goals of influencing optimization and gaining information. An adaptive weighting mechanism balances them over training without requiring tuning of that balance.

Experiments across datasets and architectures report faster training while maintaining or improving performance. On ImageNet-1k and MMLU, the authors report cost reductions exceeding 50% without performance loss. The framework also addresses scenarios involving noisy datasets. Its dataset-independent formulation and modular reward make the selection strategy adaptable across tasks, while the results show that tracking changing sample utility can reduce training effort substantially.
summary.tldr: Data Agent learns an evolving sample-selection policy that accelerates training, with reported cost reductions above 50% without performance loss on ImageNet-1k and MMLU.

title: Data Agent: Learning to Select Data via End-to-End Dynamic Optimization

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, yet they remain vulnerable to sequential jailbreaks that exploit multi-turn interaction to circumvent safety mechanisms. Current safety evaluations are largely outcome-based, offering little insight into the latent decision processes that lead to unsafe compliance. We propose an interpretable cognitive modeling framework that couples a controlled elicitation paradigm, the Contextual Iowa Gambling Task (C-IGT), with a Generalized Rescorla–Wagner (GRW) architecture to decompose behavior into measurable mechanisms. Across a diverse set of mainstream LLMs, we find that sequential vulnerability is not explained by scale alone but emerges from interactions among cognitive factors, including optimism-biased learning, perceptual reward amplification, and choice inertia. Moreover, counterfactual feedback and psychologically framed rewards (e.g., regret, authority, threat) substantially accelerate the transition from refusal to compliance. These results yield principled cognitive profiles of LLM "irrationality" and provide insights for interdisciplinary research on LLM agents at the intersection of machine learning and human behavioral science.

paragraphs: Sequential jailbreaks use multiple conversational turns to move a language model toward unsafe compliance. Evaluations that record only the final outcome reveal little about how that transition occurs. This paper develops an interpretable behavioral framework to distinguish measurable mechanisms associated with vulnerability over an interaction.

The framework pairs a controlled elicitation task, the Contextual Iowa Gambling Task, with a Generalized Rescorla–Wagner model. Across a diverse collection of mainstream language models, the analysis links vulnerability to interactions among optimism-biased learning, amplified perception of rewards, and a tendency to repeat previous choices. Model scale alone does not explain the observed differences.

The authors also find that counterfactual feedback and rewards framed through concepts such as regret, authority, and threat substantially accelerate movement from refusal to compliance. These results provide cognitive profiles of observed model behavior, expanding evaluation beyond a single success or failure judgment. The contribution is an interpretable account of how interaction and feedback relate to unsafe behavior, connecting language-agent research with methods from human behavioral science.
summary.tldr: Cognitive modeling links sequential jailbreak vulnerability to interacting behavioral factors and feedback effects that model size alone does not explain.

title: Profiling the Irrational Agent: Cognitive Modeling of LLM Behaviors in Sequential Jailbreaks

abstract: This paper proposes Omni Dense Captioning, a novel task designed to generate continuous, fine-grained, and structured audio-visual narratives with explicit timestamps. To ensure dense semantic coverage, we introduce a six-dimensional structural schema to create "script-like" captions, enabling readers to vividly imagine the video content scene by scene, akin to a cinematographic screenplay. To facilitate research, we construct OmniDCBench, a high-quality, human-annotated benchmark, and propose SodaM, a unified metric that evaluates time-aware detailed descriptions while mitigating scene boundary ambiguity. Furthermore, we construct a training dataset, TimeChatCap-42K, and present TimeChat-Captioner-7B, a strong baseline trained via SFT and GRPO with task-specific rewards. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TimeChat-Captioner achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing Gemini-2.5-Pro, while its generated dense descriptions significantly boost downstream capabilities in audio-visual reasoning (DailyOmni and WorldSense) and temporal grounding (Charades-STA). All datasets, models, and code are publicly available at https://github.com/yaolinli/TimeChat-Captioner.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Omni Dense Captioning, a task that turns video into detailed, timestamped narratives covering both sound and visual content. A six-dimensional structural schema organizes the captions into a script-like description of successive scenes. The goal is to preserve continuous, fine-grained meaning so that a reader can imagine how the video unfolds.

The authors build OmniDCBench with human annotations and introduce SodaM, an evaluation metric for detailed descriptions that accounts for timing while reducing ambiguity around scene boundaries. They also create the TimeChatCap-42K training dataset and train TimeChat-Captioner-7B through supervised fine-tuning and GRPO, using rewards designed for the captioning task.

Experiments report state-of-the-art captioning performance, including results above Gemini-2.5-Pro. The generated descriptions also significantly improve downstream audio-visual reasoning on DailyOmni and WorldSense and temporal grounding on Charades-STA. These findings give the captions two roles: a readable account of a video and a useful representation for subsequent tasks that require understanding events and locating them in time.
summary.tldr: TimeChat-Captioner generates structured, timestamped audio-visual narratives that improve dense captioning and downstream video reasoning and grounding.

title: TimeChat-Captioner: Scripting Multi-Scene Videos with Time-Aware and Structural Audio-Visual Captions

abstract: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into time series tasks has yielded impressive performance. While some works aim to enhance accuracy by explicitly designing step-by-step reasoning into prompts, such explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approaches are difficult to generalize to time series. This is because it is difficult to clearly define the reasoning trajectories of time series. In addition, the high heterogeneity across time series often requires specialized prompt designs, limiting the model’s scalability. To address these challenges, we propose Hi-Time, a hierarchical latent prediction framework based on temporal semantic codes for multivariate time series classification. This framework automatically constructs scenario-specific coarse-to-fine prediction trajectories based on the characteristics of time series, thereby providing structured supervision for the LLM. Specifically, Hi-Time first performs temporal representation pre-training with a multi-view temporal representation fusion to acquire high-quality temporal embeddings. We then discretize these temporal embeddings into hierarchical temporal semantic codes that form the coarse-to-fine prediction trajectory. Finally, the LLM predicts temporal semantic codes in a stepwise manner and then infers the final label, thereby establishing a coarse-to-fine decision process. Experiments on ten public multivariate time series datasets demonstrate that Hi-Time effectively adapts to diverse datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/qianlima-lab/Hi-Time.

paragraphs: Hi-Time studies how language models can classify multivariate time series through a structured decision process. Writing explicit reasoning prompts is difficult because useful reasoning steps are hard to define for temporal signals, and different datasets may require specialized prompts. The framework instead learns a hierarchy of temporal representations that supplies intermediate prediction targets.

It first pretrains temporal representations, combining multiple views to obtain informative embeddings. These embeddings are discretized into hierarchical temporal semantic codes. The codes define a progression from coarse information to finer detail, adapted to the characteristics of the time series. A language model learns to predict these codes step by step before producing the final class label.

This construction gives the model structured supervision without requiring a manually written reasoning trajectory for each scenario. Across ten public multivariate time series datasets, the authors report adaptation to diverse datasets and performance exceeding state-of-the-art methods. The findings support learned temporal code hierarchies as a practical way to organize language-model decisions for time series classification.
summary.tldr: Hi-Time trains language models to classify time series by predicting learned temporal codes from coarse to fine.

title: Hi-Time: Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Multivariate Time Series Classification

abstract: Recent Uniform-state Diffusion Models (USDMs), initialized from a uniform prior, offer the promise of fast text generation due to their inherent self-correction ability compared to masked diffusion models. However, they still rely on complex loss formulations with additional computational overhead, which hinders scalability. In this work, we explore a simplified denoising-based loss for USDMs that optimizes only noise-replaced tokens, stabilizing training while matching the performance of prior methods with more complex objectives. In addition, we introduce an efficient regularization term to mitigate corruption toward uniform output distributions, which further improves performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our simple and improved loss formulations by pretraining models on widely used text datasets for USDMs. More importantly, our conclusions scale to larger models, showing strong potential for large-scale training.

paragraphs: Uniform-state diffusion language models begin from a uniform prior and refine text through denoising. Their ability to correct earlier choices offers the prospect of fast generation compared with masked diffusion models. However, existing training objectives can be complex and computationally costly, creating an obstacle to scaling these models.

This paper studies a simpler denoising loss that optimizes only tokens replaced by noise. Concentrating the objective on those positions stabilizes training while matching the performance of earlier, more elaborate objectives. The authors also introduce an efficient regularization term to discourage corruption toward uniform output distributions. This addition further improves performance within the proposed training approach.

Pretraining experiments on commonly used text datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of both the simplified objective and its regularized version. The conclusions also extend to larger models, supporting the approach’s potential for large-scale training. The contribution is a simpler way to train uniform-state diffusion models while retaining their performance, together with a targeted correction for an undesirable output-distribution behavior.
summary.tldr: A loss focused on noise-replaced tokens simplifies diffusion-language-model training, while an efficient regularizer further improves performance.

title: Simple Denoising Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Multimodal learning has seen remarkable progress, particularly with large-scale pre-training across various modalities. Most current approaches are built on the assumption of a deterministic one-to-one alignment between modalities. However, this oversimplifies real-world multimodal relationships, where their nature is inherently many-to-many. The many-to-many property, or multiplicity, is not a side-effect of noise or annotation error, but an inevitable outcome of intra-modal variability, representational asymmetry, and task-dependent ambiguity in multimodal tasks. We argue that multiplicity is a fundamental bottleneck that affects all stages of the multimodal learning pipeline: from data construction to model training and evaluation benchmarks. By formalizing its causes and consequences, we demonstrate how ignoring multiplicity leads to training uncertainty, unreliable evaluation, and degraded dataset quality. This position paper calls for new research directions on multimodal learning, including multiplicity-aware learning frameworks and dataset construction and evaluation protocols.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges a common assumption in multimodal learning: that items in different modalities have a single, determinate correspondence. The authors argue that real relationships are inherently many-to-many. They call this multiplicity and treat it as a property of the learning problem, rather than something explained away by noisy data or annotation mistakes.

The paper formalizes sources of multiplicity, including variation within a modality, differences in what representations express, and ambiguity that depends on the task. These causes matter throughout the pipeline. The authors describe how overlooking them creates uncertainty during training, makes evaluations unreliable, and reduces the quality of constructed datasets.

Their proposed research agenda therefore extends beyond changing the model alone. They call for learning frameworks, dataset construction practices, and evaluation protocols that explicitly account for multiplicity. The central implication is that treating one correspondence as uniquely correct can misrepresent the task itself. Progress requires handling the range of relationships the data legitimately support.
summary.tldr: Multimodal learning should account for inherently many-to-many relationships throughout data construction, training, and evaluation.

title: Position: Multiplicity is an Inevitable and Inherent Challenge in Multimodal Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in qualitative data analysis, yet the field lacks a shared way to state what kinds of process LLM-based pipelines intend to produce. This position paper proposes an explicit specification perspective: separating meaning-making from modeling, and making both visible as part of the analytic. We introduce a 4$\times$4 landscape that crosses levels of meaning-making with levels of modeling, and use it to situate and compare qualitative outputs across both human-led studies and LLM-assisted workflows. A structured analysis of prior work suggests that many current LLM pipelines emphasize surface organization and static representations, with fewer systems making explicit commitments to richer causal or dynamical models. We demonstrate that the landscape can be applied consistently through strong agreement in independent labeling, including an LLM-based annotation pass. We conclude with a research agenda for LLM-assisted qualitative analysis focused on explicit level selection, evidence-linked outputs, and governance mechanisms aligned with the strength of semantic and representational claims.

This paper proposes making two aspects explicit: how analysts construct meaning and how they represent that meaning in a model. Separating these aspects helps clarify the claims attached to an analytic output.

The authors introduce a four-by-four landscape crossing levels of meaning-making with levels of modeling. They use it to compare human-led studies and LLM-assisted workflows. Their structured review suggests that many current pipelines organize material at a surface level or produce static representations, while fewer explicitly commit to richer causal or changing-system models. This describes a pattern in the reviewed work, rather than a universal restriction on LLM analysis.

Independent labeling showed strong agreement, including an annotation pass performed by an LLM, supporting the framework’s consistent application. The resulting agenda asks researchers to select analytic levels explicitly, connect outputs to supporting evidence, and match governance to the strength of their claims. The practical value is clearer comparison between workflows that might otherwise use similar language while offering substantially different kinds of interpretation.
summary.tldr: A four-by-four framework makes qualitative analysis workflows explicit about the meaning they construct and the models they claim to produce.

abstract: Modeling of conditional quantiles requires specification of the quantile being estimated and can thus be viewed as a parameterized predictive modeling problem. Quantile loss is typically used, and it is indeed parameterized by a quantile parameter. In this paper we show how to follow the path of cross validated solutions to regularized kernel quantile regression. Even though the bi-level optimization problem we encounter for every quantile is non-convex, the manner in which the optimal cross-validated solution evolves with the parameter of the loss function allows tracking of this solution. We prove this property, construct the resulting algorithm, and demonstrate it on data. This algorithm allows us to efficiently solve the whole family of bi-level problems.

paragraphs: Quantile regression predicts a chosen point in a conditional distribution, so changing the requested quantile changes the predictive modeling problem. Its loss function explicitly depends on that choice. With regularized kernel quantile regression and cross-validation, finding models across quantiles therefore produces a family of related optimization problems.

The paper shows how to follow the path of cross-validated solutions as the quantile parameter changes. Each individual problem has a non-convex, bi-level structure, making direct optimization challenging. Nevertheless, the authors prove that the way the optimal cross-validated solution evolves permits it to be tracked. The key opportunity lies in the relationship among solutions at different quantiles.

They turn this property into an algorithm and demonstrate it on data. Following the solution path allows efficient treatment of the entire family of bi-level problems. The contribution is thus more than fitting a model for one requested quantile: it provides a proven way to organize the computation across varying quantiles while retaining cross-validation within the problem.
summary.tldr: A proven path-following method efficiently tracks cross-validated kernel quantile regression solutions as the requested quantile changes.

title: Bi-level path following for cross validated solution of kernel quantile regression

abstract: In this paper we propose an algorithm for polynomial-time reinforcement learning in factored Markov decision processes (FMDPs). The factored optimistic initial model (FOIM) algorithm, maintains an empirical model of the FMDP in a conventional way, and always follows a greedy policy with respect to its model. The only trick of the algorithm is that the model is initialized optimistically. We prove that with suitable initialization (i) FOIM converges to the fixed point of approximate value iteration (AVI); (ii) the number of steps when the agent makes non-near-optimal decisions (with respect to the solution of AVI) is polynomial in all relevant quantities; (iii) the per-step costs of the algorithm are also polynomial. To our best knowledge, FOIM is the first algorithm with these properties.

The factored optimistic initial model (FOIM) algorithm, maintains an empirical model of the FMDP in a conventional way, and always follows a greedy policy with respect to its model. The only trick of the algorithm is that the model is initialized optimistically. We prove that with suitable initialization (i) FOIM converges to the fixed point of approximate value iteration (AVI); (ii) the number of steps when the agent makes non-near-optimal decisions (with respect to the solution of AVI) is polynomial in all relevant quantities; (iii) the per-step costs of the algorithm are also polynomial. To our best knowledge, FOIM is the first algorithm with these properties.

paragraphs: The factored optimistic initial model algorithm, or FOIM, learns in factored Markov decision processes. It maintains an empirical model and always selects actions greedily according to that model. Its distinctive design choice is to initialize the model optimistically, making the starting model central to the algorithm's learning behavior.

With suitable initialization, the authors prove three properties. FOIM converges to the fixed point of approximate value iteration. The number of steps on which its decisions are not near-optimal relative to the approximate value iteration solution is polynomial in the relevant quantities. Its computational cost at each step is also polynomial.

These guarantees connect a simple action-selection rule with bounds on both learning behavior and computation. Their reference point is the solution of approximate value iteration, so the near-optimality statement must be understood relative to that solution. The authors describe FOIM as, to their knowledge, the first algorithm to combine these properties. Suitable optimistic initialization is an explicit condition of the results.
summary.tldr: With suitable optimistic initialization, greedy FOIM has polynomial learning and computation guarantees relative to approximate value iteration.

title: Optimistic initialization and greediness lead to polynomial time learning in factored MDPs

abstract: Developing robots capable of fine manipulation skills is of major importance in order to build truly assistive robots. These robots need to be compliant in their actuation and control in order to operate safely in human environments. Manipulation tasks imply complex contact interactions with the external world, and involve reasoning about the forces and torques to be applied. Planning under contact conditions is usually impractical due to computational complexity, and a lack of precise dynamics models of the environment. We present an approach to acquiring manipulation skills on compliant robots through reinforcement learning. The initial position control policy for manipulation is initialized through kinesthetic demonstration. This policy is augmented with a force/torque profile to be controlled in combination with the position trajectories. The Policy Improvement with Path Integrals (PI^2) algorithm is used to learn these force/torque profiles by optimizing a cost function that measures task success. We introduce a policy representation that ensures trajectory smoothness during exploration and learning. Our approach is demonstrated on the Barrett WAM robot arm equipped with a 6-DOF force/torque sensor on two different manipulation tasks: opening a door with a lever door handle, and picking up a pen off the table. We show that the learnt force control policies allow successful, robust execution of the tasks.

paragraphs: Fine robotic manipulation involves controlling contact as well as motion. A robot opening a door or picking up an object must apply appropriate forces and torques while remaining compliant. Planning these interactions directly can be impractical because contact dynamics are complex and precise models of the environment may be unavailable.

The paper begins with a position-control policy obtained through kinesthetic demonstration, where the robot is physically guided through a movement. It then adds a force and torque profile to accompany the position trajectory. The PI^2 reinforcement learning algorithm improves that profile using a cost function measuring task success. A specially designed policy representation ensures smooth trajectories during exploration and learning.

The authors demonstrate the approach on a Barrett WAM arm with a six-degree-of-freedom force and torque sensor. The tasks are opening a door with a lever handle and picking up a pen from a table. Learned force-control policies enable successful, robust execution of both tasks. These results show how demonstration-based motion and learned contact control can work together on compliant manipulation problems.
summary.tldr: A compliant robot learns force and torque profiles alongside demonstrated motions, enabling robust door opening and pen pickup.

title: Learning Force Control Policies for Compliant Robotic Manipulation
